pg006_n0008: This textbook, Physics for Secondary Schools, is written specifically for Form Two students in the United Republic of Tanzania.
pg006_n0009: It is prepared in accordance with the Revised 2023 Physics Syllabus for Ordinary Secondary Education, Form I-IV, issued by the Ministry of Education, Science, and Technology (MoEST).
pg006_n0010: It is a revised edition of Physics for Secondary Schools Student’s Book for Form Two that was published in 2021 in accordance with the 2007 syllabus issued by the then Ministry of Education and Vocational Training (MoEVT).
pg006_n0012: The book consists of six chapters: Static electricity, Current electricity, Magnetism, Nature and reflection of light, Refraction and dispersion of light, and Optical instruments.
pg006_n0013: Each chapter contains illustrations, activities, and exercises.
pg006_n0014: You are encouraged to do all the activities and exercises together with other assignments that the teacher will provide.
pg006_n0015: You are also required to prepare a portfolio for keeping records of activities performed in different lessons.
pg006_n0016: Doing so will enhance your understanding and promote the development of the intended competencies for this level.

pg007_n0008: Clothes containing nylon often crackle when they are taken off the body.
pg007_n0009: Brushing a latex balloon against one’s face results in the balloon trying to stick to the face.
pg007_n0010: This is due to static electricity, which results from an imbalance of electric charges within or on the surface of a material.
pg007_n0011: In this chapter, you will learn the concept of static electricity, the origin of charges, the fundamental law of static electricity and the detection of charges.
pg007_n0012: You will also learn about conductors and insulators, capacitors, charge distribution along the surface of a conductor and lightning conductors.
pg007_n0013: The competencies developed will enable you to recognise the effects and applications of static electricity in everyday life.
pg007_n0016: Application of static electricity in daily life
pg007_n0020: Have you ever noticed that a nylon garment crackles when taken off the body?
pg007_n0021: Sometimes, tiny sparks are often experienced when undressing in the dark.
pg007_n0022: The crackling sound is caused by small electric sparks caused by charge-discharge.
pg007_n0023: The charge is caused by friction between the nylon and your skin, giving rise to static electricity.
pg007_n0024: Pens and combs made of certain plastic materials attract tiny pieces of paper after being rubbed on the hair or synthetic clothing, as shown in Figure 1.1.

pg008_n0005: Static electricity results from the accumulation of static electric charges on a material that does not conduct electricity.
pg008_n0009: Static electricity is generated through the transfer of electrons between materials.
pg008_n0010: This happens when two objects come into contact and are separated, causing one material to gain electrons (becoming negatively charged) and the other to lose electrons (becoming positively charged).
pg008_n0011: Common examples include rubbing a glass rod with cloth (Figure 1.2 (a)), and walking across a carpet (Figure 1.2 (b)) or rubbing a balloon with woollen cloth (Figure 1.2 (c)).
pg008_n0012: The magnitude of the static charge depends on several factors, including the materials involved, the surface properties, and the environmental conditions, such as humidity.
pg008_n0013: This charge build-up can lead to electrostatic discharge, such as a spark.

pg008_n0047: To demonstrate the charging of an object
pg008_n0055: 1. Align two transparent plastic sheets on top of a book.
pg008_n0057: 2. Rub the two plastic sheets with the wool jumper several times.
pg009_n0005: 3. Slowly separate the two plastic sheets and listen to what occurs.
pg009_n0007: 4. Bring the plastic sheets closer and observe the reaction.
pg009_n0009: 5. Separate the plastic sheets, then rub them individually with the wool jumper several times.
pg009_n0011: 6. Bring the sheets close to one another and observe the effect.
pg009_n0015: (a) What happened when the two plastic sheets were separated after rubbing them?
pg009_n0017: (b) Did the plastic sheets attract or repel each other when brought close?
pg009_n0019: (c) Why do you think the plastic sheets behave differently after being rubbed separately?
pg009_n0021: When the two plastic sheets are separated, a distinct cracking sound can be heard, and when they are brought together, they attract each other.
pg009_n0022: This phenomenon occurs because the upper sheet acquires a different charge from the lower sheet.
pg009_n0023: Conversely, when the two plastic sheets are rubbed separately and then brought closer, they tend to repel one another due to both sheets acquiring the same charge.
pg009_n0024: The process of charging through rubbing involves the removal or addition of electrons.
pg009_n0025: For instance, when the plastic sheets are rubbed against a sweater, electrons transfer from the sweater to the upper plastic sheet.
pg009_n0026: Meanwhile, the protons in the lower plastic sheet attract the electrons from the upper sheet.
pg009_n0027: This interaction explains why the sheets attract each other after being rubbed together.

pg009_n0085: Electric charge is something that exists inside atoms.
pg009_n0086: In 1890, a scientist named J.J. Thomson found out that all materials have tiny, light particles with a negative charge.
pg009_n0088: Later, between 1909 and 1911, another scientist named Ernest Rutherford discovered that atoms also have a heavy centre called the nucleus, which has a positive charge.
pg009_n0089: Normally, an atom is neutral, which means it is not charged, because the positive charge in the nucleus and the negative charge from the electrons are equal and cancel each other out.
pg009_n0090: But if the atom gets extra energy, it can lose one of its outer electrons.
pg009_n0091: When this happens, the atom has more positive charge than negative charge, so it becomes positively charged.
pg009_n0092: The electron that was removed can stay by itself or join another atom.
pg009_n0093: If it joins another atom, that atom gets a more negative charge and becomes
pg010_n0005: So, gaining or losing electric charge is really about moving electrons from one atom to another.
pg010_n0006: The charge on the electron equals negative one point six times ten to the minus nineteen coulombs.
pg010_n0007: The proton has a charge of the same magnitude as that of the electron but with an opposite charge.
pg010_n0008: Electrons surround the nucleus in shells.

pg011_n0045: Air as a conductor: Air is an insulator.
pg011_n0046: However, under certain conditions, sparks or lightning occur, allowing charge to move through the air as if it were a conductor.
pg011_n0047: The sparks that jump between your fingers and a doorknob after you have rubbed your feet on the carpet discharge you.
pg011_n0048: That is, you have become neutral because the excess charges have left you.
pg011_n0049: Similarly, lightning discharges from a thundercloud.
pg011_n0050: In both cases, for a brief moment, air becomes a conductor.
pg011_n0054: If two neutral objects are rubbed together, each can become charged.
pg011_n0055: For instance, when rubber and wool are rubbed together, electrons from the atoms of the wool are transferred to the rubber, as shown in Figure 1.6 (a) and (b).
pg011_n0056: The extra electrons on the rubber result in a
pg012_n0003: net negative charge, while the electrons missing from the wool lead to a net positive charge.
pg012_n0004: The combined total charge of the two objects remains the same.
pg012_n0005: Charging is conserved, which means that individual charges are neither created nor destroyed.
pg012_n0006: All that happened was that the positive and negative charges were separated through the transfer of electrons.

pg012_n0021: A charge is a characteristic of matter that causes it to create and experience electrical and magnetic effects.
pg012_n0022: The underlying idea behind charge conservation is that the system’s overall charge is conserved.
pg012_n0023: It can be defined as follows:
pg012_n0026: According to the rule of conservation of charge, the total charge of an isolated system will always remain constant.
pg012_n0027: At any time intervals, any system that is not exchanging mass or energy with its surroundings will have the same total charge.
pg012_n0029: When two objects in an isolated system each have a net charge of zero, and one body transfers one million electrons to the other, the object with the surplus electrons will be negatively charged, while the object with fewer electrons will have a positive charge of the same magnitude.
pg012_n0030: The total charge of the system has never changed and will never change.
pg012_n0035: The interaction between static electric charges produces a force known as the electrostatic force.
pg012_n0036: For instance, when plastic rods are charged by rubbing them with fur, they repel each other.
pg012_n0037: Similarly, glass rods rubbed with silk also become charged and repel one another.
pg012_n0038: Additionally, plastic rods attract the fur, while glass rods attract the silk.
pg012_n0040: French physicist Charles Coulomb measured the force between two charged objects using a torsional balance, establishing a unit of electrical charge named the coulomb in his honour.
pg012_n0041: A coulomb is a much larger quantity of charge than that normally produced by rubbing.

pg015_n0005: A neutral object has the same number of positive and negative charges, so they balance each other out.
pg015_n0006: When you bring another neutral object close to it or touch them together, nothing special usually happens because both objects have balanced charges.
pg015_n0008: However, if something causes one of the objects to have more positive or negative charges than the other, this is called an imbalance of charges.
pg015_n0009: Creating this imbalance is known as charging an object.
pg015_n0011: There are different ways to charge objects:
pg015_n0014: (a) Friction: Rubbing two objects together can move electrons from one object to another.
pg015_n0016: (b) Contact (or conduction): Touching a charged object to a neutral object can transfer electrons.
pg015_n0018: (c) Induction: Bringing a charged object close to a neutral object can rearrange the charges inside the neutral object, even without touching.
pg015_n0020: These methods all involve moving electrons to create an imbalance of charges, which makes the object either positively or negatively charged.
pg015_n0024: Charging by friction is the oldest method of generating electric charge, and it plays a fundamental role in understanding static electricity.
pg015_n0025: This process occurs when two objects in contact are rubbed against each other, leading to the transfer of electrons from one object to another.
pg015_n0029: When two insulating materials are rubbed together, friction generates an imbalance of electric charges.
pg015_n0030: Electrons, which are negatively charged particles, are transferred from one object to another.
pg015_n0031: The object that loses electrons becomes positively charged, while the object that gains electrons becomes negatively charged.
pg015_n0032: This transfer of charge is governed by the principle of conservation of charge, meaning that the total charge before and after the rubbing process remains constant.
pg015_n0033: For example, when an ebonite rod is rubbed with fur, electrons move from the fur to the ebonite rod as shown in Figure 1.10.
pg015_n0034: As a result, the fur becomes positively charged (due to the loss of electrons), while the ebonite rod becomes negatively charged (due to the gain of electrons).
pg015_im002: Hands rubbing a rod with a cloth to demonstrate charging by friction.
pg015_n0038: Every day examples of charging by friction
pg015_n0041: 1. Combing hair: When you comb your hair with a plastic comb, electrons are transferred from your hair to the comb.
pg015_n0042: This causes the comb to become negatively charged, allowing
pg016_n0003: it to attract small bits of paper when brought close.
pg016_n0004: 2. Rubbing a glass rod with silk: When a glass rod is rubbed with silk, the glass rod loses electrons and becomes positively charged, while the silk gains electrons and becomes negatively charged.
pg016_n0005: 3. Wool Sweater and Human Skin: In colder months, when you take off a wool sweater, you may notice sparks or hear crackling sounds.
pg016_n0006: This is due to the static electricity generated as electrons transfer from the wool to your skin.
pg016_n0008: The Role of insulators and conductors
pg016_n0010: Not all materials can be charged by friction.
pg016_n0011: Only insulating materials can be effectively charged through this method because their electrons are not free to move.
pg016_n0012: In contrast, conductors allow electrons to move freely, which means they cannot hold a static charge.
pg016_n0013: Common insulating materials include rubber, glass, and plastic, while metals are good conductors.
pg016_n0017: The triboelectric series is a ranking of materials based on their propensity to gain or lose electrons through contact or friction.
pg016_n0018: The position of a material in the series indicates whether it will tend to become positively or negatively charged when rubbed against another material (see Figure 1.11).
pg016_n0019: Materials higher on the list tend to become positive, while those lower become negative.
pg016_n0020: This effect is due to the transfer of electrons between the materials, leading to static electricity.
pg016_n0021: The series is a useful tool for predicting the outcome of charge transfer in various scenarios.
pg016_im008: Triboelectric series chart ranking materials from positive at the top to negative at the bottom: human skin, rabbit fur, glass, human hair, wool, silk, cotton, wood, amber, polystyrene, and ebonite, with a balloon shown near the negative end.
pg016_n0025: When two materials from this series are rubbed together, the one higher in the series will lose electrons, while the one lower will gain electrons.
pg016_n0026: For example, if you rub a glass rod with silk, the glass rod will lose electrons and become positively charged, while the silk will gain electrons and become negatively charged.
pg016_n0030: Charging by contact is achieved by bringing a charged body into contact with an uncharged one.
pg016_n0031: Charges are transferred from the charged body to the uncharged

pg017_n0029: Charging by induction is a method of charging an object without actually touching it with any other charged object.

pg017_n0051: Step 4: The negatively charged rod is removed.

pg019_n0010: Electroscopes detect the presence of electric charges on a body.
pg019_n0011: The most commonly used type of this instrument is the leaf electroscope.
pg019_n0015: A leaf electroscope was previously referred to as a gold leaf electroscope.
pg019_n0016: It is an instrument used to detect electric charge on an object.
pg019_n0017: It consists of a metal cap mounted on a metal rod, having at its lower end a small metal plate with a thin metal leaf attached to it.

pg025_n0016: You have learnt that like charges repel each other, and unlike charges attract each other.
pg025_n0017: Therefore, work must be done to overcome the repulsive force in moving a positive charge towards another positive charge.
pg025_n0018: Likewise, work is done to overcome the attractive force to move a negative charge away from a positive charge.
pg025_n0019: The above processes apply to all points in the region surrounding any charges.
pg025_n0020: This means an electrostatic force field around a charge exists.
pg025_n0021: The work required to move a unit charge from a reference point to a specific point against the electrostatic force field of another charge is called the electrostatic potential at the specific point.
pg025_n0022: Therefore, there is a difference in electrostatic potential between any two points in the electrostatic force field.
pg025_n0026: A charged body is considered to be at a positive potential if, upon grounding, electrons flow from the earth to the body.
pg025_n0027: Similarly, if electrons move from the body to the earth upon contact, the body is at a negative potential.
pg025_n0028: This electron flow continues until the body’s potential matches that of the Earth, which is defined as zero potential as indicated in Figure 1.24.
pg025_n0029: Therefore, any grounded conductor is considered to be at zero potential by definition.

pg038_n0011: Lightning, a dramatic electrostatic phenomenon, results from charge separation within storm clouds.
pg038_n0012: Ice crystals and water droplets collide, creating positive and negative charges that segregate.
pg038_n0013: A stepped leader, an ionised air channel, descends from the cloud, meeting a positive charge rising from the ground.
pg038_n0014: This interaction forms the return stroke, the visible lightning flash.
pg038_n0015: The rapid heating of air by lightning causes its expansion, resulting in the sound waves we recognise as thunder.
pg038_n0018: Lightning is a large spark due to electrostatic discharge within a cloud, between two clouds or between a cloud and the ground.
pg038_n0019: Interaction between updrafts and downdrafts in the cloud produces static charge by friction.
pg038_n0020: The lower portion of the cloud becomes negatively charged, and the upper part is positively charged.
pg038_n0021: The ground beneath the cloud can become positively charged by induction.

pg038_n0030: Hence, a large current suddenly passes, ionising the air molecules on its way, accompanied by the sudden expansion of the air.
pg038_n0031: The ionisation of air results in the observed flash of light (lightning), as shown in Figure 1.45.
pg038_n0032: Sudden expansion results in the booming sound (thunder) that is heard a few seconds after the flash is seen.

pg039_n0003: The electrical current and heat generated by lightning can lead to significant damage to both property and lives.
pg039_n0004: Lightning can reach temperatures of approximately 27,000 degrees Celsius.
pg039_n0005: When lightning strikes, it creates a tunnel-like gap in the air known as a channel.
pg039_n0006: Once the lightning disappears, this channel collapses, and the resulting sound from this collapse is what we hear as thunder.
pg039_n0010: Lightning cannot be prevented, but protection against destruction is possible by using lightning conductors.
pg039_n0011: A lightning conductor works because the charge concentrates more on sharp points, such as mountains, trees, and tall houses.
pg039_n0012: These sharp points have a high density of earth charges, so they are liable to be struck by lightning.

pg039_n0021: A lightning conductor, also known as a lightning rod, is a metal rod, typically made of copper, installed atop a structure to protect it from lightning strikes.
pg039_n0023: It offers a low-resistance path for the electrical current of a lightning strike to travel safely to the ground, thereby preventing damage to the building.
pg039_n0024: This system usually comprises a copper wire connecting the rod to a grounding system, such as a deep underground copper earth pole.
pg039_n0025: The lightning conductor should be taller than the house to be protected.
pg039_n0026: When lightning strikes the conductor, electric charges flow along the wire and are dissipated to the ground, where they cause no harm and thereby protect the building.

pg046_n0003: Electric current, I, is defined as the rate of flow of electric charge, Q, through a conductor over time, t.
pg046_n0004: This relationship is expressed mathematically as
pg046_n0005: I equals charge, Q, divided by time, t.
pg046_n0008: where n is the number of electrons and e is the charge of an electron.
pg046_n0010: I equals n e divided by t.
pg046_n0012: In simpler terms, current measures the amount of charge that passes a given point in a circuit per unit of time.
pg046_n0013: This charge is carried by charged particles such as electrons or ions.
pg046_n0014: A higher current indicates a greater flow of charge.
pg046_n0019: Given that the charge of an electron is one point six times ten to the power of minus nineteen coulombs, find the number of electrons that pass in one second through any cross-section of a conductor with a steady current of 1 ampere.
pg046_n0022: I equals n e divided by t.
pg046_n0023: n equals I t divided by e equals 1 ampere times 1 second divided by one point six times ten to the power of minus nineteen coulombs equals six point two five times ten to the power of eighteen.
pg046_n0025: Therefore, the number of electrons is six point two five times ten to the power of eighteen.
pg046_n0029: The electromotive force (e.m.f) is the potential difference across the terminals of a source when no current is flowing.
pg046_n0030: It provides the energy required to move electrons through a conductor, leading to an electric current.
pg046_n0031: Note that the word “force” in this case does not mean the force of interaction between bodies.
pg046_n0032: One may draw an analogy of e.m.f to water pressure.
pg046_n0033: When the pressure is high, more water flows through a pipe.
pg046_n0034: Similarly, with higher e.m.f, more electrons flow through a conductor.
pg046_n0035: Sources of e.m.f include electrochemical cells such as dry cells and car batteries, thermoelectric devices, solar cells and electric generators.
pg046_n0036: Labels of potential difference values written on a battery or cell refer to its e.m.f.

pg047_n0023: The e.m.f. of a cell and p.d are measured using a high resistance device called a voltmeter.
pg047_n0024: A voltmeter measures the difference in potential between two points.
pg047_n0025: It is always connected in parallel with the cell or the load because the e.m.f. of a cell is compared to the p.d across the voltmeter’s terminals.
pg047_n0026: To measure e.m.f. and p.d, the positive terminal of the voltmeter is connected to the positive terminal of a cell, and the negative terminal of the voltmeter is connected to the negative terminal of the cell.
pg047_n0027: Note: Measuring e.m.f by a voltmeter only provides an estimated value, since a small amount of current is drawn by the meter contrary to the requirement that no current is drawn for e.m.f measurement.

pg048_n0057: When drawing a circuit diagram, follow the following steps.
pg048_n0059: Voltmeter connection: A voltmeter must be connected in parallel with the component across which the voltage is being measured.
pg049_n0003: Ammeter connection: An ammeter, which measures current, is always connected in series with the circuit component(s) to ensure that the current flowing through the component(s) also flows through, and is measured by, the ammeter.
pg049_n0005: Components: For beginners, connect a single component, e.g., a resistor, bulb, in series with a source of e.m.f.
pg049_n0006: However, depending on the requirement, if multiple components are used, they may be connected in parallel and/or series configurations, and then the system is connected in series with the source of e.m.f.

pg049_n0047: The flow of charge through a wire in a circuit can be compared to the flow of water through a pipe connecting two water reservoirs.
pg049_n0048: Water flows through the pipe if there is a pressure difference between the two reservoirs.
pg049_n0049: As it flows through a pipe, it loses energy due to friction between the moving water molecules and the pipe’s inner walls.
pg049_n0050: Similarly, electric charges will flow between two points of a conductor if one point has a higher electric potential than the other; that is, there is a potential difference.
pg049_n0051: As charges flow in a material, they encounter numerous collisions with atoms, resulting in a resistance to the flow of charges.
pg049_n0052: This is known as electrical resistance, denoted by the letter R.
pg049_n0053: In other words, electrical resistance is the opposition to the flow of electrical current through a material.
pg049_n0055: Any material that offers low resistance to the current flow is termed a conductor.
pg049_n0056: On the other hand, a material is said to be an insulator if it does not allow the flow of electric current through it.
pg049_n0057: Some materials, known as semiconductors, have resistance between that of conductors and insulators.
pg049_n0058: The SI unit of electrical resistance is the ohm, denoted by the symbol Ω.
pg049_n0059: It is worth noting that electrical current loses its energy as it flows through a conductor.
pg050_n0005: A resistor is an electrical component with two terminals used to restrict the flow of electric current in a circuit.
pg050_n0006: That is, resistors control the magnitude of the current in a circuit in accordance with Ohm’s law.
pg050_n0007: There are two basic types of resistors depending on their applications and characteristics.
pg050_n0008: These are fixed resistors and variable resistors.
pg050_n0012: The most commonly used type of resistor is the fixed resistor.
pg050_n0013: A fixed resistor has a constant value of resistance.
pg050_n0014: Applications of fixed resistors include protecting electrical components from excess current, dividing voltage in a circuit, and controlling the working of some circuits.
pg050_n0015: In a circuit, the fixed resistor is represented by the symbols shown in Figure 2.8.

pg050_n0019: Diverse resistor materials are used to fabricate fixed resistors.
pg050_n0020: These materials influence the resistor’s properties, such as tolerance and noise.
pg050_n0021: Fixed resistors can be made of carbon, wound wire, metal oxide and metal films.
pg050_n0026: Use library or online resources to outline characteristics, internal structure, and applications of carbon, wound wire, metal oxide and metal films resistors.
pg050_n0030: These are resistors whose electric resistance can be adjusted (from zero to its maximum value) to suit the requirements of a circuit.
pg050_n0031: Examples of variable resistors include rheostats, voltage dividers, thermistors, photoresistors and magneto-resistors.

pg062_n0085: Factors that determine the resistance of a conductor
pg062_n0087: The resistance of a conductor is determined by its temperature, length, cross-sectional area and type of material.
pg063_n0005: As temperature rises, the atoms in the conductor vibrate more, leading to increased collisions between electrons and atoms, which raises resistance.
pg063_n0006: In some materials, the resistance varies almost linearly with temperature.
pg063_n0007: For instance, the resistance of copper (Cu) varies approximately linearly with temperature.
pg063_n0008: For some other materials, resistance does not vary linearly with temperature.
pg063_n0009: However, the effect of temperature on the resistance of some alloys, such as constantan and manganin, is minimal.
pg063_n0013: When the length of a conductor is increased, while other factors are kept constant, the resistance of the conductor also increases.
pg063_n0014: This is because electrons and atoms collide more in a long conductor than in a short conductor.
pg063_n0015: This means that the resistance (R) of the wire is proportional to the length (l) of the wire.
pg063_n0021: A conductor with a larger cross-sectional area has more charge carriers to carry the electrical current than of a smaller cross area.
pg063_n0022: This means the resistance R of a conductor is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area A of the conductor, that is,
pg063_n0023: R is proportional to one over A.
pg063_n0027: The resistance of a conductor also depends on the material used to make the conductor.
pg063_n0028: For example, a conductor made from steel will have higher resistance than one made of copper of identical dimensions at the same temperature.
pg063_n0029: For example, steel has a higher resistivity than copper.
pg063_n0030: A material’s property that resists current flow is known as the material’s resistivity, denoted by rho.
pg063_n0031: Since, R is proportional to l and R is proportional to one over A; then,
pg063_n0032: R is proportional to l over A.
pg063_n0035: R equals r times l over A.
pg063_n0037: where r is the constant of proportionality.
pg063_n0038: This constant of proportionality is the resistivity of the material, given as:
pg063_n0039: rho equals R A over l.
pg063_n0041: Resistivity is, therefore, the measure of the ability of a material to oppose the flow of an electric current.
pg063_n0042: The SI unit of resistivity is the ohm-metre (Ωm).
pg063_n0043: Activity 2.6 will aid in developing practical knowledge on determination of resistivity of wires.

pg066_n0012: Resistance measurement is essential in electrical circuits.
pg066_n0013: Two accurate methods used are the Wheatstone bridge, which balances known and unknown resistances, and the potentiometer, which compares voltage drops to determine resistance.
pg066_n0014: These methods are clearly explained in the sections below, providing step-by-step procedures, principles of operation, and practical applications to enhance understanding.
pg066_n0018: From Activity 2.5, Ohm’s law was used to determine the value of the unknown resistance of a conductor.
pg066_n0019: A similar approach cannot be applied to accurately measure a very low value of resistance in the milli-Ohms (mΩ) range.
pg066_n0020: However, when resistors are connected in the series-parallel arrangement as shown in Figure 2.28, the value of the unknown resistance of a conductor, even in mΩ, can be measured.
pg066_n0021: This diamond-like arrangement is called the Wheatstone bridge circuit.
pg066_n0023: It consists mainly of four resistors known as the bridge arms and a galvanometer in between them.

pg066_n0027: Working principle of a Wheatstone bridge
pg066_n0029: To understand how the Wheatstone bridge works, let us consider a bridge circuit in Figure 2.29.
pg066_im012: Wheatstone bridge circuit with four resistors in a rectangular bridge, a central branch between the upper and lower midpoints, and a 9 V battery connected across the outer terminals.
pg066_n0033: If the resistors, P equals 5 ohms, Q equals 1 ohm, R equals 10 ohms, X equals 2 ohms and J equals 6 ohms, what is the current flowing through the circuit?
pg066_n0035: The circuit in Figure 2.29 does not have any resistors arranged in series or in parallel.
pg067_n0003: circuit to an equivalent resistance using parallel and series formulae.
pg067_n0004: However, if you observe the circuit carefully, you realize that, the resistors on one side of the joint resistor, J, are in the same ratio as the resistor on the other side of J.
pg067_n0006: P over Q equals 5 ohms over 1 ohm and R over X equals 10 ohms over 2 ohms equals 5.
pg067_n0007: Therefore, P over Q equals R over X.
pg067_n0009: A bridge circuit that has this property is said to be a balanced Wheatstone bridge.
pg067_n0010: Now, suppose the resistor J, is removed from the circuit so that resistor P, is in series with resistor R, and resistor Q is in series with resistor X.
pg067_n0011: Moreover, the resistors P and R are in parallel with resistors Q and X.
pg067_n0012: Therefore, the voltages at points E and F are the same.
pg067_n0014: P over Q equals R over X,
pg067_n0016: the voltage drop at P is the same as the voltage drop at Q, meaning that voltage at point B, V sub B, is the same as voltage at point C, V sub C.
pg067_n0017: This means the potential difference between points B and C is zero.
pg067_n0018: Thus, when the resistor J is connected, current through it is zero.
pg067_n0019: That is, when the bridge circuit is balanced, I sub J equals 0 ampere.
pg067_n0020: Suppose a resistor J is replaced with a galvanometer G as shown in Figure 2.29.
pg067_n0021: The variable resistor R sub v, can be varied to a point where the current through the galvanometer I sub G equals 0 ampere.
pg067_n0023: At this point, the bridge circuit is balanced, and therefore,
pg067_n0024: P over Q equals R sub v over X,
pg067_n0026: X equals Q R sub v over P

pg068_n0024: A slide wire bridge (Metre bridge) is a modified Wheatstone bridge.
pg068_n0025: It is made of one known resistor R, an unknown resistor R sub x, and a wire of uniform cross section area, as shown in Figure 2.30.

pg068_n0029: The ratio R sub B over R sub A is adjusted by sliding a jockey along the length of the wire.
pg068_n0030: Because the wire has a uniform cross-sectional area, the ratio R sub B over R sub A is equivalent to respective lengths L sub B and L sub A.
pg068_n0032: R sub B over R sub A equals rho L sub B over A, over rho L sub A over A, equals L sub B over L sub A
pg068_n0034: R sub B over R sub A equals R sub X over R, implies L sub B over L sub A equals R sub X over R
pg068_n0036: This expression can therefore be written as,
pg068_n0037: R sub x equals L sub B over L sub A times R
pg068_n0039: This expression can be used to determine the value of the unknown resistor.

pg071_n0006: Theoretically, the e.m.f E one of cell P balances the p.d. V one on the wire because no current flows in G at the balance point N.

pg072_n0026: Heating effect of an electric current
pg072_n0028: When an electric current flows through a conductor, the electrical energy is converted into thermal energy, and the conductor heats up.
pg072_n0029: This is a demonstration of the heating effect of an electric current.
pg072_n0030: In an electric iron, the electrical energy is converted to heat, making the iron hot.
pg072_n0031: Other electrical appliances that work on the heating effect of electric current include immersion water heaters, hot plates, electric kettles and filament lamps.

pg079_n0023: Electricity is a highly convenient and clean source of power.
pg079_n0024: Electricity is supplied in houses by low-resistance wires (copper or aluminium) insulated with rubber.
pg079_n0025: The cables are rated according to the maximum current they can carry.
pg079_n0029: Domestic electricity is supplied through two cables: the live cable (L), coloured brown or red, and the neutral cable (N), usually coloured blue or black.
pg079_n0030: For a single-phase system, the live cable is at a potential of 240 V relative to the neutral line.
pg079_n0031: The current in the cable alternates 60 times a second (60 Hz).
pg079_n0032: The neutral cable is earthed; it is connected to the ground at the power station.
pg079_n0033: This ensures that even though current flows through this cable, it remains at zero potential.
pg079_n0034: In this situation, it cannot give an electric shock when touched.
pg079_n0035: To provide extra safety, especially in electrical appliances, a third cable called earth (E), coloured yellow or green, is also provided and is earthed by connecting it to the ground via a thick copper rod.
pg079_n0036: This cable connects the metal body of an electrical appliance to the ground through a three-pin plug.
pg079_n0037: A three-pin plug and electrical wiring cables are connected as shown in Figure 2.41.
pg079_im020: Inside view of a three-pin plug showing the fuse and the earth, live, and neutral wires connected to their terminals.
pg079_im018: Exterior view of a three-pin plug with three metal pins on a white plug top.
pg080_n0003: A fuse is connected to the live cable to ensure that if it blows, the appliance’s body is cut off from the live electrical connection, preventing potential danger to users.
pg080_n0004: The earth pin on the plug is generally longer than the other two pins, enabling it to open the safety shutter to the terminals of the socket.
pg080_n0005: It also ensures an appliance is earthed before being connected to a power source.
pg080_n0006: When connecting a three-pin plug, the colour code must be strictly adhered to avoid an electric shock.
pg080_n0007: The switch must be OFF when pushing the plug into the socket.
pg080_n0008: The two-pin plug does not have a fuse or an earth pin.
pg080_n0009: Thus, an appliance using a two-pin plug does not have its body connected to the earth.
pg080_n0011: The connections for this plug follow the same colour code as the three-pin plug.

pg080_n0015: A fuse and a circuit breaker
pg080_n0017: When an electric current exceeds the rated value of an electrical appliance, it causes damage to the device.
pg080_n0018: To protect an appliance against this damage, a fuse or a circuit breaker is used.
pg080_n0019: A fuse consists of an element, usually a piece of copper or tin-lead alloy wire, that melts when current exceeds a predetermined value.
pg080_n0020: The element is contained in a suitable casing and placed in series with the circuit to be protected.
pg080_n0022: Fuses are categorised into two types; rewirable fuses and cartridge fuses.
pg080_n0023: In rewireable fuse, the fuse element is carried in a removable fuse link that is. made of porcelain or other suitable insulating material.
pg080_n0024: This ensures no danger to an operator when removing the fuse link.
pg080_im013: Rewirable fuse with a black insulating top and two metal blades.
pg080_n0029: Cartridge fuses consist of a porcelain tube with metal end caps attached to the fuse element.
pg080_im014: Cartridge fuse with metal end caps and a white body labeled 12 A.
pg080_n0036: Blowing (melting) of a fuse occurs when a circuit is overloaded or a short circuit occurs.
pg080_n0037: A short-circuit fault is an unwanted connection allowing current to flow along a path not part of a circuit design.
pg081_n0003: some or all of the current flows from the designed path.
pg081_n0004: Short-circuit faults can be identified because the circuit or a section of the circuit draws an unusually high current (leading to fuse blowing).
pg081_n0005: The potential difference between two points joined by a short circuit is zero or much lower than expected.

pg082_n0006: A circuit breaker like the ones shown in Figure 2.47 is a type of switch that cuts off the flow of current when the current in a circuit exceeds a specific value.
pg082_n0007: It operates by opening the circuit in the event of excess current.
pg082_n0008: Unlike a fuse, a circuit breaker can be reset once the current in a circuit has returned to normal.
pg082_n0009: However, like a fuse, a circuit breaker is connected in series with the circuit it controls.
pg082_n0011: In a circuit breaker, switch contacts are held closed by a latch mechanism that releases the contacts quickly to open the circuit.

pg082_n0017: The power company connects power to a house up to the meter and leaves cables to be connected to the consumer unit where the house wiring starts.
pg082_n0018: A consumer unit is a type of distribution board that distributes electricity from the main supply to separate circuits.
pg082_n0019: From the consumer unit, the cables branch into several parallel circuits which carry current to the various parts of the house.
pg082_n0020: There are two methods of wiring a house from the main switch: the ring and tree systems.
pg082_n0023: In many houses, the main sockets are connected to a ring main.
pg082_n0024: This cable begins and ends at the consumer unit.
pg082_n0025: It has live, neutral, and earth wires, each forming a ring around the house or part of the house.
pg082_n0026: In a circuit, the current has two parts, so thin cables can be used.
pg082_n0027: The sockets usually have a 30 A fuse at the consumer unit.
pg082_n0028: Figure 2.48 shows a typical ring main circuit.

pg082_n0035: Figure 2.48: Consumer unit and a ring main in a house
pg082_n0037: The tree system method uses a cable from the main switch to the distribution box as shown in Figure 2.49.
pg082_n0038: Of these two methods of wiring, the ring system is more convenient for wiring modern houses than the tree system.

pg083_n0005: In the distribution box, there are lighting fuses and power fuses.
pg083_n0006: For example, there are separate fuses for lighting in corridors, bedrooms, the living room and the kitchen.
pg083_n0007: Most houses have light fuses rated 5 A and fuses for power sockets usually rated 15 A.
pg083_n0008: Hence, cables for power points are different from those for lights.
pg083_n0009: Lighting circuits control the lighting fixtures in a house.
pg083_n0010: Unlike the ring circuit, the lighting circuit does not form a loop returning to the consumer unit.
pg083_n0011: Instead, the consumer unit is normally connected to the first lamp, which in turn is connected to the second lamp, and so on.
pg083_n0012: There are two types of lighting circuits: loop-in lighting circuits and junction box lighting circuits.
pg083_n0014: In the loop-in lighting circuit, the live, neutral, and earth wires run from the consumer unit to each of the ceiling designs, one after the other.
pg083_n0015: From each rose, another set of wires runs to the switch, which operates the light.

pg083_n0025: In the junction box lighting circuit, neutral and earth wires run to one junction box after another.
pg083_n0026: From the junction box, one wire runs to the light and the other runs to the switch for that light.

pg084_n0041: Checking electrical faults in domestic appliances
pg084_n0043: Identifying electrical faults in domestic appliances is essential for ensuring safety and optimal performance.
pg084_n0044: Common issues like short circuits and faulty wiring can lead to malfunctions and pose hazards, making regular inspections and maintenance crucial.
pg084_n0045: Two devices are useful when checking electrical appliance faults.
pg084_n0046: These are the multimeter and the live mains lead indicator.
pg084_n0047: Multimeters are tools used for measuring a variety of electrical variables.
pg084_n0048: The most basic parameters measured are voltage and current (both a.c and d.c.).
pg084_n0049: They also have a range switch so that precise readings can be taken.
pg084_n0050: There are moving coils and digital multimeters.
pg084_n0051: The moving-coil multimeters (analogue) (Figure 2.52 (a)) have some disadvantages as they involve various settings when in use.
pg084_n0052: The digital multimeter (Figure 2.52 (b)), has no moving parts, thus, easy to use.
pg084_im017_seg001_v1: Analogue multimeter with a needle display and central rotary range selector.
pg084_im017_seg002_v1_crop_v1: Digital multimeter with LCD display reading 0.00 and a central rotary range selector.
pg085_n0003: The live mains lead indicator, commonly called a tester, is made up of a form of a screwdriver with a hollow insulating handle containing a tiny neon discharge tube.
pg085_n0004: One electrode of the neon tube is usually in contact with the metal probe of the screwdriver.
pg085_n0005: The other is connected to the metal cap of the handle through a high-carbon resistor.
pg085_n0006: When one inserts the metal probe into a live socket and touches a metal cap with a finger, current leaks to the earth through the body and the neon tube glows.
pg085_n0007: Owing to the high resistance, this current is very low, so there is no risk of electric shock.
pg085_im007: Live mains lead indicator tester with a transparent yellow handle and a metal probe tip.
pg085_n0012: Most of the faults that occur in electrical appliances are simple and can be repaired easily.
pg085_n0013: If, for example, an electric kettle fails to work, the first thing to check is whether there is power in the socket.
pg085_n0014: This is done using the tester.
pg085_n0015: The next step is to check the cable from the socket to the appliance.
pg085_n0016: The plug should be opened to check the fuse if no fault is detected.
pg085_n0017: Also, check each cable for continuity using a multimeter.
pg085_n0018: If these components function correctly, the heating element is the next thing to check for faults.
pg085_n0019: This can be checked for continuity or short circuits using a multimeter.
pg085_n0021: If the element is faulty, it must be replaced, as repair may not be possible.
pg085_n0022: If the element is not faulty, then look for loose connections.
pg085_n0024: Connections should be made firm and/or cleaned of rust and other dirt.
pg085_n0026: Repairs in electrical appliances should be limited to connections to the power supply only.
pg085_n0027: Beyond that, an electrical technician should be consulted.
pg085_n0028: Care should be taken to avoid electric shocks during such repairs.
pg085_n0029: Simple repairs on electrical connections in a domestic system can also be carried out.
pg085_n0030: When a fuse blows, it is very likely to be due to a fault in an appliance.
pg085_n0031: If the fault is detected and corrected, then the fuse can be replaced (or the circuit breaker switched ON).
pg085_n0033: Other faults occur due to wire cutting or joining, sockets getting dirty and switch breakage.
pg085_n0034: All repairs should be done with the mains switched OFF.
pg085_n0035: When replacing switches and sockets, the colour code should be followed strictly.

pg086_n0027: A cell is a set-up used to cause a flow of electric current in a conductor.
pg086_n0028: The flow of current is caused by reactions releasing and accepting electrons at different ends of a conductor.
pg086_n0029: There are two common types of electrochemical cells, namely primary cells and secondary cells.
pg086_n0033: Primary cells, also known as voltaic cells, are formed by dipping two different electrodes (usually made of metals) into an electrolyte.
pg086_n0034: In a primary cell, reactants are used up after some time and must be replaced.

pg086_n0052: Zinc goes into solution as zinc ions, Z n two plus, releasing two electrons which travel along the wire (external circuit) to the copper electrode.

pg087_n0007: This movement of electrons through the wire is called the electric current.
pg087_n0008: The conventional direction of electric current is from the positive terminal to the negative terminal of the cell, which is the opposite of the direction of flow of electrons.

pg089_n0038: When the simple cell is in operation, the current drops to a very small value after some time.
pg089_n0039: A simple cell has two main defects which cause the current to diminish quickly when the cell is being used.
pg089_n0040: These defects are local action and polarization.
pg089_n0044: The local action of a cell is the deterioration of the battery due to currents that are flowing from and to the same electrode.
pg089_n0045: The deterioration is caused by embedded impurities such as iron, lead and carbon in a zinc electrode.
pg089_n0046: The impurities act as positive electrodes and create electric currents between zinc and this positive (impurities) electrode.
pg089_n0047: Local action can be reduced by using pure zinc or by rubbing mercury on the zinc plate to form an amalgam.
pg089_n0051: Polarization is a defect that occurs in simple electric cells due to the accumulation of hydrogen gas around a positive electrode.
pg089_n0052: The hydrogen gas produced in chemical reactions inside the cell can accumulate around the electrodes resulting in insulation.
pg089_n0053: Polarization in cells can be minimized using depolarizers such as potassium dichromate or manganese oxide, which oxidizes hydrogen to water.

pg090_n0005: In this type of cell, the current is produced from non-recoverable or irreversible chemical reactions.
pg090_n0006: For example, when all zinc has been dissolved in a simple cell, it will never be recovered to its original form by passing a current through the cell in the opposite direction.
pg090_n0010: Unlike primary cells, secondary cells can be recharged after they have run down.
pg090_n0011: Examples of secondary cells are the lead-acid cell and the nickel-ferrous cell.
pg090_n0012: Secondary cells are also called accumulators.
pg090_n0014: Mode of action of lead-acid accumulator
pg090_n0016: The lead-acid battery consists of several lead-acid cells.
pg090_n0017: Each cell has two groups of lead plates.
pg090_n0018: One group forms a positive terminal while the other group forms a negative terminal.
pg090_n0019: All positive terminal plates are connected with a connecting strap.
pg090_n0020: This is also the case for negative terminal plates.
pg090_n0021: The positive and negative terminal plates are connected so that they alternate.
pg090_n0022: Between the plates are sheets of insulating material called separators.
pg090_n0023: These are made up of porous wood or fibreglass.
pg090_n0024: The separators prevent the positive and negative plates from coming into contact thereby avoiding the production of a short circuit.
pg090_n0025: The positive plates are made of lead dioxide while the negative plates are made of porous lead metal.
pg090_n0026: The two sets of plates with the separators between them are placed in a container filled with a dilute solution of sulphuric acid.
pg090_n0027: The term lead-acid refers to the lead plates and the sulphuric acid which are the main components of the battery.

pg094_n0004: Uses of current electricity in daily life
pg094_n0009: Electricity is essential for domestic tasks like cooking, preserving food, and doing laundry.
pg094_n0010: It powers appliances such as stoves, refrigerators, washing machines, and irons.
pg094_n0011: It also provides lighting, entertainment through TVs and computers, and comfort using fans, heaters, and air conditioners.
pg094_n0012: Other common devices include kettles, vacuums, and hairdryers.
pg094_n0017: Current electricity is used in transportation to power various electric vehicles.
pg094_n0018: For example, standard gauge railway trains use electricity for efficient and eco-friendly travel.
pg094_n0019: Additionally, electric cars like the Tesla Model 3, electric buses in urban areas, trams in cities, and electric scooters also rely on current electricity for operation.

pg094_n0029: Welding machines, and electric drills also rely on current electricity.

pg095_n0008: Electromotive force (e.m.f), is the maximum potential difference between two terminals of a battery or a cell when no current is drawn from the battery or cell.
pg095_n0009: In other words, it is the electrical intensity or pressure developed by a source of electrical energy.
pg095_n0012: Electric potential difference (p.d) is the work done per unit charge in moving the electric charge from one point to another point of a conductor.
pg095_n0015: Electric current, I, is defined as the rate at which electric charge, Q, passes a given point by a unit of the ampere, A, and is measured by an instrument called an ammeter.
pg095_n0018: Resistance is the opposition to the flow of electric current in a conductor.
pg095_n0022: The resistance of a conductor is affected by: temperature, its length, cross-sectional area and material of the conductor.
pg095_n0025: When resistors are connected in series, the total resistance in the circuit is equal to the sum of the individual resistances.
pg095_n0028: When resistors are connected in parallel, the reciprocal of the total resistance is equal to the sum of the reciprocals of the individual resistances.
pg095_n0031: When an electric current flow through a conductor of high resistance, the electrical energy gets converted into thermal energy and heats the conductor.
pg095_n0032: This is known as the heating effect of an electric current.
pg095_n0035: Every electrical appliance should carry a label stating the potential difference for which it has been designed and the power it can convert when operating at the stated potential difference.
pg095_n0038: Electricity is supplied in consumers’ places by low-resistance wire made up of either copper or aluminium material insulated with plastic.
pg095_n0041: The wires used in electrical installation are rated according to the maximum current they can carry.
pg095_n0044: Domestic electricity is supplied by two cables; the live cable (L), coloured brown or red, and the neutral cable (N) usually coloured blue or black.
pg095_n0047: The rate at which an appliance dissipates energy is called the rating of that appliance and is usually marked on the body of the appliance.
pg095_n0050: There are two common types of electrochemical cells, namely primary and secondary cells.
pg095_n0053: The total voltage across cells connected in series is equal to the sum of the voltages of the individual cells while in parallel connection, the effective voltage is equal to the voltage of one of the cells (for identical cells).

pg100_n0009: Knowledge of magnetism has provided several useful applications in daily life, starting from the historical navigation by the Greeks to the present-day digital world.
pg100_n0010: In this chapter, you will learn the concept of magnetism and how materials can be magnetised or demagnetised.
pg100_n0011: You will also learn about magnetic fields, including the Earth’s magnetic field.
pg100_n0012: The competencies developed will enable you to apply the knowledge of magnetism in various contexts.
pg100_n0015: Life without the existence of magnetism
pg100_n0019: Magnetism is a phenomenon produced by the motion of electric charges that results in an attractive and repulsive force between objects.
pg100_n0020: The earliest observation of magnetism was recorded in 600 BC by the Greek philosopher Thales.
pg100_n0021: He observed that pieces of iron were attracted to a natural mineral iron ore called magnetite.
pg100_n0022: The lodestone is an example of a magnetised piece of the mineral magnetite.
pg100_im060: Dark, irregular lump of iron ore with a rough, shiny surface.
pg100_n0027: The lodestone tends to attract certain metals more strongly at specific points on its surface than others.
pg100_n0028: Any material that has properties similar to those of the lodestone is called a magnet.
pg100_n0029: When magnets attract or repel each other, they exert a force called magnetic force.
pg100_n0030: Magnetism arises from two types of electron motion as shown in Figure 3.2.
pg100_n0031: The first is the motion of electrons around the nucleus of an atom.
pg100_n0032: The second type of motion is the spin of electrons about their axes.
pg100_n0033: These motions of charged particles independently impart a magnetic effect, causing an atom to behave like a tiny magnet.
pg101_im006: Electron moving in an elliptical orbit around a central nucleus, with a small arrow showing the electron’s spin.
pg101_n0007: Figure 3.2: Orbit of a spinning electron around the nucleus of an atom
pg101_n0009: In many atoms, these magnetic effects cancel each other, while in other atoms they do not cancel completely.
pg101_n0013: When a magnet is brought near different objects, some will be attracted or repelled, and others will not.
pg101_n0014: Objects that are attracted are said to possess induced magnetism.
pg101_n0015: The process by which a material becomes a magnet due to its closeness or contact with a magnet is called induction.
pg101_n0016: The induced magnetism can be temporary or permanent upon the removal of the magnet in contact.
pg101_n0017: The nature of the material being magnetised determines how long the induced magnetism lasts.
pg101_n0018: For example, iron exhibits temporary magnetism while materials like steel tend to retain their magnetism for a long time.
pg101_n0019: Materials which are not affected by a magnet are called non-magnetic materials.
pg101_im005: Two students carrying out a magnetism activity at a table, with a bar magnet and another test object between them.

pg101_n0039: Metallic materials like iron, nickel and cobalt become magnetised when exposed to the influence of a magnet.
pg101_n0041: Magnetic materials are those which can be magnetised by even weak magnets.
pg101_n0042: Materials that are attracted to a magnet and can be strongly magnetised are called ferromagnetic materials.
pg101_n0043: Ferromagnetic materials contain either iron, nickel or cobalt.
pg101_n0044: These materials are grouped as magnetically hard or soft depending on how well they retain their magnetism when magnetised.
pg101_n0046: Magnetically hard materials such as steel do not readily lose their magnetism, though they are difficult to magnetise.
pg101_n0047: They are used to make permanent magnets.
pg101_n0048: On the other hand, soft magnetic materials like iron can be easily magnetised, but they tend to lose their magnetism easily.
pg101_n0049: As a result, they are used in the cores
pg101_sec001_ans_item-1: The knife, blade and iron nail were attracted to the magnet. They have in common that they are made of magnetic materials containing iron.
pg101_sec001_ans_item-2: Some metals are attracted because they are magnetic and can be magnetised, especially metals containing iron, nickel or cobalt. Other metals are not attracted because they are non-magnetic.
pg101_sec001_ans_item-3: Materials attracted by a magnet are classified as magnetic materials, while materials not attracted by a magnet are classified as non-magnetic materials.
pg102_n0004: Brass, copper, tin, zinc and aluminium are non-magnetic materials.
pg102_n0005: These materials are not attracted by a magnet.
pg102_n0006: Non-metals, for example, plastic, rubber, water, wood and ceramics are also non-magnetic.
pg102_n0011: Magnets are categorised according to their sources of magnetism.
pg102_n0015: These acquire magnetism due to an applied external magnetic field but lose their magnetism when the external field is removed.
pg102_n0016: These magnets retain magnetism in a short time (i.e., the time during which the magnetising field is present).
pg102_n0017: For example, the magnetism that is induced in iron is temporary and is lost once the external magnet is withdrawn.
pg102_n0018: Iron nails and paper clips shown in Figure 3.3 (a) are good examples of objects that can be temporarily magnetised.
pg102_n0019: An electromagnet used in magnetic cranes, as shown in Figure 3.3 (b), is an example of a temporary magnet.

pg102_n0031: Other examples of temporary magnetism are electromagnets.
pg102_n0032: These are temporary magnets created by an electric current flowing through a coil, often with an iron core to enhance the magnetic field.
pg102_n0033: They can be quickly turned on and off, and their magnetic strength can be adjusted by changing the current.
pg102_n0034: However, they require a continuous power supply to maintain magnetism, which disappears when the current stops.
pg102_n0035: Electromagnets are widely used in applications needing strong, controllable magnetic fields, such as railroad tracks, electric motors, microphones, hard drives, MRI machines, security systems, cranes, and various computer and television hardware.
pg102_im009: An electric motor showing a practical application of electromagnets.
pg103_n0004: These retain some magnetism even after the external magnetic field is removed.
pg103_n0005: Such materials include an alloy composed of aluminium, nickel and cobalt (Alnico), or ceramic-like material made from a mixture of iron oxides with nickel, strontium, or cobalt (ferrites) that become magnetised in a magnetic field.
pg103_n0006: These magnets may be naturally occurring “rare earth” elements or chemical compounds.

pg103_n0014: Every magnet, regardless of its shape and size, has two poles.
pg103_n0015: N represents a North pole and S represents a South pole as shown in Figure 3.6.

pg103_n0019: These poles are always marked during the process of manufacturing for easy identification.
pg103_n0020: Colouring is also used to mark the poles as shown in Figure 3.6.

pg104_n0029: Some of the properties of magnets and magnetism include:
pg104_n0032: 1. All magnets have two poles, the north and south poles.
pg104_n0034: 2. Magnets exert a force on some materials and do not on others.
pg104_n0036: 3. Magnets attract ferromagnetic materials such as iron, nickel and cobalt.
pg104_n0038: 4. The magnetic force is an action-at-a-distance force.
pg104_n0040: 5. In a bar magnet, more iron filings stick to the poles, meaning that the magnetic force is the strongest near the poles of a magnet, and that the poles have equal strength.
pg104_n0042: 6. When two magnets are brought together, like poles repel each other while unlike poles attract, as shown in Figure 3.9.
pg104_n0043: This is the basic law of magnetism.

pg104_im012_seg004_v1: Bar magnet with arrows showing attraction as unlike poles pull together.

pg105_n0003: 7. A freely suspended bar magnet always points in a north–south direction.
pg105_n0004: The north pole of a freely suspended magnet points in the north direction, and the south pole points in the south direction of the Earth.
pg105_n0005: Likewise, the arrow of a compass needle points towards the north.
pg105_n0009: Magnets are of different types, and they work in different ways.
pg105_n0010: They differ in materials, shapes, sizes, functions, forces and applications.
pg105_n0011: For example, magnets can have different shapes, which include bar, horseshoe and disc as shown in Figure 3.10.
pg105_n0012: Magnets also vary in size from tiny discs used in speakers to large magnets used in commercial power-generating plants.
pg105_n0013: One of the largest magnets is perhaps the Earth itself.

pg107_n0034: Magnets are manufactured by aligning the tiny atomic magnets of a material.
pg107_n0035: The process of making a magnet is called magnetisation.
pg107_n0036: Likewise, demagnetisation is the process of destroying or removing the magnetism in a magnetised material.
pg107_n0040: The atoms of most materials act like tiny magnets called atomic dipoles.
pg107_n0041: If the material is not yet magnetised, its atomic dipoles randomly align, forming magnetic domains as shown in Figure 3.16.
pg107_im011: Magnetic domains with atomic dipoles aligned in different directions in separate regions of an unmagnetised material.
pg107_n0045: Figure 3.16: Random alignment of atomic dipoles in unmagnetised material
pg107_im012: Two magnetic domains with atomic dipoles aligned within each domain but oriented differently from one another.
pg107_im014: Adjacent magnetic domains showing atomic dipoles aligned within each domain but pointing in different directions overall.
pg108_n0005: If atomic dipoles arrange in such a way that N poles of all the dipoles face in one common direction, the material is said to be magnetised.
pg108_n0008: Magnetisation is the process of aligning the atomic dipoles in a material in one direction to produce a net effect of attraction or repulsion.
pg108_n0010: The domains may show a net magnetic behaviour in the absence of an external magnetic field.
pg108_n0011: On applying an external magnetic field, all dipoles align themselves in the direction of the applied field.
pg108_n0012: In this way the material is strongly magnetised in the direction parallel to the magnetising field as shown in Figure 3.17.
pg108_im011_crop_v1: Aligned atomic dipoles inside a magnetised material, all pointing in the same direction parallel to an external magnetic field.
pg108_n0015: Figure 3.17: Aligned atomic dipoles in a magnetised material
pg108_n0017: Materials in which it is possible to cause this alignment are either ferromagnetic or paramagnetic.
pg108_n0018: Ferromagnetic materials such as steel, nickel and cobalt can form permanent magnets, while paramagnetic materials such as aluminium and chromium can only be weakly magnetised and do not retain any magnetism once the external field is removed.
pg108_n0019: The alignment of domains in these materials can be achieved through one of the following: heating or vibration, stroking, and the electric method.
pg108_n0021: In the first method of magnetisation, an external magnetic field is required.
pg108_n0022: Placing an object in an external magnetic field will result in some degree of alignment.
pg108_n0023: Vibrating or heating the object can increase the amount of alignment by causing the atomic dipoles to move and eventually become aligned.
pg108_n0024: Many natural magnetic materials start out as part of lava (molten rock).
pg108_n0025: If the lava contains ferromagnetic minerals, the atoms align with the Earth’s magnetic field which is subject to vibration while the rock is still liquid.
pg108_n0026: As the rock cools and solidifies, the alignment becomes permanent.

pg109_n0024: In the second magnetisation method, a piece of unmagnetised material is stroked using a magnet.
pg109_n0025: An existing magnet is moved from one end of the material to the other in the same direction.
pg109_n0026: This process is repeated several times.
pg109_n0027: The pole produced at the end of the stroke is always the opposite of that at the end of the magnet used for stroking.
pg109_n0028: For example, if the north pole of the magnet is used for stroking, then the rod will be magnetised such that its starting end will act as the north pole and the other end as the south pole, as shown in Figure 3.19.
pg109_im008: Single-touch magnetisation: a bar magnet is stroked along an iron nail in one direction, then lifted and returned for repeated strokes.
pg109_n0033: After completing stroking, care has to be taken not to move the magnet close to the nail because this is taken as a repeat stroke.
pg109_n0034: It disorganises the already aligned dipoles.
pg109_n0035: The stroking method, whereby only one magnetising magnet is used, is called a single-touch method.
pg109_n0036: When two magnets are used, the method is called a double-touch method.
pg109_n0037: In this process, the ends of two magnets of different polarities are positioned at the middle of the iron nail.
pg109_n0038: The two magnets are then moved in a curved motion in the opposite directions as shown in Figure 3.20.
pg109_n0039: The iron nail is stroked a few times along its length.
pg109_n0040: This procedure must be done with care to ensure the proper magnetisation of the iron nail.

pg110_n0054: The third method of magnetisation relies on the fact that an electric current produces a magnetic field.
pg110_n0055: A long wire is wrapped around an object, such as a nail and connected to a battery as shown in Figure 3.21.

pg110_n0057: The combined effect of all the turns of wire produces a field similar to that of a bar magnet.
pg110_n0058: A wire coil of several turns is called a solenoid.

pg111_n0005: This is an industrial way of making a magnet.

pg111_n0010: Polarity of a magnet can be determined by the direction of the current.
pg111_n0011: When looking at the nail, the end that has current flowing in a clockwise direction is the S pole.
pg111_n0012: If it flows anticlockwise, the end acts as the N pole.
pg111_n0014: This is the rule for magnetic polarity.

pg112_n0012: Demagnetisation is the process of destroying the magnetic property of a material.
pg112_n0014: The process involves the destruction of the dipole alignment in the magnetised material.
pg112_n0015: This process can be done in the following ways:
pg112_n0019: If a permanent magnet is heated or vibrated in the absence of an external field, the magnetisation can be destroyed.
pg112_n0022: Randomly stroking one magnet with another can demagnetise the magnet being stroked.
pg112_n0025: Wrapping a wire coil around the magnet and connecting the coil to a source of alternating current will eliminate the magnetic alignment.
pg112_n0028: Repeated hammering or dropping the magnet in the absence of external magnetic field can also distort dipoles alignment.
pg112_n0031: During heating, the dipoles gain thermal energy and start to vibrate randomly losing alignment.
pg112_n0032: Randomly stroking makes the individual dipoles orient in different directions.
pg112_n0033: Alternating current repeatedly realign the dipoles in different directions making them settle in random orientations.
pg112_n0034: Hammering or dropping induce physical force into dipoles that disaligns them.

pg116_n0040: Properties of magnetic lines of force
pg116_n0042: Some of the properties of magnetic lines of force are as follows:
pg116_n0045: 1. Magnetic lines of force are continuous and always form closed loops.
pg116_n0047: 2. Lines of force from the bar magnet leave the north pole
pg117_n0004: and enter the south pole, and back to the north pole, forming a closed loop.
pg117_n0006: 3. Magnetic lines of force are close together where the magnetic force is stronger, and they are far apart where the magnetic force is weaker.
pg117_n0008: 4. Magnetic lines of force never cross one another.
pg117_n0010: 5. Parallel magnetic lines of force in the same direction repel one another.
pg117_n0011: Parallel magnetic lines of force in opposite directions attract one another as shown in Figure 3.34.

pg117_n0020: 6. Magnetic lines of force pass through magnetic and non-magnetic materials.
pg117_n0022: 7. Magnetic lines of force always enter or leave a magnetic material at right angles to the surface.
pg117_n0024: Neutral points in a magnetic field
pg117_n0027: At any point where two different magnetic fields exist, a stronger field is created if they are in the same direction, but a weaker field arises if they are in opposite directions.
pg117_n0028: The two fields can balance each other at one point.
pg117_n0030: A neutral point is a location where the total magnetic field equals zero.
pg117_n0032: For instance, if two bar magnets are positioned close to each other as illustrated in Figure 3.35, their magnetic fields oppose one another.
pg117_n0033: At a certain spot, these fields exactly cancel out, creating a neutral point labelled X.
pg117_n0034: As a result, there is no magnetic force present at neutral points.

pg122_n0010: Direction of the Earth’s magnetic field
pg122_n0012: Magnetic fields have both magnitude and direction.
pg122_n0013: The SI unit for magnitude of a magnetic field is the Tesla, T.
pg122_n0014: The magnitude of the Earth’s field varies from one location to another, ranging from 25µT to 65µT.
pg122_n0015: A compass may be used to determine the direction of the Earth’s magnetic field.
pg122_n0016: A compass is a device with a magnetised needle that is free to rotate in a horizontal plane and align itself with the horizontal component of the Earth’s magnetic field.
pg122_n0017: The head of a compass needle is a magnetic north pole, and the tail is a magnetic south pole.
pg122_n0019: The compass needle points toward the north pole, which means it will point toward the Earth’s MSP.
pg122_n0020: Therefore, a compass needle points in the general north direction of the Earth as shown in Figure 3.46.
pg122_n0021: For this reason, the magnetic north pole of the compass needle is referred to as a north-seeking pole, and the general direction it indicates is often called the “magnetic north".

pg125_n0005: If we position a compass on its side so that its needle can rotate within a vertical plane, the needle will align itself with the Earth’s magnetic field.
pg125_n0008: The angle formed between the direction of the resulting magnetic field and its horizontal component is known as the angle of inclination, or dip angle, denoted by I.
pg125_n0010: This angle is positive when the magnetic field vector points downward (as in the Northern Hemisphere) and negative when it points upward (as in the Southern Hemisphere).
pg125_n0011: The angle of inclination ranges from 0° at the magnetic equator to 90° at the magnetic poles.
pg125_n0012: It is measured using a dip needle, which is a magnetised needle mounted on a pivot allowing it to rotate freely in a vertical plane, as shown in Figure 3.53.
pg125_im002: Dip needle mounted in a circular frame on a stand, with the magnetised needle free to rotate in a vertical plane.
pg125_n0016: In practice, a compass is used to align the dip needle with the horizontal component of the magnetic field, and the dip needle rotates vertically to align with the total field.
pg125_n0017: The magnetic dip produces a vertical moment, causing the needle in a compass to rotate vertically.
pg125_n0018: This produces friction in the pivot, which hinders the free rotation of the needle.
pg125_n0019: To compensate for the dip, a small mass is added to one end of the needle to produce an opposite gravitational moment so as to maintain the needle in vertical equilibrium.
pg125_n0020: A compass to be used in the northern hemisphere, whereby the vertical component points down, has the mass added to the tail end of the needle.

pg126_n0005: Applications of the Earth’s magnetic field
pg126_n0007: The Earth’s magnetic field has very important applications in our daily life.
pg126_n0010: It is used by map-readers to find locations of different places.
pg126_n0012: It gives useful information in the search for minerals.
pg126_n0014: Reversals of the Earth’s magnetic field provide the basis for dating rocks and sediments.
pg126_n0016: Map-readers with a magnetic compass can locate the direction of the magnetic north using the compass.
pg126_n0018: It protects the Earth from cosmic radiation (potentially damaging high-energy particles from the sun).

pg130_n0008: Light is essential for many everyday activities, most notably our ability to see objects around us.
pg130_n0009: It allows us to perceive colours, shapes and details and navigate our environments safely.
pg130_n0010: In this Chapter, you will learn the concept of light, sources of light, propagation and transmission of light, reflection of light through plane mirrors and curved mirrors, and uses of curved mirrors in daily life.
pg130_n0011: The competencies developed will enable you to analyse and describe the characteristics of images formed by plane and curved mirrors.
pg130_n0012: Also, you will be able to apply the principles of light reflection in different everyday situations.
pg130_n0019: Light is a fundamental aspect of our universe, influencing both the physical world and our perception of it.
pg130_n0020: It is a type of energy that we can see with our eyes, which helps us understand what is around us.
pg130_n0021: When light encounters different materials, it can be absorbed, reflected, or refracted, leading to various visual effects.
pg130_n0023: The concept of light extends beyond mere visibility; it shapes our experiences, influences our environment, and carries profound significance in both science and culture.
pg130_n0024: Understanding light allows us to appreciate its role in our lives and the world around us.
pg130_n0026: Light is a form of energy which stimulates the sense of vision.
pg130_n0028: Light has some distinct features that differentiate it from other forms of energy.
pg130_n0032: 1. Light is given out from its source.
pg130_n0033: Lines known as light rays are used to show the direction of light.
pg130_n0035: 2. Light travels in a straight line.
pg130_n0036: This means that light can be observed as a beam of light.
pg130_n0037: A beam is a bundle of rays.
pg130_n0040: Objects gain energy when they absorb light.
pg130_n0041: For example, solar panels absorb light
pg131_n0003: from the Sun (solar energy) and convert it into electrical energy.
pg131_n0005: Light does not require a material medium to travel.
pg131_n0006: 5. Light travels at the speed of 3 times 10 to the power of 8 meters per second, which is the highest speed recorded on Earth.
pg131_n0010: Light sources can be classified into two main types: natural and artificial.
pg131_n0011: Some objects are luminous, meaning they produce their own light, whereas others are non-luminous and only reflect or scatter light from other sources.
pg131_n0012: Bioluminescence is a natural occurrence in certain glowing organisms, especially in dark forest settings.

pg137_n0041: Reflection of light through the plane mirror
pg137_n0043: We see objects because they reflect the light falling on them.
pg137_n0044: When light rays fall on the surface of an object, they are either absorbed, transmitted, or reflected.
pg137_n0045: Sometimes, a combination of the above processes may occur.
pg137_n0046: When light strikes a surface, how it is reflected depends on the nature of the surface.
pg137_n0049: Reflection of light is the phenomenon in which light rays are bounced back when they strike a highly polished surface like a mirror.
pg137_n0051: While one cannot usually see behind oneself, by the use of a mirror, one can see an object which is approaching from behind.
pg137_n0052: This is possible because the light from the object, on falling on the mirror, is thrown back to the observer’s eyes.
pg138_n0003: Therefore, this throwing back of light from the mirror is called reflection.
pg138_n0004: It is possible to see an object because it either emits or reflects light.
pg138_n0006: When using a plane mirror, a reflected ray bounces off the mirror.
pg138_n0007: A plane mirror is a thin glass whose surface (the bottom/back) is silvered to obtain a shiny reflecting surface.
pg138_n0008: Figure 4.9 shows the reflection of light rays from a plane mirror.
pg138_n0009: A polished metal surface can also reflect light rays like a plane mirror.
pg138_im008: Reflection of light on a plane mirror showing an incident ray, a reflected ray, and the normal at the point of incidence.
pg138_n0015: Figure 4.9: Reflection of light on a plane mirror
pg138_n0017: Regular and irregular reflection of light
pg138_n0019: There are two types of reflection: regular or specular reflection, and irregular or diffuse reflection.
pg138_n0023: In regular reflection, the reflecting surface is so smooth that an image of the object that reflects the light is very clear.
pg138_n0024: In regular reflection, all the reflected rays are in one direction.
pg138_n0025: The rays are also parallel, as shown in Figure 4.10.
pg138_n0026: Examples of such surfaces are mirrors and polished metal surfaces like highly reflective aluminium sheets.
pg138_n0028: When viewing the image of an object in a plane mirror, rays of light originate from the object and travel parallel along a straight line to the mirror.
pg138_n0029: The same rays reach the eye after reflection, appearing as if originating from the image, resulting in a very sharp image.
pg138_im009: Regular reflection of light: parallel incident rays strike a smooth surface and reflect as parallel rays.
pg138_n0037: Irregular reflection is the type of reflection in which light rays meet a rough reflecting surface.
pg138_n0038: This is shown by the incident light rays reflected in different directions as shown in Figure 4.11.
pg138_n0039: In irregular reflection, the reflected rays are not parallel, causing them to scatter in many directions.
pg138_n0040: This results in the formation of distorted images.
pg138_im010: Diffuse reflection of light: incoming rays strike a rough surface and reflect in different directions.
pg138_n0048: The phenomenon of reflection is fundamental to the behaviour of light and serves as a foundation in the study of
pg139_n0004: When light encounters a surface, it predictably changes direction, following specific principles known as the laws of reflection.
pg139_n0005: These laws govern how light interacts with reflective surfaces, such as mirrors (Figure 4.12) and determine the path of the reflected rays.
pg139_n0006: They are essential for understanding the behaviour of optical systems and have practical applications in fields ranging from astronomy to everyday technologies like periscopes, cameras, and fibre optics.
pg139_n0007: Activity 4.4 aids in experimental exploration on laws governing reflection of light.
