pg139_n0018: Figure 4.12: Reflection of light from the plane mirror
pg139_n0020: There are two laws of reflection that can be stated as follows:
pg139_n0024: The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.
pg139_n0025: This means the angle at which the incoming light ray strikes a surface (the angle of incidence) is identical to the angle at which it is reflected away (the angle of reflection).
pg139_n0028: The incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal to the reflective surface all lie in the same plane.
pg139_n0030: This ensures that the reflection is constrained to a two-dimensional plane defined by the light ray and perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence.

pg141_n0017: Characteristics of images formed in a plane mirror
pg141_n0019: A plane mirror is a simple glass with a flat surface.
pg141_n0020: The only difference from other types of glass is that its back has been silvered.
pg141_n0021: The image formed by a plane mirror has several characteristics.
pg141_n0025: 1. The image formed is virtual (not real).
pg141_n0027: When an object is placed in front of the plane mirror, its image will appear to be in a position behind the mirror.
pg141_n0028: This image is said to be virtual, that is not real, since it is in a location where the light does not reach, even though it appears like it does.
pg141_n0029: It only appears to the observer as though the light is coming from this point.
pg141_n0033: If you stand in front of a plane mirror, your image appears upright; that is, the image of your head appear at the top and that of your feet at the bottom.
pg141_n0034: This is because plane mirrors form upright images, not inverted images.
pg141_n0036: 3. The image is the same size as the object.
pg141_n0038: The image of an object placed in front of a plane mirror is the same size as the object.
pg141_n0039: The ratio of the image size to the object size is called magnification.
pg141_n0040: Plane mirrors produce images which have a magnification of 1.
pg141_n0042: 4. The image is the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front of the mirror.
pg141_n0044: If you stand a distance of three metres from the plane mirror you must focus at a location three metres behind the mirror to view your image.
pg141_n0046: 5. The image has a left-right reversal.
pg141_n0048: If you view your image in a plane mirror, you will notice that it appears to be laterally inverted.
pg141_n0049: This means that when, for example, you raise your left hand, the image appears to indicate a raised right hand.
pg141_n0050: If you are wearing a shirt with lettering, for example, WAY, it would appear as YAW.
pg142_n0003: both the order and orientation of the letters are reversed.
pg142_n0005: The alphabets that will have the image appear the same as the alphabet when kept in front of a plane mirror are A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, and Y.
pg142_n0007: That means if we cut the letters in half, both halves will look similar.
pg142_n0008: There won’t be any change in appearance when the letter is flipped sideways.
pg142_n0010: Lateral inversion is the phenomenon in which the image of the object turns 180° about the vertical axis, such that the right side of the object appears as the left side of the object and vice versa.
pg142_n0011: For example, a card printed with word, REEL when viewed through the mirror the word would appear as ⅃ƎƎЯ.

pg146_n0021: A mirror with a curved reflecting surface is called a curved mirror.
pg146_n0022: It is formed by silvering a piece of curved glass.
pg146_n0023: If the glass is considered a portion of a hollow sphere, then the resulting mirror is called a spherical or curved mirror.
pg146_n0024: The type of curved mirror depends on which side of the curved glass is silvered.
pg146_n0025: If the outer side of the curved glass is silvered such that the inner side becomes reflective, the mirror is called a concave mirror (Figure 4.20(a)).
pg146_n0026: Conversely, if the inner side of the curved glass is silvered so that the outer surface becomes reflective, the mirror is called a convex mirror (Figure 4.20 (b)).

pg146_n0040: Understanding spherical mirrors involves key terms such as principal axis, focal point, mirror vertex, focal length, and centre of curvature.
pg146_n0041: The centre of curvature (C) is the centre of the sphere from which the mirror is derived.
pg146_n0042: The principal axis is the line through the sphere’s centre that intersects the mirror at the pole (P), which is the mirror’s vertex.
pg146_n0043: These concepts are essential for understanding how light reflects off curved mirrors.
pg147_im003: Concave mirror ray diagram showing parallel incident rays reflected to meet at the principal focus in front of the mirror, with the focal length marked.
pg147_im002: Convex mirror ray diagram showing parallel incident rays reflected outward, with dashed extensions meeting at the virtual principal focus behind the mirror and the focal length marked.
pg147_n0021: The pole acts as the centre of the mirror, with the principal focus (F) positioned halfway between the pole and the centre of curvature (C).
pg147_n0022: In concave mirrors, the focal point is where all parallel rays of light come together; in contrast, for convex mirrors, the focal point appears as a location from which light rays spread out.
pg147_n0023: The radius of curvature (R) refers to the radius of the sphere from which the mirror originates, and the focal length (f) is half that radius, indicating the distance from the mirror to the focal point.
pg147_n0024: Figure 4.21 shows the geometry of curved mirrors.
pg147_n0026: A virtual image is formed when light rays appear to originate but cannot be focused onto a screen, while a real image is created where actual light rays intersect and can be projected onto a screen.
pg147_n0027: The image distance v is the distance from the image point to the pole, and the object distance u is the distance from the object to the pole.
pg147_n0028: Magnification m is the ratio of the image height h sub i to the object height h sub o, and it can also be expressed as the ratio of the image distance to the object distance.
pg147_n0029: We perceive an image because light from the object reflects off a mirror and travels to our eyes, similar to how we see the object itself.

pg149_n0005: The rules of reflection for concave mirrors are used to locate an image formed by a concave mirror.
pg149_n0009: 1. An incident ray that travels parallel to the principal axis of the mirror is reflected through the focal point.
pg149_n0011: 2. An incident ray that passes through the focal point is reflected parallel to the principal axis.
pg149_n0013: 3. An incident ray that passes through the centre of curvature is reflected along its path.
pg149_n0015: 4. An incident ray striking the pole of the mirror at an angle to the principal axis is reflected such that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, measured with respect to the principal axis.

pg149_n0018: Each reflected ray converges at the image location and then diverges to the eye of an observer.
pg149_n0019: Every observer can observe the same image location, and every light ray follows the laws of reflection.
pg149_n0020: However, only two of these rays are needed to determine the image location since it only requires two rays to find the intersection point.

pg152_n0027: In convex mirrors, the the centre of curvature, C, and the focal point, F, are located behind the mirror, that is, on the side of the mirror opposite the reflecting surface.
pg152_n0028: Thus, a convex mirror has a negative focal length.
pg152_n0030: A convex mirror is sometimes referred to as a diverging mirror because incident light rays diverge upon reflection from the mirror surface.
pg152_n0031: As a result, the reflected light rays never intersect on the object side (front side) of the mirror; instead, they appear to converge behind the mirror when extended backwards.
pg152_n0032: For this reason, convex mirrors produce virtual images that are located somewhere behind the mirror.
pg152_n0033: To determine the image location, only a pair of incident and reflected rays needs to be drawn.
pg152_n0034: These rays are the same as those used in concave mirror ray diagrams, except that in this case, the rays appear to diverge from a point behind the convex mirror.
pg152_n0035: The divergence point can be determined using the laws of reflection for convex mirrors (Figure 4.27), stated as:
pg152_n0038: 1. Any incident ray travelling parallel to the principal axis will be reflected in such a manner that the reflected ray extended backwards pass through the focal point of the mirror.
pg152_n0040: 2. Any incident ray travelling toward a convex mirror such that its extension passes through the focal point will be reflected parallel to the principal axis.
pg152_n0042: 3. An incident ray, not parallel to the principal axis, that strikes the pole of the convex mirror is reflected such
pg153_n0003: that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
pg153_n0004: 4. Any incident ray travelling toward a convex mirror such that its extension passes through the centre of curvature will be reflected along its path.
pg153_n0007: The image of an object can be located by drawing any two of the stated rays.

pg155_n0016: Ray diagrams provide valuable information for determining the approximate location and size of the image.

pg155_n0019: Therefore, to obtain more precise numerical information, one should use the mirror equation and the magnification equation.

pg163_n0005: Curved mirrors have various applications in our daily lives.
pg163_n0006: Depending on the purpose, some applications utilise concave mirrors while others utilise convex mirrors.
pg163_n0010: Convex mirrors provide a wide field of view compared to other mirrors, forming diminished images.
pg163_n0011: Therefore, they are used when a broad field of view is preferred over the size of the image.
pg163_n0012: The following are some applications of convex mirrors:
pg163_n0014: Convex mirrors are used as side mirrors for cars.
pg163_n0015: This allows the driver to gain a wide angle rear view, as shown in Figure 4.33.
pg163_n0016: However, these mirrors have the disadvantage of making objects appear farther away than they actually are.
pg163_n0017: This occurs because the image is always formed between the mirror and the focal point of the mirror, regardless of the object’s distance.
pg163_n0018: Hence, images appear small, and the brain interprets smaller images as farther away.
pg163_im002: Car side mirror showing a wide rear view of the road and a smaller car behind.
pg163_n0020: Figure 4.33: A side mirror of a car
pg163_n0022: Reflecting light in streetlights: A convex mirror is a reflector in street lamps.
pg163_n0023: Due to the wide view offered by the diverging mirror, light from the lamp spreads over a larger area.
pg163_n0024: Figure 4.34 illustrates light diverging from the streetlights.
pg163_im003: Two streetlights with light spreading outward over a wide area.
pg163_n0026: Figure 4.34: Divergence of light from a streetlight
pg163_n0028: Seeing around corners: Convex mirrors are placed at road junctions and the corners of places like parking lots and supermarkets.
pg163_n0029: This enables people to see around the corners to avoid collisions between vehicles or supermarket trolleys.
pg163_n0030: Figure 4.35 shows a convex mirror used as a safety mirror at a road junction.
pg163_im004: Convex road safety mirror reflecting a curved road and an approaching car around a corner.
pg163_n0032: Figure 4.35: A safety convex mirror around a corner
pg164_n0005: Security and investigation: Due to their wide field of view, convex mirrors are used to investigate business establishments and security installations.
pg164_n0006: An example of a convex mirror employed for security purposes is illustrated in Figure 4.36.
pg164_im008: Convex security mirror reflecting a wide view of a clothing shop with rows of garments and a sale sign.
pg164_n0008: Figure 4.36: A security convex mirror in a shop
pg164_n0012: Concave mirrors are helpful because of their ability to produce enlarged images, focus faint light and produce a parallel beam of light.
pg164_n0013: The following are some applications of concave mirrors:
pg164_n0015: Headlights in a car: A powerful light source is positioned at the focal point of a concave mirror in a small space at the back of a headlight.
pg164_n0016: Any light that strikes the mirror from the focus will be reflected parallel to the axis of the concave mirror.
pg164_n0017: This creates an intense beam of light in front of the car, as illustrated in Figure 4.37.
pg164_im010: Front of a car in the dark with bright headlights projecting two intense parallel beams of light.
pg164_n0021: Dentist’s mirror: A concave mirror helps the dentist to focus light on the tooth to be examined inside the mouth.
pg164_n0022: Figure 4.38 shows a dentist mirror in use to examine a tooth.
pg164_im009: Dentist using a small mirror to examine a child’s teeth inside the mouth.
pg164_n0024: Figure 4.38: A dentist mirror in use
pg164_n0026: Shaving mirrors: A concave mirror produces a magnified and upright image of the object when the object is positioned between the principal focus and the pole.
pg164_n0027: Thus, concave mirrors are used as shaving mirrors, creating an enlarged reflection of the face when it is held within the focus of the mirror.
pg164_n0028: A concave mirror, as shown in Figure 4.39, serves as an example of a shaving mirror.
pg165_im002: Wall-mounted circular shaving mirror on an adjustable arm.
pg165_n0005: Reflecting telescopes: A concave mirror (primary mirror) forms images of distant stars at the focal point.
pg165_n0006: A plane mirror (secondary mirror) is then used to project the rays to the side where the image can be viewed through a lens, as shown in Figure 4.40.

pg165_im023_seg002_v1: Cross-section of a reflecting telescope showing the concave primary mirror, slanted secondary mirror, and eyepiece.
pg165_n0016: In some cases, the concept of light reflection off concave surfaces is used for applications beyond light and image formation, outlined as follows:
pg165_n0017: Satellite dishes: Satellite dishes are specialized antennas designed to receive and transmit signals to and from satellites in orbit.
pg165_im013: Two large satellite dish antennas pointed toward the sky.
pg166_n0003: Parabolic solar cookers: These solar cookers convert sunlight directly into heat by concentrating it through a parabolic arrangement of reflectors.

pg166_sec001_ans_item-1: Concave mirrors can form real images when the object is beyond the focal point because reflected rays actually meet, and virtual images when the object is between the pole and the focal point because the reflected rays only appear to meet behind the mirror. Convex mirrors always diverge reflected rays, so they can form only virtual images.
pg166_sec001_ans_item-2: Using 1/f = 1/u + 1/v with f = 10 cm and u = 30 cm: 1/v = 1/10 - 1/30 = 2/30 = 1/15, so v = 15 cm. Magnification m = v/u = 15/30 = 0.5, so image height = 0.5 × 6 = 3 cm. The image is formed 15 cm in front of the mirror, real, inverted, and diminished.
pg166_sec001_ans_item-3: For a diverging mirror, take u = 15 cm and v = -10 cm. Using 1/f = 1/u + 1/v = 1/15 - 1/10 = -1/30, therefore f = -30 cm. The focal length is -30 cm.
pg166_sec001_ans_item-4: Radius of curvature R = 12 cm, so focal length f = R/2 = 6 cm. Using 1/f = 1/u + 1/v with u = 10 cm: 1/v = 1/6 - 1/10 = 1/15, so v = 15 cm. Magnification m = v/u = 15/10 = 1.5, so image height = 1.5 × 4 = 6 cm. The image is real, inverted, and enlarged.
pg166_sec001_ans_item-5: Using 1/f = 1/u + 1/v with f = 15 cm and u = 30 cm: 1/v = 1/15 - 1/30 = 1/30, so v = 30 cm. Magnification m = -v/u = -30/30 = -1. Thus the image distance is 30 cm and the magnification is -1. The image is real and inverted.
pg166_sec001_ans_item-6: Concave mirrors: shaving or make-up mirrors, dentists' mirrors, reflectors in headlights or torches. Convex mirrors: vehicle rear-view mirrors, security mirrors in shops, mirrors at road bends or blind corners.
pg167_n0005: 6. A convex mirror is a mirror that curves outward, producing smaller images and a wider field of view.
pg167_n0007: 7. A virtual image is formed by the apparent divergence of light rays, which cannot be projected onto a screen (e.g., images in a plane mirror).
pg167_n0009: 8. Real image is an image formed by the actual convergence of light rays, which can be projected onto a screen.
pg167_n0011: 9. Focal point is the point at which parallel light rays converge after reflecting off a concave mirror.
pg167_n0013: 10. Magnification, m, is the ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object, indicating how much larger or smaller the image is compared to the object.

pg169_n0007: The principles, theories, and concepts surrounding the refraction of light are integral to our daily lives, significantly impacting both natural phenomena and technological advancements.
pg169_n0008: Key applications include vision correction, the design of various optical instruments, the functionality of optical fibres, the creation of various colours by prisms and rainbows, and the development of magnification tools.
pg169_n0009: In this chapter, you will explore how light refracts through glass prisms and lenses.
pg169_n0010: The competencies developed will enable you to design optical instruments and use them in different contexts.
pg169_n0013: Importance of optical fibres in our daily lives
pg169_n0017: In the previous chapter, it was learnt that, as light travels through a given medium, it travels in a straight line.
pg169_n0018: However, when light passes from one medium to other medium, the light beam tends to bend.
pg169_n0019: The bending of light is referred to as the refraction of light.
pg169_n0020: The direction of a ray of light changes as it passes obliquely from one medium into another.
pg169_n0022: Refraction occurs because different media have different optical densities.
pg169_n0023: If the speed of light in one medium is lower than that in the other medium, the first medium is said to have a higher optical density than the second medium.
pg169_n0024: Thus, the optical density of a medium can be determined by using the speed of light in that medium.
pg169_n0025: Refraction occurs only at a boundary.
pg169_n0026: Once the light has crossed the boundary between the two media, it continues to travel in a straight line.

pg170_n0036: Angle of incidence and angle of refraction
pg170_n0038: When light passes from a medium such as air to another medium such as glass, which is optically denser than the first medium, its velocity decreases.
pg170_n0039: Conversely, when light passes from an optically denser medium such as glass to a medium that is optically less dense like air, its velocity increases.
pg170_n0040: The line that is perpendicular to the boundary between the two media through which light travels is called the normal line.
pg170_n0041: The ray of light in the first medium is called the incident ray and the ray of light in the second medium is called the refracted ray.
pg170_n0042: The angle between the incident ray and the normal line is known as the angle of incidence and is denoted by the letter i.
pg170_n0043: On the other hand, the angle between the refracted ray and the normal line is called the angle of refraction, denoted by r.

pg171_n0015: Refraction of light by a glass prism
pg171_n0017: Glass prisms come in various types, including rectangular and triangular.
pg171_n0018: Refraction occurs when light passes through the prism, bending at the interfaces due to changes in speed as it enters and exits the glass.
pg171_n0019: When light enters the prism from air, it slows down and bends towards the normal line, which is perpendicular to the surface at the entry point.
pg171_n0020: Conversely, as light exits the prism back into the air, it speeds up and bends away from the normal.
pg171_n0022: Refraction of light by a rectangular prism
pg171_n0024: When a light ray passes from air into a rectangular glass prism, it undergoes refraction at the point where it enters the glass.
pg171_n0025: Inside the prism, the light travels in a straight line until it reaches the opposite boundary, where it is refracted again as it exits back into the air.
pg171_n0026: Since the opposite sides of a rectangular glass prism are parallel, the emerging light ray continues in the same direction it had before entering the prism.
pg171_n0027: As a result, there is no overall deviation in the path of the light.
pg171_n0028: This behaviour is illustrated in Figure 5.3.
pg171_im006: Light ray passing through a rectangular glass block, bending at both surfaces and emerging parallel to the original direction but laterally displaced.

pg173_n0014: When a beam of light passes through two different media via an interface, it bends.
pg173_n0015: The amount of bending depends on the optical densities of the two media and the angle of incidence of the light beam.
pg173_n0016: Note that, the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction differ in proportion to the difference in the optical densities of the two media.
pg173_n0017: If a light ray passes from the optically less dense medium to the optically denser medium, it is bent towards the normal.
pg173_n0018: However, if the ray travels from a medium of higher optical density to a medium of lower optical density, it bends away from the normal.
pg173_n0019: Following various experimental observations, two laws govern the behaviour of a light ray as it strikes the interface between two media of different optical densities.
pg173_n0020: These laws are known as the laws of refraction of light.

pg174_n0080: Several deductions can be made from the results of the above experiment:
pg174_n0083: 1. Whenever the pins are set in line and viewed from one side, they appear to be in line.
pg174_n0084: This is also the case when pins are viewed from the other side.
pg174_n0085: This illustrates the principle of reversibility of light, which states that; "light will follow exactly the same path if its direction of travel is reversed".
pg174_n0086: The implication of the law of reversibility of light in a rectangular glass prism is that, if i is the angle of incidence from air to glass and r is the angle of refraction, then, r becomes the angle of incidence for glass to air and i becomes the angle of refraction.
pg174_n0088: 2. As a ray of light travels from air to glass (from an optically less dense medium to a denser medium), it is bent towards the normal at the boundary between the two media.
pg174_n0089: Conversely, when a ray of light travels from glass to air (from an optically denser
pg175_n0003: medium to a less dense medium), it is bent away from the normal.
pg175_n0004: 3. The ratio sine of i over sine of r is the same, constant, for the different angles of incidence.
pg175_n0005: 4. The points E and F, the normal line, the incident ray and the refracted ray lie on the same plane.
pg175_n0006: This may not have been obvious.
pg175_n0007: However, you can observe this if you lift one edge of the glass block above the other edge of the block after setting the pins in a line.
pg175_n0008: You will immediately notice that the linearity of pins A, B, C and D disappears.
pg175_n0009: These important observations lead to two important conclusions that are essentially the laws of refraction of light.
pg175_n0011: (a) At the point of incidence, the incident ray, the normal line and the refracted ray all lie on the same plane.
pg175_n0012: (b) For a particular material, the ratio sine of i over sine of r is constant.
pg175_n0013: This law is also referred to as Snell’s law of refraction.
pg175_n0017: In Activity 5.4, you observed that, for a given material or medium, the ratio sine of i over sine of r is constant regardless of the size of the angle of incidence.
pg175_n0018: This constant is known as the refractive index of the material (medium).
pg175_n0019: It is a dimensionless, it has no unit, constant denoted by the Greek letter eta.
pg175_n0020: The refractive index of a material is a measure of the influence of the material on the speed of light as it passes through it.
pg175_n0021: Therefore, the refractive index of a material is also obtained from the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum, c, to the speed of light in the material, v.
pg175_n0023: That is, eta equals c over v.
pg175_n0025: To be specific, the ratio eta equals c over v is known as the absolute refractive index of a material.
pg175_n0026: If the ratio is obtained from the speed of light v one in one material, to the speed of light v two in the other material, then eta equals v one over v two.
pg175_n0028: In this case, the ratio is called the relative refractive index.
pg175_n0030: Normally, the speed of light in air is considered as the speed of light in vacuum, c.
pg175_n0031: Therefore, if light travels from air to water and from air to glass, it will have different speeds in water and glass because air, water and glass have different optical densities.

pg175_n0040: This implies that, c equals eta two v two.

pg177_n0095: It has been established that when light travels from a lighter medium to a denser one, eta one is less than eta two, the refracted light ray bends towards the normal.
pg178_n0003: light travels from a denser medium to a lighter one, eta one is less than eta two, the refracted light ray bends away from the normal.
pg178_n0004: It is also known that the angle of refraction and hence the amount by which light bends away from the normal depends on the angle of incidence.
pg178_n0005: Therefore, the larger the angle of incidence, the more the light bends away from normal.
pg178_n0006: Yet, one could ask, when light travels from a denser medium to a less dense medium, how far away from normal can light bend?
pg178_n0008: The answer to this question is that the bending of light can only get as far as 90° without leaving the medium.
pg178_n0009: Therefore, there is an angle of incidence of light for which the angle of refraction is 90°.
pg178_n0010: This angle of incidence is known as the critical angle and is typically denoted by a letter c.
pg178_n0011: When the angle of incidence becomes greater than the critical angle, light is not refracted anymore; instead, light is reflected back into the same medium from which it is coming.
pg178_n0012: This phenomenon is known as total internal reflection.
pg178_n0016: Total internal reflection (TIR) is a physical phenomenon in which all the light travelling in an optically denser medium is reflected back upon striking the interface with an optically less dense medium.
pg178_im008: Diagram of total internal reflection at the boundary between medium a, below, and less dense medium b, above: a ray from point P refracts away from the normal into medium b, a second ray at the critical angle produces a refracted ray along the surface with θb = 90°, and a third ray with angle of incidence greater than θcrit is totally internally reflected back into medium a.
pg178_n0018: Figure 5.8: Occurrence of the total internal reflection
pg178_n0020: Total internal reflection only takes place when both of the following two conditions are met:
pg178_n0023: 1. Light travels from an optically denser medium towards a less dense medium.
pg178_n0025: 2. The angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle.
pg178_n0027: Total internal reflection will not take place unless the incident light is travelling within the more optically dense medium towards the less optically dense medium.
pg178_n0030: TIR will happen for light travelling from water towards air, but it will not happen for light travelling from air towards water.
pg178_n0031: On the other hand, TIR occurs only if the angle of refraction exceeds 90°.

pg179_n0045: In the previous discussion, it has been established that light tends to bend when it strikes an interface between two media that have different refractive indices.
pg179_n0046: After passing the boundary, the light travels in a straight line within the new medium.
pg179_n0047: However, the discussion has presumed that the media in which light travels are of uniform optical density.
pg179_n0048: Nevertheless, not every medium is uniform and even air can sometimes form a non-uniform medium.
pg179_n0049: When the medium is optically non-uniform, refraction of light can occur as the light travels within the medium.
pg179_n0050: This leads to an interesting phenomenon; the formation of mirages.
pg179_n0051: A mirage is an optical phenomenon that produces illusion images due to the refraction of light through a non-uniform medium.
pg180_n0003: Mirages can commonly be observed when you walk down a tarmac roadway on a sunny day.
pg180_n0004: As you walk down the roadway, there appears to be a puddle of water on the road several metres (about 100 m) ahead of you.
pg180_n0005: Yet, when you arrive at the perceived location of the puddle, you recognise that the puddle is not there.
pg180_n0006: Instead, the puddle of water appears to be another one hundred metres before you.
pg180_n0007: The appearance of the puddle of water is simply an illusion because of the mirage.
pg180_n0009: Mirages occur on sunny days because the sun heats the roadway to high temperatures.
pg180_n0010: The heated roadway, in turn, heats the surrounding air, keeping the air just above the roadway at a higher temperature than the air above.
pg180_n0011: Hot air tends to be optically less dense than cooler air.
pg180_n0012: Thus, the layers of air just above the roadway are optically less dense than the air further above the roadway.
pg180_n0013: This creates a non-uniform optical medium.
pg180_n0014: Consequently, as light travels from the sun, it passes through the cooler air layers towards the hot air layers.
pg180_n0015: This means light travels from an optically denser medium to a less dense medium.
pg180_n0016: Thus, light will be refracted upon striking the boundary between the two layers of air.
pg180_n0018: As the light continues to traverse different air layers, it is bent more upwards to the extent that it reaches your eyes instead of hitting the road.
pg180_n0019: Your brain traces the light straight back along the direction from which it comes to your eyes.
pg180_n0020: Figure 5.10 (a) shows an image of the sky, which is refracted by air with non-uniform optical density, appearing as a puddle of water just above the roadway.
pg180_n0021: Figure 5.10 (b) illustrates the formation of an atmospheric mirage.
pg180_n0022: The mirage phenomenon can also occur in bodies of water such as seas, lakes, ponds, and deserts.

pg181_n0045: A triangular glass prism is a transparent object having two triangular and three rectangular faces.
pg181_n0046: The refraction of light by a triangular glass prism is different from the refraction by a rectangular glass prism.
pg181_n0047: For a triangular glass prism, the emergent ray of light is not parallel to the incident ray of light.
pg181_n0048: This is because, when a ray of light enters the glass prism, it gets deviated two times.
pg181_n0049: First, light is refracted when it enters the glass prism and then refracted for the second time when it comes out of the prism as shown in Figure 5.11.
pg181_n0050: This is possible because the refracting surfaces of the prism are not parallel to each other, therefore when the ray of light passes through the prism it bends towards the normal, which is oriented towards the prism’s base.
pg181_n0051: The amount by which light bends is dependent on the angle of incidence, the wavelength of the light, and the refractive indices of the materials through which light travels.

pg187_n0005: The major source of light for the Earth is the Sun.
pg187_n0006: What is the colour of sunlight?
pg187_n0007: Sometimes we see in the sky a rainbow consisting of different colours.
pg187_n0008: In addition, during sunset or sunrise, the sky appears orange or red.
pg187_n0009: Can we conclude from these observations that sunlight is made of different colours?
pg187_n0013: White light is known to consist of seven colours.
pg187_n0014: If a beam of white light is passed through a triangular glass prism, it splits into a band of seven colours.
pg187_n0015: Figure 5.16 shows a band of colours formed when white light passes through a triangular glass prism.
pg187_n0016: This band is known as the spectrum of white light.
pg187_n0017: Colours that form the spectrum of white light are red (R), orange (O), yellow (Y), green (G), blue (B), indigo (I) and violet (V).
pg187_n0018: For the sake of remembering the arrangement of these colours, an abbreviation ROYGBIV is commonly used.
pg187_im002: White light entering a triangular glass prism splits into a spectrum of seven colours—red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet—with red deviating least and violet most.
pg187_n0022: Figure 5.16: Dispersion of white light by a triangular glass prism
pg187_n0024: Dispersion of light is a phenomenon in which white light splits into its colour components upon passing through a medium such as a triangular glass prism.
pg187_n0025: This phenomenon happens because when a beam of white light enters a transparent medium, each colour component is refracted at a different angle of refraction, resulting in different angles of deviation.
pg187_n0026: For example, red colour deviates least while violet colour deviates most.
pg187_n0027: The result is the splitting of the white light into its components to form a spectrum with red colour being at the upper part of the spectrum, and the violet colour being at the bottom of the spectrum, as shown in Figure 5.16.
pg187_n0028: Each component has a different wavelength, which falls well within the visible part of the electromagnetic spectrum.
pg187_n0032: Light dispersion can also occur when light passes through other transparent materials, such as water droplets and soap bubbles.
pg187_n0033: One consequence of light dispersion by water droplets in the atmosphere is the formation of a rainbow.
pg187_n0034: A rainbow is a natural phenomenon caused by the dispersion of white light.
pg187_n0035: It is caused by the refraction and reflection of white light by falling water droplets.
pg188_n0005: The rainbow phenomenon can be observed when there are water droplets in the atmosphere as the sun shines from behind the observer at a low altitude.
pg188_n0006: The rainbow’s appearance is caused by the dispersion of sunlight as it is refracted by nearly circular raindrops.
pg188_n0007: The white light from the sun is first refracted as it enters the surface of the raindrops.
pg188_n0009: When light travels from a less dense medium to a light denser medium, it bends towards the normal.
pg188_n0010: However, not all colours bend equally.
pg188_n0011: As in a glass prism, red light bends the least while violet bends the most.
pg188_n0012: At the back of the raindrops, some of the dispersed light is reflected back over a wide range of angles and again refracted as it leaves the raindrop.
pg188_n0013: In most cases, the violet light leaves the raindrop at a smaller angle relative to incident sunlight compared to red light as shown in Figure 5.17 (a).
pg188_n0014: As a result, the observer sees an image of well-arranged coloured bands in the atmosphere called a rainbow, with red light appearing on top and violet at the bottom of the spectrum as shown in Figure 5.17 (b).

pg189_n0012: When you look at a rainbow, you see seven colours.
pg189_n0013: They are always in the same order.
pg189_n0014: That is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet.
pg189_n0015: An easy way to remember the colours and the order is to think of the name ROYGBIV, spelt from the first letter of each colour.
pg189_n0018: This rainbow forms at an angle of approximately 40° to 42° from the antisolar point.
pg189_n0019: The light undergoes one internal reflection within the water droplets (see Figure 5.18(a)), creating the primary rainbow we observe.
pg189_n0020: It is the brightest and most common rainbow with the red colour being on the outside (on top) and the violet colour in the inside (bottom);

pg189_n0029: A secondary rainbow forms outside a primary rainbow, resulting from light undergoing two internal reflections within raindrops (see Figure 5.18(b)).
pg189_n0030: This double reflection causes the colours of the secondary rainbow to appear in reverse order compared to the primary rainbow.
pg189_n0031: The secondary rainbow is also considerably fainter than the primary one.
pg189_n0032: This phenomenon showcases the complex interaction of light with water droplets, demonstrating how multiple reflections alter the path and appearance of the light.
pg189_n0035: We have seen that upon falling on a transparent medium such as a triangular glass prism or water droplet, white light splits into its colour components.
pg189_n0036: What happens when the components of white light are passed through a second prism
pg190_n0003: that is identical to the first prism?
pg190_n0004: If the second prism is arranged similarly to the first prism, no further splitting of white light can be observed.
pg190_n0005: But if the second prism is inverted with respect to the first prism, a beam of white light is observed to emerge from the other side of the second prism.
pg190_n0006: This means that the dispersed colours of white light can be recombined to form white light, as illustrated by Figure 5.19.
pg190_n0007: This phenomenon is known as the white colour recombination.
pg190_im008: White light enters the first prism and is dispersed into coloured rays, which pass through an inverted second prism and recombine into white light.
pg190_n0009: Figure 5.19: Dispersion and recombination of white light
pg190_n0011: The experiment of recombination of the spectrum of light can be extended to observe the recombination of two or more individual colours.
pg190_n0012: Sir Isaac Newton did this for the first time using prisms and mirrors.
pg190_n0013: He discovered that when the light from the red, green, and blue regions of the spectrum are recombined, they regenerate white light.
pg190_n0014: Therefore, he called red, green, and blue the primary colours.
pg190_n0016: Newton also observed that when two primary colours are combined, other colours are formed.
pg190_n0017: For example, when blue and green lights are combined, cyan light is formed.
pg190_n0018: Furthermore, green and red lights combine to give yellow light, while red and blue lights combine to form magenta light.
pg190_n0019: Newton named the colours that resulted from recombining two primary colours as secondary colours.
pg190_n0020: Secondary colours include yellow, cyan and magenta.
pg190_n0021: He finally organised his findings in a colour wheel showing the three “primary colours” separated by the three “secondary colours”, as shown in Figure 5.20.
pg190_n0023: This colour wheel is famously known as the Newton colour wheel or disc.
pg190_n0024: When the disc is rotated about its axis at high speed, all the colours blend to form a white colour.
pg190_n0025: However, as the disc slows down, individual colours are seen again.
pg190_im012: Newton’s colour wheel divided into six equal sectors: cyan, blue, magenta, red, yellow, and green.
pg190_n0035: Since magenta was not a part of the light spectrum, its origin posed a mystery.
pg190_n0036: This mystery was resolved by Hermann von Helmholtz, who established that the human eye consists of three types of colour receptors.
pg190_n0037: One of the primary colours (red, blue and green) can stimulate only one receptor type.
pg190_n0038: Moreover, the eye perceives all of the variations in colour by internally combining the signals from these receptors.
pg190_n0039: Therefore, white light is seen when red, blue and green light enters the eye.
pg190_n0040: However, when both red and blue light but no green light enters the eye, magenta is seen even though the light is not magenta.
pg190_n0041: Similarly, when red and green light enters the eye, a yellow light is seen, and
pg191_n0003: when blue and green light enter the eye, a cyan light is seen.

pg191_n0010: Appearance of objects under white light
pg191_n0012: When one looks at an object, the object is seen when it reflects light into the eye of the observer.
pg191_n0013: Objects may absorb certain colours of the light falling on them and reflect other colours.
pg191_n0014: Therefore, the colour appearance of objects depends on the colour of the light that the object reflects or absorbs and the colour of the light falling on the object.
pg191_n0015: The selective absorption or reflection of light by an object gives the object its characteristic colour as perceived by an observer.
pg191_n0019: When white light falls on an object, and the object reflects the entire colour spectrum in the light, the object appears white.
pg191_n0020: Conversely, the object appears black if it absorbs all colours of the white light falling on it.
pg191_n0021: If the object reflects some of the colours and absorbs the others, the object appears coloured.
pg191_n0022: For example, some flowers in Figure 5.21 appear yellow because they absorb all other colours except the yellow colour, which is reflected into the observer’s eyes.
pg191_n0023: Other flowers also absorb all the colours of white light except their respective colours, as seen in the Figure 5.21.
pg191_im015: Garden bed with pink and yellow flowers among green leaves, showing different flower colours under white light.
pg191_n0029: An object is seen as white because it reflects all colours of the white light falling on it.
pg191_n0030: Therefore, when a white object is viewed under the coloured light, it will reflect the coloured light and hence appear to have the colour of the light.
pg191_n0031: For example, when a white object is viewed under the blue light, it appears as a blue object.
pg191_n0032: Similarly, an object will appear red or green when viewed under red or green light, respectively.

pg192_n0016: When white light is transmitted through a colour filter, the filter allows only a specific light colour to pass through it.
pg192_n0017: Therefore, the filtered light will have a colour depending on the colour of the filter.
pg192_n0018: For example, the light will be yellow, green, blue or red if the filter used is respectively yellow, green, blue or red.
pg192_n0019: Consequently, if light from one filter is passed through another filter of different colour, the light is absorbed by the second filter.
pg192_n0020: Now, when the light through a filter of a given colour falls on the white object, the object reflects that light into the observer’s sight.
pg192_n0021: Therefore, the object appears to have the colour of the filtered light.

pg192_n0042: Primary, secondary and complementary colours of light
pg192_n0044: What happens when a physicist simultaneously casts the blue, green and red light beams on a spot on a white screen?
pg192_n0046: Experiments with beams of various coloured lights have demonstrated that many colours in the light spectrum can be created by mixing other colours.
pg192_n0047: For instance, when light from one end of the spectrum is combined with light from the middle, we can produce all the colours found in that half of the spectrum.
pg192_n0048: Similarly, by mixing lights from both ends of the spectrum with light from the middle, we can generate all the colours that lie in between them.
pg192_n0050: White light can also be produced by combining only three distinct light colours, provided that they are widely separated on the visible light spectrum.
pg192_n0051: Any three colours of light that produce white light when combined with the correct intensity are called primary
pg193_n0004: These include red (R), blue (B) and green (G) as shown in Figure 5.23.
pg193_n0005: Moreover, mixing together two or all of these three primary light colours with varying degrees of intensity can produce a wide range of other light colours.
pg193_n0006: Many television sets and computer monitors produce a wide range of colours on the monitor by using red, green and blue light-emitting phosphors.
pg193_im018: Three adjacent colour blocks labeled Red, Blue, and Green, representing the primary colours of light.
pg193_n0010: Light colours formed by combining the primary colours are referred to as secondary colours.
pg193_n0011: These include cyan, magenta, and yellow, as shown in Figure 5.24.
pg193_im019: Three adjacent colour blocks labeled Cyan, Magenta, and Yellow, representing the secondary colours of light.
pg193_n0015: On the other hand, white light can sometimes be formed by mixing any two colours of the light spectrum.
pg193_n0016: Therefore, the two colours that mix in definite ratios to form white light are termed complementary colours.
pg193_n0017: Examples of complementary colours are blue and yellow, red and cyan, and green and magenta.

pg194_n0009: Addition and subtraction of light colours
pg194_n0011: When you look at an object and perceive a distinct colour, you are not necessarily seeing a single colour of light, rather a combination of different colours.
pg194_n0012: Consider, for instance, that you are looking at a shirt that appears yellow.
pg194_n0013: There may be several colours of light with varying intensity that strike your eye after being reflected by the shirt.
pg194_n0014: Yet your eye-brain system interprets the colours that strike your eye, and the shirt is perceived to be yellow.
pg194_n0015: Understanding how different colours are perceived requires knowledge of adding and subtracting light colours.
pg194_n0019: Generation of various colours of light by mixing of the three primary colours of light is known as colour addition.
pg194_n0020: The colour addition principles can be used to make predictions of the colours that would result when different coloured lights are mixed.
pg194_n0021: For example, red (R) light and green (G) light add together to produce yellow (Y) light.
pg194_n0022: Red light and blue light add together to produce magenta (M) light.
pg194_n0023: Green light and blue (B) light add together to produce cyan (C) light.
pg194_n0024: Finally, red light, green light and blue light add together to produce white light.
pg194_n0025: Moreover, addition of complementary colours of light produces white light.

pg195_n0005: The principles of colour addition govern the perceived colour resulting from mixing of different colours of light.
pg195_n0006: However, understanding colour perceptions cannot be complete without an understanding of the principles of colour subtraction.
pg195_n0007: Some materials contain atoms and molecules that are capable of selectively absorbing one or more colours of light.
pg195_n0008: Therefore, if a beam of white light falls on such a material, some light colours are absorbed and some are reflected to the observer’s eye.
pg195_n0009: This is the basis of subtraction of light colours.
pg195_n0011: Yellow filter absorbs blue light, magenta filter absorbs green light, and cyan filter absorbs red light.

pg196_n0004: Generally, the rules of subtraction of light colour are:
pg196_n0007: 1. Red colour absorbs green and blue light and reflects red light.
pg196_n0009: 2. Blue colour absorbs green and red light and reflects blue light.
pg196_n0011: 3. Green colour absorbs blue and red light while reflecting green light.
pg196_n0013: 4. Cyan colour absorbs red light and reflects cyan light (blue + green).
pg196_n0015: 5. Magenta colour absorbs green light and reflects magenta light (red + blue).
pg196_n0017: 6. Yellow colour absorbs blue light and reflects yellow light (red + green).
pg196_n0019: These rules are very important concepts for understanding colour appearance in objects.

pg196_n0024: Additive and subtractive mixing of colours
pg196_n0026: Following our discussion on the addition and subtraction of colours of light, you may have realised that objects can appear in different colours depending on the combination of light that reaches our eyes.
pg196_n0027: This idea is very useful in the synthesis of colours, which we refer to as colour mixing.
pg196_n0028: Since colour-mixing uses the concepts of addition and subtraction of light colours, there are two main types of colour mixing.
pg196_n0029: These are additive colour mixing and subtractive colour mixing.
pg196_n0033: Additive colour mixing is the process of creating a new colour by adding one set of colours to another set of colours.
pg196_n0034: When we add all of the different colours of sunlight, we see white light rather than many individual colours.
pg196_n0035: Thus, this type of colour mixing is called additive colour mixing because all of the wavelengths still reach our eyes, but the observed colour depends on the combinations of different colours.
pg196_n0037: Normally, primary colours used in additive colour mixing are red, blue and green and secondary colours are cyan, magenta and yellow.
pg196_n0038: Additive colour mixing is commonly used to generate colours on televisions and computer monitors using RGB (red, green and blue) system.
pg196_n0039: Activity 5.10 that you performed earlier demonstrates the process of additive mixing of colours.
pg196_n0043: When colour pigments are mixed, both paints continue to absorb the same colours as they did before being mixed, the result is
pg197_n0003: the colour that both pigments reflect in common.
pg197_n0004: This process is therefore called subtractive colour mixing because, when colour pigments mix, each may absorb some of the colours that the other pigment reflects, reducing the range of colours seen compared to before mixing.
pg197_n0005: Since we only see light that is reflected by the paints, the primary colours in the subtractive colour mixing are cyan, magenta and yellow while secondary colours are red, blue, and green.
pg197_n0006: Even addition of primary colours gives black colour, which simply means all colours have been absorbed and no light is reflected.
pg197_n0007: Subtractive colour mixing is commonly used in coloured printers and production of different paints using a CMY (cyan, magenta and yellow) system.
pg197_n0009: It is important to note that each primary colour of paint pigment absorbs one primary colour of light.
pg197_n0010: The colour absorbed by a primary colour paint pigment is the complementary colour of that paint pigment.
pg197_n0020: On the other hand, each secondary colour paint pigment absorbs two secondary colours of light.
pg197_n0024: (a) Blue paint absorbs cyan and magenta.
pg197_n0026: (b) Green paint absorbs yellow and cyan.
pg197_n0028: (c) Red paint absorbs magenta and yellow.

pg197_n0057: Note that, both additive and subtractive colour mixing are of paramount importance for understanding our perception of different colours.
pg198_n0003: Differences between additive and subtractive colour mixing
pg198_n0005: The easy way to remember the difference between additive and subtractive colour mixing is that, additive colour mixing is what happens when we mix lights of different colours whereas subtractive colour mixing occurs when we mix paints or other coloured material.

pg199_n0020: A piece of glass or other transparent material may be shaped in such a way that, parallel incident light rays passing through it would either converge to a point or appear to diverge from a point.
pg199_n0021: A piece of glass that has such a shape is referred to as a lens.
pg199_n0022: Though most lenses are made of glass, it is possible to make lenses from various transparent materials.
pg199_n0023: In recent times, the use of plastic for making lenses has been increasing.
pg199_n0024: A lens is therefore a carefully molded piece of transparent material that refracts light rays in such a way that an image is formed.
pg199_n0025: Lenses can be thought of as a series of tiny refracting prisms, each of which refracts light to produce their own image.
pg199_n0026: When these prisms act together, they produce a bright image focused at a point as shown in Figure 5.30.
pg199_im151: Converging lens shape formed by stacked prisms, thicker at the centre and thinner at the edges.
pg199_n0028: Figure 5.30: A set of prisms packed to converge or diverge light rays
pg199_n0036: Lenses differ from one another in terms of their shape and the materials from which they are made.
pg199_n0037: Based on their shapes, there are two major types of lenses.
pg199_n0038: These are the convex (converging) lenses and concave (diverging) lenses.
pg199_n0040: A convex lens is a lens that converges rays of light that pass through it.
pg199_n0041: Convex lenses are relatively thicker across their middle and thinner at their edges as shown in Figure 5.31.
pg199_n0042: At least one side of a convex lens curves outwards.
pg199_n0043: Convex lenses can be further categorized depending on their specific shapes.
pg199_n0044: These include bi-convex lenses, plano-convex lenses and convex meniscus lenses as depicted in Figure 5.31.
pg199_n0045: Task 5.5 demonstrates the action of a convex lens.
pg199_im153: Converging meniscus lens, curved inward on one side and outward on the other, thicker at the centre.
pg199_im152: Diverging lens shape formed by stacked prisms, thinner at the centre and thicker at the edges.

pg200_n0012: A concave lens is a lens that diverges rays of light that pass through it.
pg200_n0013: Concave lenses are relatively thinner across their middle and thicker at their edges.
pg200_n0014: At least one side of a concave lens curves inwards.
pg200_n0015: Types of concave lenses include biconcave lens, plano-concave lens and the concave meniscus.
pg200_n0016: Figure 5.32 shows the types of concave lenses.
pg200_n0025: The discussion of refraction of light rays and the formation of images by lenses requires the use of a variety of terms.
pg200_n0026: If one face of a lens is thought of as being a portion of a spherical surface, then the imaginary line passing through the centre of the sphere and the exact centre of the lens is called the principal axis of the lens.
pg200_n0027: A lens also has an imaginary vertical line that bisects it symmetrically into two halves.
pg200_n0028: This line is the vertical axis of the lens.
pg200_n0029: The point of intersection between the vertical axis and the principal axis is called the optical centre of the lens.
pg200_n0031: Light rays incident to a lens and travelling parallel to the principal axis will either converge or diverge.
pg200_n0032: In a convex lens, the light rays converge to to a point called the focal point or principal focus.
pg200_n0033: In a concave lens, the light rays diverge, but when traced backwards, they appear to come from a common point, also called a focal point.
pg200_n0034: In both cases, the focal point is denoted by the letter F.
pg200_n0035: The distance between the focal point and the optical centre is the focal length, denoted by the letter, f.
pg200_n0037: Note that, unlike mirrors, lenses allow light to pass through either face.
pg200_n0038: Therefore, a lens has two focal points on each side of the lens.
pg200_n0039: A lens also has an imaginary point called the centre of curvature, which is the centre of the sphere of which the surface of a lens is a part.
pg200_n0040: The centre of curvature lies on the principal axis and its distance from the optical centre is called the radius of curvature R.
pg200_n0041: The lens has two centres of curvature, on each side of the lens.
pg200_n0042: Note that, the focal point, F is real for a convex lens and virtual for a concave lens.
pg201_n0003: Other common terms used are; real image, virtual image, image distance, v, object distance, u and magnification, m.
pg201_n0004: All these terms take the same meaning as they were defined in the case of image formation by curved mirrors.
pg201_n0005: Figure 5.33 illustrates the terms used in discussing lenses.
pg201_n0007: It is important to note that, for thin lenses, the pole and the optical centre merely coincide.
pg201_n0008: Moreover, the plane through the principal focus, which is perpendicular to the principal axis, is called the focal plane.
pg201_im066: Diagram of a converging convex lens showing the optical centre, vertical axis, principal axis, focal points F on both sides, and the focal length from the optical centre to the focus.
pg201_im067: Diagram of a diverging concave lens showing the optical centre, vertical axis, principal axis, focal points F on both sides, and the focal length from the optical centre to the focus.
pg201_n0028: Image formation by lenses is a result of the refraction of light at both surfaces of the lens.
pg201_n0029: As light enters and exits the lens, it is refracted at each boundary.
pg201_n0030: The net effect of this refraction of light at the two boundaries is a change in direction of the light.
pg201_n0031: Because of the geometric shape of a lens, the refracted light rays either converge to a focal point or appear to diverge from a focal point forming an image as shown in Figure 5.30.
pg201_n0036: How lenses form images of objects can be shown by means of ray diagrams.
pg201_n0037: In ray diagrams, sometimes lenses are represented by vertical lines with an appropriate indication to show whether it is a converging lens or a diverging lens.
pg201_n0038: Figure 5.34 shows the representation of converging lens and diverging lenses in ray diagrams.
pg201_n0044: Figure 5.34: Representation of converging and diverging lenses in ray diagrams
pg202_n0003: Some rules are to be followed when one constructs ray diagrams for both convex and concave lenses.
pg202_n0004: These rules originate from the principles of refraction of light.
pg202_n0005: When a ray of light strikes the first face of a lens, it travels from a less dense to a denser medium, thus it bends towards the normal.
pg202_n0006: Upon exiting on the other side of the lens, the ray of light is now travelling from the denser medium to a less dense medium.
pg202_n0007: Therefore, the ray bends away from the normal as it exits the lens.
pg202_n0008: Three important rules are useful in constructing ray diagrams.
pg202_n0011: 1. Convex lens: A ray of light travelling parallel to the principal axis of a convex lens (Figure 5.35 (a)) is converged to the principal focus.
pg202_n0012: Concave lens: A ray of light travelling parallel to the principal axis of a concave lens (Figure 5.35(b)) is diverged in such a way that it appears to be coming from the principal focus.
pg202_n0016: Figure 5.35: Refraction of incident light rays that are parallel to the principal axis
pg202_n0018: 2. A ray of light travelling through the optical centre continues to travel along the same path for both convex and concave lenses as seen in Figure 5.36.
pg202_n0021: Figure 5.36: Refraction of light rays incident through the optical centre
pg202_n0023: 3. Convex lens: An incident ray of light travelling through the principal focus of a converging lens is refracted parallel to the principal axis of the convex lens as shown in Figure 5.37 (a).
pg202_n0024: Concave lens: An incident ray of light that appears to travel through the principal focus of a diverging lens is refracted parallel to the principal axis.
pg202_n0025: Figure 5.37(b) shows the path of a ray through the principal focus for concave lenses.
pg203_n0007: Figure 5.37: Refraction of light rays incident through the principal focus
pg203_n0009: Like in the case of spherical mirrors, any two of the light rays are enough to locate the image formed by a lens.
pg203_n0010: The refraction of light produced by a lens is treated as occurring at a plane through the optical centre, that is, perpendicular to the principal axis of the lens.
pg203_n0011: Whenever rays diverge after passing through the lens, they are extended backwards to locate the virtual images.

pg207_n0037: If we represent the object distance by letter u, the image distance by letter v, and the focal length by letter f, then the general formula relating the three quantities is,
pg207_n0038: 1 over f equals 1 over u plus 1 over v.
pg207_n0040: This equation is called the thin lens formula or lens equation.
pg207_n0041: It is valid for both converging and diverging lenses.
pg207_n0042: The equation is a simpler and more accurate alternative for locating the image formed by either convex or concave lens.
pg207_n0043: The formula can be verified experimentally as demonstrated in Activity 5.14.
pg208_n0005: To determine the values of u and v using the formula, a sign convention is adopted.
pg208_n0006: The convention is referred to as the real-is-positive convention.
pg208_n0007: When using this convention, all distances are measured from the optical centre.
pg208_n0008: Distances of real objects and real images are treated as positive whereas distances of virtual objects and images are taken to be negative.
pg208_n0009: Because the principal focus of a concave lens is virtual, concave lenses have negative values of focal length.

pg211_n0019: Magnification is a measure of the extent to which an optical system changes the size of an image of an object.
pg211_n0020: The linear or lateral magnification produced by a lens is the ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object.
pg211_n0021: If the image size is bigger than the object size, then the image is said to be enlarged.
pg211_n0022: On the other hand, when the image size is smaller than the object size, the image is said to be diminished.
pg211_n0023: Magnification is usually denoted by the letter m.

pg212_n0023: Lenses have different applications in our daily life.

pg217_n0010: Optical instruments enhance the human eye’s ability to see distant and tiny objects, making it possible to observe stars and microorganisms that are otherwise invisible.
pg217_n0011: These devices use light, along with lenses, mirrors, and prisms, to form clearer images.
pg217_n0012: In this chapter, you will learn how various optical instruments work, including microscopes, telescopes, and cameras.
pg217_n0013: The competencies developed will enable you to choose, use, and even construct simple optical instruments for different applications.
pg217_n0020: The size of an object as viewed by the eye is determined by the size of its image formed on the retina.
pg217_n0021: The size of the image depends on the distance from the object to the observer’s eye and the angle subtended by the object at the eye, called angular size (θ).
pg217_n0022: If you want to look closely at a small object, such as an insect, you bring the object close to your eye.
pg217_n0023: By doing so, you increase the angular size and hence make the image on the retina as large as possible.
pg217_n0024: However, your eyes cannot focus sharply on objects that are closer than a point at about 25 cm from the eye.
pg217_n0025: This point is known as the near point of the eye.
pg217_n0026: Moving an object closer to the near point of the eye increases the size of the image on your retina.
pg217_n0027: But if you still move the object closer than the near point, the image will be fuzzy or blurred because the lens of the eye will no longer focus an image on the retina.
pg217_n0028: Therefore, the closest comfortable distance for viewing an image is when an object is at this point.
pg217_n0029: Thus, an object cannot be brought closer to the eye beyond the near point.
pg217_n0030: To overcome this limitation, a converging lens can be used to enlarge the image of an object.
pg217_n0031: The object can then be moved even closer to the eye, resulting in a large image formed on the retina.
pg217_n0032: A lens used in this way forms a device known as a simple microscope.
pg218_n0005: A simple microscope is made of a biconvex lens normally held by a round-shaped frame with a handle.
pg218_n0006: It can therefore be hand-held and moved according to the user’s needs.
pg218_n0007: A simple microscope is sometimes called a magnifying glass or simply a magnifier.

pg218_n0012: Mode of action of a simple microscope
pg218_n0014: When using a simple microscope, you can simply put it over the object to be viewed.
pg218_n0015: For the comfort of the observer’s eye, the position of the magnifying glass with respect to the object is adjusted so that the object is at the focal point of the lens.
pg218_n0016: This produces a virtual, upright, and magnified image of the object.
pg218_n0017: Note that the largest image can be formed on the retina of the naked eye when the object is at the near point (D ≈ 25 cm).
pg218_n0018: Therefore, for the clear and maximum size of the image to be formed on the retina, the magnifier must have a focal length of approximately 25 cm.
pg218_n0019: The image is formed at infinity when the position of the magnifying glass or the object itself is adjusted so that the object is at the focal point of the magnifying glass.
pg218_n0020: In this way, the eyes see a magnified image such that smaller features can be observed.

pg221_n0044: The magnification of a simple microscope is limited to M less than or equal to 9 for realistic focal lengths.
pg221_n0045: This means that the object will appear 9 times larger when viewed using a simple microscope of maximum magnification.
pg221_n0046: For example, an object whose size is 1 mm will be seen to be 9 mm when viewed through a magnifier.
pg221_n0047: However, the size of bacteria, for example, is much smaller than 1 mm.
pg221_n0048: Thus, to see a bacterium, a magnification larger than 9 is required.
pg221_n0049: To achieve this, a new microscope that uses two lenses in such a way that one lens compounds the effect of the other lens is normally used.
pg221_n0050: Such a microscope is called a compound microscope.
pg221_n0054: A compound microscope is composed of a lens system, a lighting system and a focusing system.

pg222_n0006: The image formed by the objective lens serves as the object for the second lens, which is known as the eyepiece.
pg222_n0007: The eyepiece functions as a simple microscope to produce the final image, which is enlarged and virtual.
pg222_n0009: A compound microscope has a revolving nose piece that allows the user to change the objective lens according to needs.
pg222_n0010: The compound microscope also consists of the lighting system, which may be called the illumination system.
pg222_n0011: It consists of a light source, which can be an electric bulb, a light-emitting diode (LED) or sometimes natural sunlight.
pg222_n0012: There is also a mirror and a condenser which help to transmit light through an object for viewing.
pg222_n0013: On the other hand, the compound microscope has a focusing system.
pg222_n0015: This system is made of coarse and fine adjustment knobs, which are essential for moving the objective lens away or towards the object in searching for a clear image.
pg222_n0016: The system also has the inclination joint, which helps in tilting the microscope for a comfortable view.
pg222_n0017: Other parts of a compound microscope include the body tube, which separates the objective and the eyepiece and assures continuous alignment of the optics.
pg222_n0018: A stage is used for holding the object to be viewed, and the base supports the whole structure of the microscope.

pg222_n0034: Mode of action of a compound microscope
pg222_n0036: A compound microscope works by using the principle that an image formed by one optical element can serve as the object for the second optical element.
pg222_n0037: That is, an image formed by the objective lens is used as the object for the eyepiece.
pg222_n0038: The object to be viewed is placed just beyond the first focal point F o of the objective lens, which forms a real and enlarged image I one as illustrated by Figure 6.4.
pg222_n0040: In a properly designed compound microscope, the image formed by the objective lens lies just inside the focal point F e of the eyepiece.
pg222_n0041: The eyepiece, or ocular, acts as a simple magnifier and forms a final virtual image I two.
pg222_n0042: The position of I two may be anywhere between the near and far points of the eye.

pg226_n0032: The human eye has limitations when viewing objects that are very far from the observer.
pg226_n0033: When the object is at a distance far from the point 2F of the eye lens, its image is formed at the focal point of the eye lens.
pg226_n0034: However, this image is extremely small and sometimes cannot be decoded by the brain.
pg226_n0035: How can this limitation be overcome?
pg226_n0036: Astronomers use a device named an astronomical telescope to observe the universe and its components, which are extremely far from our eyes.
pg226_n0040: Just like the compound microscope, an astronomical telescope uses two convex lenses: the objective lens and the eyepiece.
pg226_n0041: It also consists of a focusing system for adjusting the sharpness and clarity of the image.
pg226_n0042: However, unlike the compound microscope, the objective lens of a telescope has a large focal length while the eyepiece has a much shorter focal length.

pg226_sec001_ans_item-14: The objective lens forms a real, inverted, magnified intermediate image of the object. This image acts as the object for the eyepiece, which then magnifies it further to produce a large virtual image.
pg226_sec001_ans_item-15: Because when the intermediate image is formed near the focal point of the eyepiece, the eyepiece acts as a magnifier and produces a highly enlarged virtual final image for comfortable viewing.
pg227_n0003: Since the astronomical telescope uses a lens as its objective glass, it is also called a refracting telescope.

pg227_n0012: Mode of action of an astronomical telescope
pg227_n0014: A telescope is used to provide angular magnification of distant objects.
pg227_n0015: Light from a distant object enters the objective lens and a real image is formed in the tube at the second focal point of the objective lens.
pg227_n0016: This image becomes the object for the eyepiece.
pg227_n0017: The position of the eyepiece lens is adjusted until the image from the objective lens falls at the focal point of the eyepiece.
pg227_n0018: The image of the eyepiece is inverted and magnified as illustrated in Figure 6.8.
pg227_n0019: Note that the main considerations with an astronomical telescope are its light-gathering power and its resolution or resolving power.
pg227_n0020: The light-gathering power depends on the area of the objective lens.
pg227_n0022: The larger the diameter of the objective lens, the brighter the image observed.
pg227_n0023: The resolving power, which is the ability to observe two close objects distinctly, also depends on the diameter of the objective lens.
pg227_n0024: So, the desire is to make astronomical telescopes with an objective lens of larger diameter.
pg227_n0025: Nevertheless, lenses with big diameters tend to be very heavy and therefore, difficult to make and to be supported by their edges.
pg227_n0026: Further, it is rather difficult and expensive to make such large-sized lenses that may form images that are free from any kind of distortions.

pg229_n0042: When you visit a national park, you cannot get very close to dangerous animals, such as lions and leopards, for safety reasons.
pg229_n0043: To closely watch such animals, one needs to use a device that can help the eye see distant objects closely.
pg229_n0044: An optical device used in such a situation is called binoculars.
pg230_n0005: Binoculars can be considered as having two telescopes that are exactly the same and placed beside each other, such that they accurately point in the same direction.
pg230_n0006: This allows the observer to use both eyes when looking at distant objects.
pg230_n0007: The main components of binoculars are the eyepiece, the objective lens and prisms.
pg230_n0008: The objective lens focuses a distant object to a point near the focal point of the eyepiece, which magnifies that image.
pg230_n0009: A pair of prisms inverts the image so that it can be seen properly upright by the eyes.
pg230_n0010: Other parts are the focusing system, which allows the lenses to be moved back and forth.
pg230_n0011: Figure 6.10 shows some parts of binoculars.
pg230_im018: Black binoculars with two large objective lenses at the front, two eyepieces at the back, and a central focusing knob between the barrels.
pg230_n0020: Two objective lenses are situated at the ends of both telescopes making the binoculars.
pg230_n0021: The purpose of the objective lens is to collect light from the object that the user is looking at and form the image of the object at or near the focal point of the eyepiece.
pg230_n0022: The eyepiece can be thought of as a magnifying glass.
pg230_n0023: It picks up the small image formed by the objective lens and magnifies it so that the observer can clearly see the object.
pg230_n0024: However, when light is refracted through the objective, the light rays cross over, resulting in an upside-down image.
pg230_n0025: The eyepiece simply magnifies this image so that the viewer sees the object upside down.
pg230_n0026: This problem can be solved by deploying a pair of prisms.
pg230_n0027: These prisms are essentially used to rotate and reflect the image using the principle of total internal reflection.
pg230_n0028: To rotate the image 180 degrees, prisms are arranged in a way that each prism effectively rotates the image 90 degrees.
pg230_n0029: Normally, two types of prisms are used in binoculars: roof prisms and porro prisms.
pg230_n0030: Figure 6.11 shows how image inversion is achieved in binoculars.

pg231_n0008: While the magnifying power affects the size of the image, the size of the objective lens affects the clarity and details of the image.
pg231_n0009: Commercial binoculars are normally imprinted with information about the objective lens size and the magnification power.

pg231_n0025: For example, binoculars are commonly used by tourists to view animals.
pg231_n0026: Also, soldiers use binoculars to view the enemy camp from a far point.
pg231_n0028: Likewise, surveyors use binoculars to survey and observe the landscape and other features.

pg231_n0041: The camera is one of the optical instruments that have been used since the discovery of lenses.
pg231_n0042: The word camera is a Latin word that means “a room or enclosure”.
pg231_n0043: Thus, the primary component of a camera is the light-tight enclosure or box.
pg231_n0044: A camera is made up of different components contained inside the light tight box.
pg231_n0045: Depending on the components, cameras may take many forms, including film cameras, digital cameras and video cameras.
pg231_n0046: In this section, we discuss the simplest form of a camera, which is known as a lens camera.
pg231_n0050: Major components of a lens camera include a biconvex lens, a film, a diaphragm, a
pg232_n0005: Figure 6.12 shows some parts of a lens camera.

pg232_n0011: Figure 6.12: Parts of a lens camera
pg232_n0013: The lens is the image-forming device in a camera.
pg232_n0014: The focal length of a lens determines the size of the image that will be formed on the film.
pg232_n0015: Therefore, four basic categories of lenses exist.
pg232_n0021: Normal lens which allows the viewing field of approximately 50 degrees, giving a picture that is normal in size relative to the background and which looks natural to the viewer.
pg232_n0025: Wide angle lens which enables a view of 90 degrees and is used when smaller objects are to be photographed.
pg232_n0029: Telephoto lens or long-focus lens which has a wider field of view than the normal lens.
pg232_n0030: It shows enlarged detail of the image over the same film area.
pg232_n0031: The telephoto lens has a long reach, allowing you to capture an object that is far away.
pg232_n0032: You have probably seen a photograph where an object is in focus but the background is blurred; this is often done with a telephoto lens.
pg232_n0036: Interchangeable lens which offers the photographer the opportunity to select a focal length that is best for a given situation.
pg232_n0037: In recent years, variable focal length or “zoom” lenses have become very popular.
pg232_n0039: The diaphragm determines the amount of light that passes through the lens by changing the size of the aperture.
pg232_n0040: The aperture is an opening whose diameter is adjustable.
pg232_n0041: The size of the aperture is measured in f-number; the larger the number the smaller the aperture.
pg232_n0042: Most cameras use an iris-type diaphragm, which consists of a number of very thin metal blades.
pg232_n0043: They are mounted so that the size of the lens opening can be changed by a rotating ring or a moving lever.
pg232_n0045: The shutter is a mechanical device that acts as a gate, controlling the duration of time that light is allowed to pass through the lens and fall on the film.
pg232_n0047: A film is a light-sensitive surface of the camera.
pg232_n0048: It is normally rolled to the back of the camera.
pg232_n0049: In most cameras, the film is wound up on a spool with an interleaving light-tight backing paper.
pg232_n0050: However, in a digital camera, an electronic detector called a charge-coupled device (CCD) array is used instead of a film.
pg232_n0051: The digital information is stored on a memory chip for play back on the screen of the camera.
pg233_n0003: Mode of action of a lens camera
pg233_n0005: To take a photograph of an object, the image of the object must be sharply focused on the film.
pg233_n0006: This is done by adjusting the distance of the lens from the film.
pg233_n0007: After focusing and correctly setting the aperture size and shutter time, the shutter release button is pressed.
pg233_n0008: The shutter opens to allow light to enter and expose the film to form an image of the object being photographed.
pg233_n0009: The film is then developed to produce a photograph of the object.
pg233_n0010: Figure 6.13 illustrates the image formation by a lens camera.
