pg235_n0012: The human eye is a natural optical instrument that is exceptionally important for human life.
pg235_n0013: It belongs to a general group of eyes found in nature called “camera-type eyes” since the optical behaviour of the eye is similar to that of a lens camera.
pg235_n0014: The human eye can respond to a range of light frequencies.
pg235_n0015: The human eye looks whitish with a central black spot as seen in Figure 6.17.
pg235_im003: Close-up of a human eye showing the brown iris, black pupil, white sclera, and upper eyelashes.
pg235_n0021: The eye is nearly spherical and is about 2.5 cm in diameter.
pg235_n0022: The front portion is somehow more sharply curved and is covered by a tough, transparent membrane called the cornea.
pg235_n0023: The region behind the cornea contains a liquid called aqueous humour.
pg235_n0024: Next to the aqueous humour, there is a crystalline lens, which is a capsule containing a fibrous jelly, hard at the centre and progressively softer at the outer portions.
pg235_n0025: The crystalline lens is held in place by ligaments that attach it to the ciliary muscles which encircle the lens.
pg235_n0026: In front of the lens, there is an aperture with a variable diameter known as the pupil.
pg235_n0028: The pupil’s size is controlled by the iris, which is attached to the ciliary muscles.
pg235_n0029: The iris is responsible for the colour of the eye.
pg235_n0030: It acts as the diaphragm in a lens camera.
pg235_n0031: Behind the lens, the eye is filled with a thin watery jelly called the vitreous humour.
pg235_n0032: This jelly helps to focus the rays of light and also maintains the shape of the eye.
pg235_n0033: After the vitreous humor, there is a lining on the rear inner surface of the eye called the retina.
pg235_n0034: The retina hosts some photosensitive cells known as cones and rods which respond to the light falling on them.
pg235_n0035: Cones and rods are connected to millions of nerves which are later joined together to form the optic nerve.
pg235_n0036: The eye is protected by a tough whitish skin known as the sclera.
pg235_n0037: Figure 6.18 shows parts of the human eye.
pg236_im052: Cross-sectional diagram of the human eye showing the cornea, lens, retina, vitreous humour, and optic nerve.
pg236_n0014: Figure 6.18: Parts of a human eye
pg236_n0016: Images formed by the human eye
pg236_n0018: When light strikes the eye, it passes through the cornea.
pg236_n0019: The cornea is shaped like a dome, so it bends the light to help the eye focus.
pg236_n0020: The light through the cornea and the aqueous humour enters the eye through the pupil.
pg236_n0021: The iris controls the size of the pupil, which in turn determines the amount of light that enters the eye.
pg236_n0022: Next, light passes through the lens.
pg236_n0023: The lens works together with the cornea to focus light correctly on the retina.
pg236_n0024: Light from the lens travels through the vitreous humor towards the retina.
pg236_n0025: The image is formed on the retina as illustrated in Figure 6.19.
pg236_n0026: When light hits the retina to form the image, the photoreceptors on the retina turn the light into electrical signals, which travel to the brain through the optic nerve.
pg236_n0028: The indices of refraction of both the aqueous humour and the vitreous humour are about 1.336, which is nearly equal to that of water.
pg236_n0029: The crystalline lens, while not homogeneous, has an average index of refraction of 1.437.
pg236_n0030: This is not very different from the indices of the aqueous and vitreous humour.
pg236_n0031: As a result, most of the refraction of light entering the eye occurs at the outer surface of the cornea, as shown in Figure 6.19.
pg236_im051: Diagram of image formation in the human eye, with light from a tree focused by the lens to form an inverted image on the retina.
pg236_n0033: Figure 6.19: Image formation by the human eye
pg237_n0005: For an object to be seen sharply, the image must be formed exactly at the location of the retina.
pg237_n0006: The eye adjusts to different object distances u by changing the focal length f of its lens.
pg237_n0007: This is because the lens-to-retina distance, corresponding to v, does not change.
pg237_n0008: However, this is different from the lens camera in which the focal length is fixed and the lens-to-sensor distance is changed.
pg237_n0009: For the normal eye, a distant object is sharply focused when the ciliary muscles are relaxed.
pg237_n0010: This causes the curvature of the lens to decrease, thereby increasing its focal length (Figure 6.20(a)).
pg237_n0011: To focus sharply on a closer object, the tension in the ciliary muscle increases, causing the ciliary muscle to contract.
pg237_n0012: This causes the lens to bulge, resulting in the increase of its curvature and decrease of its focal length (Figure 6.20(b)).
pg237_n0013: The process by which the eye focuses on objects at different distances by varying the focal length of the lens is called accommodation.
pg237_im002: Three parallel light rays entering the eye from a distant object.
pg237_im013: Front of the eye with a thinner lens and relaxed ciliary muscles bending parallel rays toward the retina for distant vision.
pg237_im014: Back of the eye where light rays converge to a focus on the retina near the optic nerve.
pg237_im003: Near focusing in the human eye: diverging rays from a nearby object enter the eye, the lens bulges as the ciliary muscles contract, and the rays are focused on the retina.
pg237_n0024: Figure 6.20: Focusing distant and near objects
pg238_n0003: The extremes of the range over which distinct vision is possible are known as the far point and the near point of the eye.
pg238_n0004: The far point of a normal eye is the maximum distance at which the light from the object can still be focused onto the retina.
pg238_n0005: The near point is the shortest distance from the eye at which the light from the object can be focused onto the retina.
pg238_n0006: The eye tends to be blind when the object is closer to the eye than the near point.
pg238_n0007: The position of the near point depends on the amount by which the ciliary muscle can increase or decrease the curvature of the crystalline lens.
pg238_n0008: The range of accommodation gradually diminishes with age because the crystalline lens grows throughout a person’s life, and the ciliary muscles become less capable of distorting a larger lens.
pg238_n0009: For this reason, the near point gradually recedes as one grows older.
pg238_n0010: The recession of the near point is a condition called presbyopia.

pg238_n0047: For an object to be seen by the human eye, light from the object must be focused on the retina.
pg238_n0048: However, there are cases when light from the object cannot be focused on the retina.
pg238_n0049: This arises mainly from incorrect distance relationships in the eye.
pg238_n0050: A normal eye can form an image on the retina for an object at infinity when the ciliary muscles are relaxed, and for a nearby object when the ciliary muscles are contracted, as illustrated in Figure 6.20.
pg238_n0051: In some cases, the size of the eyeball is defective, leading to conditions known as short-sightedness (myopia) and far-sightedness (hyperopia).
pg238_n0055: In the myopic (short-sightedness or near-sightedness) eye, the eyeball is too long from front to back in comparison with the radius of curvature of the cornea (or the cornea is too sharply curved).
pg238_n0056: This causes the rays of light from an object at infinity to be focused in front of the retina.
pg238_n0057: The most distant object for which an image can be formed on the retina is then nearer than infinity.
pg239_n0003: from short-sightedness can see nearby objects clearly but not distant objects.

pg239_n0014: To correct myopia, rays of light from a distant object should be diverged before entering the eye.
pg239_n0015: Therefore, correcting the myopic eye involves the use of a concave (diverging) lens, which forms the image of a distant object close to the eye lens.
pg239_n0016: The image formed by the glass lens is then focused onto the retina by the eye lens.

pg240_n0003: Note that lenses used for vision correction are usually described in terms of lens power, P, which is given by the reciprocal focal length expressed in metres.
pg240_n0007: The unit of lens power is the dioptre, D.
pg240_n0008: Thus, a lens with f equals 0.50 meters has a power of 2.0 D, f equals 0.250 meters corresponds to 4.0 D, and so on.
pg240_n0009: The numbers used for the prescription of the glass lenses are usually powers expressed in diopters.
pg240_n0013: In the hyperopic (long-sightedness or far-sightedness) eye, the eyeball is too short or the cornea is not curved enough.
pg240_n0014: This causes the rays of light from a near object to be focused behind the retina.
pg240_n0015: A person suffering from long sightedness can see distant objects clearly, but cannot see nearby objects clearly.
pg240_n0016: The near point of the eye may be more than a metre away, making ordinary reading difficult.
pg240_im028: Cross-section of a long-sighted (hyperopic) eye, with incoming light rays focused behind the retina.
pg240_n0024: Note that the myopic eye produces too much convergence of light rays from a distant object, while a hyperopic eye produces insufficient convergence of rays of light from a near object.
pg240_n0028: Presbyopia is the gradual loss of the eye’s ability to focus on nearby objects because of old age.
pg240_n0029: The term “presbyopia” comes from a Greek word that means “old eye.”
pg240_n0030: This defect is normally observed after the age of 40 years.
pg240_n0031: Presbyopia is caused by loss of eye lens flexibility, which is necessary to change its focal length in order to focus on objects.
pg240_n0032: This results in insufficient accommodation, leading to image formation behind the retina, as shown in Figure 6.24.
pg240_im003: Cross-section of a presbyopic eye showing insufficient accommodation, causing rays from a near object to focus behind the retina.
pg240_n0041: In the case of either a presbyopic or a hyperopic eye, the near point is farther from the eye than normal.
pg240_n0042: Therefore, to see clearly an object at a normal reading distance, which is about 25 cm, a convex
pg241_n0003: lens is required to form a virtual image at or beyond the near point.
pg241_n0004: The lens converges the rays of light from a near object to form the image at or beyond the near point.
pg241_n0005: The eye lens then focuses the image of the glass lens onto the retina.

pg241_n0020: Astigmatism is the imperfection in the curvature of the eye that causes the formation of blurred images on the retina.
pg241_n0021: It occurs when either the cornea or the lens has mismatched curves.
pg241_n0022: That is, instead of having a curve like a ground ball, the surface is egg-shaped.
pg241_n0023: This causes the lens to have different focal points when looking at the same object.
pg241_n0024: Consequently, rays of light from the object are focused at different points, leading to image formation at different positions on the retina.
pg241_n0027: Astigmatism is often present at birth and may occur in combination with near-sightedness or far-sightedness.

pg007_n0008_easy_read: Clothes with nylon often make a crackling sound when you take them off your body.
pg007_n0009_easy_read: If you rub a latex balloon on your face, the balloon may try to stick to your face.
pg007_n0010_easy_read:
This happens because of static electricity.
Static electricity comes from an uneven balance of electric charges inside a material or on its surface.
pg007_n0011_easy_read:
In this chapter, you will learn:
- the idea of static electricity
- where charges come from
- the basic law of static electricity
- how to detect charges
pg007_n0012_easy_read:
You will also learn about:
- conductors and insulators
- capacitors
- how charge spreads on the surface of a conductor
- lightning conductors
pg007_n0013_easy_read: The skills you develop will help you recognise the effects and uses of static electricity in daily life.
pg007_n0016_easy_read: Uses of static electricity in daily life
pg007_n0020_easy_read: Have you noticed that a nylon cloth makes a crackling sound when you take it off your body?
pg007_n0021_easy_read: Sometimes, you can feel tiny sparks when you undress in the dark.
pg007_n0022_easy_read: The crackling sound comes from small electric sparks during charge-discharge.
pg007_n0023_easy_read:
The charge comes from friction between the nylon and your skin.
This creates static electricity.
pg007_n0024_easy_read: Pens and combs made of some plastic materials can attract tiny pieces of paper after you rub them on hair or synthetic clothing, as shown in Figure 1.1.
pg007_n0031_easy_read: Figure 1.1: A charged comb attracts pieces of paper
pg008_n0005_easy_read: Static electricity happens when static electric charges build up on a material that does not conduct electricity.
pg008_n0009_easy_read: Static electricity is made when electrons move from one material to another.
pg008_n0010_easy_read: This happens when 2 objects touch and then separate. One material gains electrons and becomes negatively charged. The other material loses electrons and becomes positively charged.
pg008_n0011_easy_read:
Common examples are:
- rubbing a glass rod with cloth (Figure 1.2 (a))
- walking across a carpet (Figure 1.2 (b))
- rubbing a balloon with woollen cloth (Figure 1.2 (c))
pg008_n0012_easy_read:
The size of the static charge depends on several things:
- the materials used
- the surface properties
- the environmental conditions, such as humidity
pg008_n0013_easy_read: This build-up of charge can cause electrostatic discharge, such as a spark.
pg008_n0024_easy_read: (a) Rubbing a glass rod with silk
pg008_n0040_easy_read: (c) Rubbing a balloon with a woollen cloth
pg008_n0047_easy_read: To show the charging of an object
pg008_n0050_easy_read:
Materials:
- wool jumper
- dry plastic sheets
pg008_n0055_easy_read: 1. Put 2 transparent plastic sheets on top of a book.
pg008_n0057_easy_read: 2. Rub the 2 plastic sheets with the wool jumper several times.
pg009_n0005_easy_read:
3. Slowly pull the 2 plastic sheets apart.
Listen to what happens.
pg009_n0007_easy_read:
4. Move the plastic sheets closer together.
Watch what happens.
pg009_n0009_easy_read:
5. Separate the plastic sheets.
Then rub each sheet with the wool jumper several times.
pg009_n0011_easy_read:

A neutral object has the same number of positive and negative charges.
These charges balance each other.
pg015_n0006_easy_read:
When you bring another neutral object near it, or when you touch the 2 objects together, usually nothing special happens.
This happens because both objects have balanced charges.
pg015_n0008_easy_read:
But sometimes, 1 object gets more positive charges or more negative charges than the other object.
This is called an imbalance of charges.
pg015_n0009_easy_read: Creating this imbalance is called charging an object.
pg015_n0011_easy_read: There are different ways to charge objects:
pg015_n0014_easy_read: (a) Friction: When you rub 2 objects together, electrons can move from 1 object to the other.
pg015_n0016_easy_read: (b) Contact (or conduction): When a charged object touches a neutral object, electrons can move between them.
pg015_n0018_easy_read:
(c) Induction: When you bring a charged object close to a neutral object, the charges inside the neutral object can move around.
This can happen without touching.
pg015_n0020_easy_read:
All these methods move electrons.
This creates an imbalance of charges.
Then the object becomes either positively charged or negatively charged.
pg015_n0024_easy_read:
Charging by friction is the oldest way to create electric charge.
It is very important for understanding static electricity.
pg015_n0025_easy_read:
This process happens when 2 objects that touch each other are rubbed together.
Then electrons move from 1 object to the other.
pg015_n0029_easy_read: When 2 insulating materials are rubbed together, friction creates an imbalance of electric charges.
pg015_n0030_easy_read:
Electrons are negatively charged particles.
They move from 1 object to another.
pg015_n0031_easy_read:
The object that loses electrons becomes positively charged.
The object that gains electrons becomes negatively charged.
pg015_n0032_easy_read:
This transfer of charge follows the principle of conservation of charge.
This means the total charge stays the same before and after rubbing.
pg015_n0033_easy_read: For example, when an ebonite rod is rubbed with fur, electrons move from the fur to the ebonite rod, as shown in Figure 1.10.
pg015_n0034_easy_read:
As a result, the fur becomes positively charged because it loses electrons.
The ebonite rod becomes negatively charged because it gains electrons.

When 2 materials from this series are rubbed together, the material higher in the series loses electrons.
The material lower in the series gains electrons.

The silk gains electrons and becomes negatively charged.

pg025_n0016_easy_read: You have learnt that like charges repel each other. Unlike charges attract each other.

Current electricity is a basic part of engineering science.
It is important for designing, studying, and improving electric circuits, electronic devices, and power systems in different areas of technology.
pg045_n0009_easy_read: In this chapter, you will learn about current electricity, voltage, Ohm’s law, electrical components, electrical energy, and power.

pg045_n0011_easy_read: The skills you develop will also help you use electrical appliances efficiently in different situations.

A conductor, such as an electric wire (Figure 2.1(a)), contains charges, which can be negative or positive.
When these charges are forced to move, they form an electric current.
pg045_n0021_easy_read: To start this movement, we must create a potential difference across the ends of the conductor.
pg045_n0023_easy_read:
People use different methods to create a potential difference.
One method uses a battery, as shown in Figure 2.1(b).
Another method uses a charged capacitor.
pg045_n0024_easy_read:
To keep the current flowing steadily, we must use a battery.
A capacitor loses its charge as soon as the current starts to flow.
pg046_n0003_easy_read: Electric current, I, is the flow of electric charge, Q, through a conductor over time, t.
pg046_n0004_easy_read: We can write this relationship in maths as:
pg046_n0005_easy_read: I equals charge, Q, divided by time, t.
pg046_n0008_easy_read: Here, n is the number of electrons, and e is the charge of 1 electron.
pg046_n0010_easy_read: I equals n e divided by t.
pg046_n0012_easy_read: In simple words, current measures how much charge passes a point in a circuit in a unit of time.
pg046_n0013_easy_read: Charged particles carry this charge. These particles can be electrons or ions.
pg046_n0014_easy_read: A higher current means a greater flow of charge.
pg046_n0019_easy_read: The charge of 1 electron is 1.6 times 10 to the power of negative 19 coulombs. Find the number of electrons that pass in 1 second through any cross-section of a conductor with a steady current of 1 ampere.
pg046_n0022_easy_read: I equals n e divided by t.
pg046_n0023_easy_read: n equals I t divided by e, equals 1 ampere times 1 second divided by 1.6 times 10 to the power of negative 19 coulombs, equals 6.25 times 10 to the power of 18.
pg046_n0025_easy_read: So, the number of electrons is 6.25 times 10 to the power of 18.
pg046_n0029_easy_read: The electromotive force (e.m.f) is the potential difference across the terminals of a source when no current flows.
pg046_n0030_easy_read: It gives the energy needed to move electrons through a conductor. This movement produces an electric current.
pg046_n0031_easy_read: Here, the word "force" does not mean the force between bodies.
pg046_n0032_easy_read: We can compare e.m.f to water pressure.
pg046_n0033_easy_read: When the pressure is high, more water flows through a pipe.
pg046_n0034_easy_read: In the same way, when the e.m.f is higher, more electrons flow through a conductor.
pg046_n0035_easy_read:
Sources of e.m.f include:
- electrochemical cells, such as dry cells and car batteries
- thermoelectric devices
- solar cells
- electric generators

pg046_n0047_easy_read: When an electric device such as a bulb is connected to a cell, electric current flows through the device. Some electrical energy changes into light and heat.
pg046_n0048_easy_read: The energy changed per unit charge is equal to the potential difference (p.d) across the device.
pg047_n0003_easy_read: Potential difference (p.d) is the work done to move 1 unit of charge in a circuit from 1 point to another.
pg047_n0004_easy_read: Potential difference (p.d) is also called voltage.
pg047_n0005_easy_read: p d, V, equals work done, W, divided by charge, Q.
pg047_n0007_easy_read: Like e.m.f., the SI unit for p.d is the volt (V).
pg047_n0008_easy_read: 1 volt is equal to 1 joule per coulomb.

The resistance of a conductor depends on:
- temperature
- length
- cross-sectional area
- type of material
pg063_n0005_easy_read:
When temperature rises, the atoms in the conductor vibrate more.
Then electrons hit atoms more often.
This increases resistance.
pg063_n0006_easy_read: In some materials, resistance changes almost linearly with temperature.
pg063_n0007_easy_read: For example, the resistance of copper (Cu) changes approximately linearly with temperature.
pg063_n0008_easy_read: In some other materials, resistance does not change linearly with temperature.
pg063_n0009_easy_read: However, temperature has very little effect on the resistance of some alloys, such as constantan and manganin.
pg063_n0013_easy_read: When the length of a conductor increases, and the other factors stay the same, the resistance also increases.
pg063_n0014_easy_read: This happens because electrons and atoms collide more in a long conductor than in a short conductor.
pg063_n0015_easy_read: This means that the resistance, R, of the wire is proportional to the length, l, of the wire.
pg063_n0021_easy_read: A conductor with a larger cross-sectional area has more charge carriers to carry the electric current than a conductor with a smaller cross-sectional area.
pg063_n0022_easy_read:
This means that the resistance R of a conductor is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area A of the conductor.
That is,
pg063_n0023_easy_read: R is proportional to one over A.
pg063_n0027_easy_read: The resistance of a conductor also depends on the material used to make it.
pg063_n0028_easy_read: For example, a conductor made from steel has higher resistance than a conductor made from copper, if both have the same dimensions and the same temperature.
pg063_n0029_easy_read: For example, steel has higher resistivity than copper.
pg063_n0030_easy_read:
The property of a material that resists current flow is called resistivity.
It is shown by rho.
pg063_n0031_easy_read: Since R is proportional to l and R is proportional to one over A, then:
pg063_n0032_easy_read: R is proportional to l over A.
pg063_n0035_easy_read: R equals r times l over A.
pg063_n0037_easy_read: Here, r is the constant of proportionality.
pg063_n0038_easy_read:
This constant of proportionality is the resistivity of the material.
It is given as:
pg063_n0039_easy_read: rho equals R A over l.
pg063_n0041_easy_read: So, resistivity measures how much a material opposes the flow of electric current.
pg063_n0042_easy_read: The SI unit of resistivity is the ohm-metre (Ωm).
pg063_n0043_easy_read: Activity 2.6 will help you develop practical knowledge about how to determine the resistivity of wires.

Every electrical appliance should have a label.

pg076_n0036_easy_read:
The rate at which an appliance uses energy is called the rating of the appliance.
This rating is usually marked on the appliance.

You have learnt that the unit of electrical power is watt.

pg077_n0012_easy_read: However, the watt-second unit is too small for everyday commercial use of electrical energy.
pg077_n0014_easy_read:
So, a larger unit is used.
This unit is the kilowatt-hour (kWh).
pg077_n0015_easy_read: 1 kWh is the energy used in 1 hour by an appliance that works at 1 kW.
pg077_n0016_easy_read: In commercial use, 1 kWh is called 1 unit of electricity.
pg077_n0017_easy_read: For example, if a user consumes 5 units of electricity, it means the user has consumed 5 kWh of electrical energy.

pg077_n0024_easy_read: The unit kWh is used to find the cost of the electrical energy that electricity users consume.

pg079_n0023_easy_read: Electricity is a very convenient and clean source of power.
pg079_n0024_easy_read:
In houses, electricity is supplied through low-resistance wires made of copper or aluminium.
The wires are covered with rubber.
pg079_n0025_easy_read: Cables are rated by the maximum current they can carry.
pg079_n0029_easy_read:
Domestic electricity is supplied through 2 cables:
- the live cable (L), which is brown or red
- the neutral cable (N), which is usually blue or black
pg079_n0030_easy_read: In a single-phase system, the live cable has a potential of 240 V relative to the neutral line.
pg079_n0031_easy_read: The current in the cable changes direction 60 times each second (60 Hz).
pg079_n0032_easy_read:
The neutral cable is earthed.
It is connected to the ground at the power station.
pg079_n0033_easy_read: This keeps the neutral cable at zero potential, even though current flows through it.
pg079_n0034_easy_read: In this situation, the neutral cable cannot give an electric shock if someone touches it.
pg079_n0035_easy_read:
For extra safety, especially in electrical appliances, there is also a 3rd cable called earth (E).
It is yellow or green.
It is earthed by connecting it to the ground through a thick copper rod.
pg079_n0036_easy_read: The earth cable connects the metal body of an electrical appliance to the ground through a 3-pin plug.
pg079_n0037_easy_read: A 3-pin plug and electrical wiring cables are connected as shown in Figure 2.41.
pg080_n0003_easy_read:
A fuse is connected to the live cable.
If the fuse blows, the body of the appliance is cut off from the live electrical connection.
This helps prevent danger to users.
pg080_n0004_easy_read:
The earth pin on the plug is usually longer than the other 2 pins.
This lets it open the safety shutter to the terminals of the socket.
pg080_n0005_easy_read: The longer earth pin also makes sure the appliance is earthed before it is connected to a power source.
pg080_n0006_easy_read:
When you connect a 3-pin plug, you must follow the colour code exactly.
This helps avoid electric shock.
pg080_n0007_easy_read: The switch must be OFF when you push the plug into the socket.
pg080_n0008_easy_read: A 2-pin plug does not have a fuse or an earth pin.
pg080_n0009_easy_read: So, an appliance that uses a 2-pin plug does not have its body connected to the earth.
pg080_n0011_easy_read: The connections for the 2-pin plug follow the same colour code as the 3-pin plug.
pg080_n0017_easy_read: If electric current goes above the rated value of an electrical appliance, it damages the appliance.
pg080_n0018_easy_read: A fuse or a circuit breaker is used to protect an appliance from this damage.
pg080_n0019_easy_read:
A fuse has an element.
This element is usually a piece of copper or tin-lead alloy wire.
It melts when the current goes above a set value.
pg080_n0020_easy_read:
The element is inside a suitable casing.
It is placed in series with the circuit that needs protection.
pg080_n0022_easy_read:
There are 2 types of fuses:
- rewirable fuses
- cartridge fuses
pg080_n0023_easy_read:
In a rewirable fuse, the fuse element is in a removable fuse link.
The fuse link is made of porcelain or another suitable insulating material.
pg080_n0024_easy_read: This makes it safe for an operator to remove the fuse link.
pg080_n0029_easy_read:
A cartridge fuse has a porcelain tube.
Metal end caps are attached to the fuse element.
pg080_n0036_easy_read: A fuse blows, or melts, when a circuit is overloaded or when a short circuit happens.
pg080_n0037_easy_read:
A short-circuit fault is an unwanted connection.
It lets current flow through a path that is not part of the circuit design.
pg080_n0038_easy_read: The new path might change the route of the current.
pg081_n0003_easy_read: Some or all of the current flows away from the designed path.
pg081_n0004_easy_read: You can identify a short-circuit fault because the circuit, or part of the circuit, draws a very high current. This can blow the fuse.
pg081_n0005_easy_read: The potential difference between 2 points joined by a short circuit is 0 or much lower than expected.
pg081_n0006_easy_read: Activity 2.13 shows the melting of a fuse.

pg082_n0006_easy_read: A circuit breaker, like the ones in Figure 2.47, is a type of switch. It stops the flow of current when the current in a circuit goes above a set value.
pg082_n0007_easy_read: A circuit breaker works by opening the circuit when the current is too high.
pg082_n0008_easy_read: Unlike a fuse, a circuit breaker can be reset after the current in the circuit returns to normal.
pg082_n0009_easy_read: However, like a fuse, a circuit breaker is connected in series with the circuit it controls.
pg082_n0011_easy_read: In a circuit breaker, a latch keeps the switch contacts closed. The latch releases the contacts quickly to open the circuit.
pg082_n0017_easy_read: The power company brings power to a house up to the meter. Then it leaves cables to connect to the consumer unit, where the house wiring starts.
pg082_n0018_easy_read: A consumer unit is a type of distribution board. It sends electricity from the main supply to separate circuits.
pg082_n0019_easy_read: From the consumer unit, the cables split into several parallel circuits. These circuits carry current to different parts of the house.
pg082_n0020_easy_read: There are 2 ways to wire a house from the main switch: the ring system and the tree system.
pg082_n0023_easy_read: In many houses, the main sockets are connected to a ring main.
pg082_n0024_easy_read: This cable starts and ends at the consumer unit.
pg082_n0025_easy_read:
The cable has:
- live wires
- neutral wires
- earth wires
Each wire forms a ring around the house or part of the house.
pg082_n0026_easy_read: In this circuit, the current has 2 parts. So thin cables can be used.
pg082_n0027_easy_read: The sockets usually have a 30 A fuse at the consumer unit.
pg082_n0028_easy_read: Figure 2.48 shows a typical ring main circuit.
pg082_n0035_easy_read: Figure 2.48: Consumer unit and a ring main in a house
pg082_n0037_easy_read: The tree system uses a cable from the main switch to the distribution box, as shown in Figure 2.49.
pg082_n0038_easy_read: Of these 2 wiring methods, the ring system is more convenient for modern houses than the tree system.
pg083_n0003_easy_read: Figure 2.49: The tree system method of house wiring
pg083_n0005_easy_read: The distribution box has lighting fuses and power fuses.
pg083_n0006_easy_read:
For example, there are separate lighting fuses for:
- corridors
- bedrooms
- the living room
- the kitchen
pg083_n0007_easy_read:
Most houses have:
- light fuses rated 5 A
- power socket fuses usually rated 15 A
pg083_n0008_easy_read: So, cables for power points are different from cables for lights.
pg083_n0009_easy_read: Lighting circuits control the lights in a house.
pg083_n0010_easy_read:
The lighting circuit is different from the ring circuit.
The lighting circuit does not make a loop back to the consumer unit.
pg083_n0011_easy_read:
Instead, the consumer unit usually connects to the 1st lamp.
Then the 1st lamp connects to the 2nd lamp, and so on.
pg083_n0012_easy_read:
There are 2 types of lighting circuits:
- loop-in lighting circuits
- junction box lighting circuits
pg083_n0014_easy_read: In the loop-in lighting circuit, the live wire, neutral wire, and earth wire run from the consumer unit to each ceiling rose, 1 after another.
pg083_n0015_easy_read:
From each rose, another set of wires goes to the switch.
The switch operates the light.
pg083_n0025_easy_read: In the junction box lighting circuit, the neutral wire and earth wire run from 1 junction box to the next junction box.
pg083_n0026_easy_read:
From the junction box, 1 wire goes to the light.
The other wire goes to the switch for that light.
pg083_n0027_easy_read: Figure 2.51 shows the junction box lighting circuit.

pg084_n0041_easy_read: Checking electrical faults in domestic appliances
pg084_n0043_easy_read: Finding electrical faults in domestic appliances is important for safety and good performance.
pg084_n0044_easy_read:
Common problems include short circuits and faulty wiring.
These problems can cause faults and dangers.
So regular checks and maintenance are important.
pg084_n0045_easy_read: 2 devices are useful for checking faults in electrical appliances.
pg084_n0046_easy_read: These devices are the multimeter and the live mains lead indicator.
pg084_n0047_easy_read: A multimeter is a tool for measuring different electrical values.
pg084_n0048_easy_read: The most basic values it measures are voltage and current, both a.c. and d.c.
pg084_n0049_easy_read:
A multimeter also has a range switch.
This helps you take precise readings.
pg084_n0050_easy_read: There are moving-coil multimeters and digital multimeters.
pg084_n0051_easy_read:
Moving-coil multimeters, also called analogue multimeters, are shown in Figure 2.52 (a).
They have some disadvantages because you need to use different settings.
pg084_n0052_easy_read:
The digital multimeter, shown in Figure 2.52 (b), has no moving parts.
So it is easy to use.
pg085_n0003_easy_read: The live mains lead indicator, usually called a tester, is like a screwdriver. It has a hollow insulated handle with a very small neon tube inside.
pg085_n0004_easy_read: 1 electrode of the neon tube usually touches the metal tip of the screwdriver.
pg085_n0005_easy_read: The other electrode is connected to the metal cap on the handle through a high-carbon resistor.
pg085_n0006_easy_read: When a person puts the metal tip into a live socket and touches the metal cap with a finger, current passes through the body to the earth. Then the neon tube glows.
pg085_n0007_easy_read: The resistance is high, so the current is very low. There is no risk of electric shock.
pg085_n0012_easy_read: Most faults in electrical appliances are simple and easy to repair.
pg085_n0013_easy_read: For example, if an electric kettle does not work, first check if the socket has power.
pg085_n0014_easy_read: Use the tester to check this.
pg085_n0015_easy_read: The next step is to check the cable from the socket to the appliance.
pg085_n0016_easy_read: If you do not find a fault, open the plug and check the fuse.
pg085_n0017_easy_read: Also, use a multimeter to check each cable for continuity.
pg085_n0018_easy_read: If these parts work properly, check the heating element next for faults.
pg085_n0019_easy_read: Use a multimeter to check this for continuity or short circuits.
pg085_n0021_easy_read: If the element is faulty, replace it. Repair may not be possible.
pg085_n0022_easy_read: If the element is not faulty, look for loose connections.
pg085_n0024_easy_read: Make the connections firm. Clean off rust and other dirt if needed.
pg085_n0026_easy_read: Repairs in electrical appliances should only be on the connections to the power supply.
pg085_n0027_easy_read: For any repair beyond that, ask an electrical technician.
pg085_n0028_easy_read: Take care to avoid electric shocks during these repairs.
pg085_n0029_easy_read: You can also do simple repairs on electrical connections in a domestic system.
pg085_n0030_easy_read: When a fuse blows, the cause is very likely a fault in an appliance.
pg085_n0031_easy_read: If you find and correct the fault, you can replace the fuse or switch the circuit breaker ON.
pg085_n0033_easy_read:
Other faults happen because of:
- wire cutting
- wire joining
- dirty sockets
- broken switches
pg085_n0034_easy_read: Do all repairs with the mains switched OFF.
pg085_n0035_easy_read: When replacing switches and sockets, follow the colour code strictly.

pg086_n0027_easy_read: A cell is a device that makes electric current flow in a conductor.
pg086_n0028_easy_read: Current flows because reactions release and accept electrons at different ends of a conductor.
pg086_n0029_easy_read:
There are 2 common types of electrochemical cells:
- primary cells
- secondary cells
pg086_n0033_easy_read:
Primary cells are also called voltaic cells.
People make them by putting 2 different electrodes, usually metals, into an electrolyte.
pg086_n0034_easy_read:
In a primary cell, the reactants are used up after some time.
They must be replaced.
pg086_n0035_easy_read: Figure 2.54 shows the parts of a simple primary cell.
pg086_n0045_easy_read:
The electrodes in a simple cell can be copper, which is positive, and zinc, which is negative.
The electrolyte is dilute sulphuric acid.
pg086_n0047_easy_read: These processes happen when the cell is working:
pg086_n0049_easy_read: The dilute sulphuric acid ionises into sulphate ions, S O 4 two minus, and hydrogen ions, H plus:
pg086_n0050_easy_read: H 2 S O 4 yields 2 H plus plus S O 4 two minus
pg086_n0052_easy_read:
Zinc goes into the solution as zinc ions, Z n two plus.
It releases 2 electrons.
The electrons travel along the wire, called the external circuit, to the copper electrode.
pg086_n0053_easy_read: The zinc ions combine with the sulphate ions to form zinc sulphate, Z n S O 4.
pg087_n0003_easy_read:
At the same time, zinc ions go into solution.
The same number of hydrogen ions move to the copper electrode.
There, the hydrogen ions gain electrons and become hydrogen gas bubbles:
pg087_n0004_easy_read: 2 H plus plus 2 e minus yields H 2 gas
pg087_n0006_easy_read:
When copper loses electrons, it becomes positively charged.
Then it attracts electrons from zinc through the connecting wire.
pg087_n0007_easy_read: This movement of electrons through the wire is called electric current.
pg087_n0008_easy_read:
The usual direction of electric current is from the positive terminal to the negative terminal of the cell.
This is the opposite of the direction of electron flow.
pg087_n0012_easy_read:
The Leclanché cell has:
- carbon as the positive electrode
- zinc as the negative electrode
pg087_n0013_easy_read:
The electrolyte in this cell is ammonium chloride (NH4Cl).
It is also called Sal-ammoniac.
pg087_n0015_easy_read:
A dry cell is a changed Leclanché cell.
Its main electrolyte can be a liquid or a paste.
pg087_n0016_easy_read: If the electrolyte is a liquid, the cell is called a wet cell.
pg087_n0017_easy_read: So, the Leclanché cell is a wet cell.
pg087_n0018_easy_read: If the electrolyte is a paste, the cell is called a dry cell.
pg087_n0019_easy_read:
Figure 2.55 shows:
- the internal structure of a dry cell
- different dry cells
pg087_n0025_easy_read: Mixture of manganese chloride and zinc chloride
pg087_n0031_easy_read:
The parts of a dry cell are the same as the parts of the Leclanché cell.
But the dry cell does not use ammonium chloride solution.
Instead, the cell is filled with a paste of manganese dioxide, ammonium chloride, and zinc chloride.
pg087_n0032_easy_read:
The 2 salts below act as the electrolyte:
- ammonium chloride
- zinc chloride
pg087_n0033_easy_read:
The negative electrode is zinc.
It contains the electrolyte and depolarizer.
pg088_n0006_easy_read: A battery is made when 2 or more cells are connected.
pg088_n0007_easy_read: Cells can be connected in series or in parallel.

pg089_n0039_easy_read: A simple cell has 2 main defects. These defects make the current decrease quickly when the cell is being used.
pg089_n0040_easy_read: The 2 defects are local action and polarization.
pg089_n0044_easy_read: Local action in a cell is damage to the battery. It happens because currents flow from and to the same electrode.
pg089_n0045_easy_read:
This damage is caused by impurities in a zinc electrode, such as:
- iron
- lead
- carbon
pg089_n0046_easy_read: The impurities act like positive electrodes. They create electric currents between the zinc and this positive electrode.
pg089_n0047_easy_read: You can reduce local action by using pure zinc. You can also rub mercury on the zinc plate to form an amalgam.
pg089_n0051_easy_read: Polarization is a defect in simple electric cells. It happens because hydrogen gas builds up around a positive electrode.
pg089_n0052_easy_read: The hydrogen gas is produced by chemical reactions inside the cell. The gas can build up around the electrodes and cause insulation.
pg089_n0053_easy_read:
You can reduce polarization in cells by using depolarizers, such as:
- potassium dichromate
- manganese oxide
These oxidize hydrogen to water.

pg090_n0004_easy_read: These are all called primary cells.
pg090_n0005_easy_read: In this type of cell, the current comes from chemical reactions that cannot be reversed.
pg090_n0006_easy_read: For example, in a simple cell, all the zinc can dissolve. If this happens, the zinc cannot return to its original form by passing current through the cell in the opposite direction.
pg090_n0010_easy_read: Secondary cells are different from primary cells. You can recharge them after they run down.
pg090_n0011_easy_read: Examples of secondary cells are the lead-acid cell and the nickel-ferrous cell.
pg090_n0012_easy_read: Secondary cells are also called accumulators.
pg090_n0016_easy_read: A lead-acid battery is made of several lead-acid cells.
pg090_n0017_easy_read: Each cell has 2 groups of lead plates.
pg090_n0018_easy_read: 1 group makes the positive terminal. The other group makes the negative terminal.
pg090_n0019_easy_read: All the positive terminal plates are joined by a connecting strap.
pg090_n0020_easy_read: The negative terminal plates are connected in the same way.
pg090_n0021_easy_read: The positive and negative terminal plates are connected in an alternating order.
pg090_n0022_easy_read: Sheets of insulating material are placed between the plates. These sheets are called separators.
pg090_n0023_easy_read: The separators are made of porous wood or fibreglass.
pg090_n0024_easy_read: The separators stop the positive and negative plates from touching. This prevents a short circuit.
pg090_n0025_easy_read: The positive plates are made of lead dioxide. The negative plates are made of porous lead metal.
pg090_n0026_easy_read: The 2 sets of plates are placed in a container. Separators are between the plates. The container is filled with a dilute solution of sulphuric acid.
pg090_n0027_easy_read: The name lead-acid refers to the lead plates and the sulphuric acid. These are the main parts of the battery.
pg090_n0028_easy_read: Figure 2.59 shows the parts of the lead-acid accumulator.
pg090_n0043_easy_read: When the battery gives energy, it is discharging.
pg090_n0044_easy_read: The energy is produced when the acid (electrolyte) slowly combines with the active material of the electrodes.
pg090_n0045_easy_read: This makes the sulphuric acid less concentrated.
pg090_n0047_easy_read: Charging a lead-acid battery means driving all the acid out of the plates and returning it to the electrolyte.
pg090_n0048_easy_read: During charging (Figure 2.60(b)), direct current passes through the battery in the opposite direction from the direction during discharge (Figure 2.60(a)).
pg090_n0049_easy_read: The negative terminal of the battery charger connects to the negative terminal of the battery. The positive terminal of the charger connects to the positive terminal of the battery.
pg090_n0050_easy_read: This reverses the discharge process and restores the battery to its
pg091_n0004_easy_read: When the battery is fully charged, the active material on the positive plates is lead peroxide. The active material on the negative plate is porous lead metal.
pg091_n0005_easy_read: The acid concentration is highest when the battery is charged.
pg091_n0014_easy_read: Porous lead changes to lead sulphate.
pg091_n0015_easy_read: Lead peroxide changes to lead sulphate.
pg091_n0021_easy_read: The electrolyte returns to its normal strength.
pg091_n0024_easy_read: Lead sulphate changes to porous lead.
pg091_n0025_easy_read: Lead sulphate changes to lead peroxide.
pg091_n0029_easy_read: If the battery is only partly discharged, you can recharge it with a battery charger, as shown in Figure 2.61(b).
pg091_n0030_easy_read: Do not let lead-acid batteries become completely discharged.
pg091_n0031_easy_read: The maximum recommended discharge is 75% of the maximum voltage, depending on the type of battery.
pg091_n0032_easy_read: When the battery is completely discharged, both electrodes change fully into lead sulphate.
pg091_n0033_easy_read: In this state, the battery is called sulphated. It will no longer work because it cannot be recharged.
pg091_n0034_easy_read: The main advantage of the lead-acid accumulator is that you can recharge it.
pg091_n0035_easy_read: The main disadvantages are its large size and weight.

pg092_n0035_easy_read: If people take good care of lead-acid batteries, the batteries can last a long time.
pg092_n0036_easy_read: Here are some guidelines for taking care of lead-acid batteries:

pg095_n0008_easy_read: Electromotive force (e.m.f) is the highest potential difference between the 2 terminals of a battery or a cell when no current is taken from the battery or cell.
pg095_n0009_easy_read: In other words, it is the electrical pressure produced by a source of electrical energy.
pg095_n0012_easy_read: Electric potential difference (p.d) is the work done per unit charge to move electric charge from 1 point to another point in a conductor.
pg095_n0015_easy_read: Electric current, I, is the rate at which electric charge, Q, passes a given point. The unit is the ampere, A. An ammeter measures electric current.
pg095_n0018_easy_read: Resistance is the opposition to the flow of electric current in a conductor.
pg095_n0022_easy_read:
The resistance of a conductor depends on:
- temperature
- length
- cross-sectional area
- the material of the conductor
pg095_n0025_easy_read: When resistors are connected in series, the total resistance in the circuit is the sum of the individual resistances.
pg095_n0028_easy_read: When resistors are connected in parallel, the reciprocal of the total resistance is the sum of the reciprocals of the individual resistances.
pg095_n0031_easy_read: When electric current flows through a conductor with high resistance, electrical energy changes into thermal energy and heats the conductor.
pg095_n0032_easy_read: This is called the heating effect of electric current.
pg095_n0035_easy_read: Every electrical appliance should have a label. The label should state the potential difference the appliance was designed for and the power it can convert when it works at that potential difference.
pg095_n0038_easy_read: Electricity is supplied in consumers’ places through low-resistance wire made of copper or aluminium and covered with plastic insulation.
pg095_n0041_easy_read: The wires used in electrical installation are rated by the maximum current they can carry.

pg100_n0009_easy_read: Knowledge of magnetism has led to many useful uses in daily life, from Greek navigation in the past to the digital world today.
pg100_n0010_easy_read:
In this chapter, you will learn what magnetism is.
You will also learn how materials can become magnetised or demagnetised.
pg100_n0011_easy_read: You will also learn about magnetic fields, including the Earth's magnetic field.
pg100_n0012_easy_read: The skills you develop will help you use knowledge of magnetism in different situations.
pg100_n0019_easy_read:
Magnetism is a phenomenon caused by moving electric charges.
It creates forces that make objects attract or repel each other.
pg100_n0020_easy_read:
The first recorded observation of magnetism was in 600 BC.
The Greek philosopher Thales recorded it.
pg100_n0021_easy_read: Thales observed that pieces of iron were attracted to a natural iron ore mineral called magnetite.
pg100_n0022_easy_read: A lodestone is a magnetised piece of the mineral magnetite.
pg100_n0027_easy_read: A lodestone attracts some metals more strongly at certain points on its surface than at other points.
pg100_n0028_easy_read: Any material with properties like a lodestone is called a magnet.
pg100_n0029_easy_read: When magnets attract or repel each other, they apply a force called magnetic force.
pg100_n0030_easy_read: Magnetism comes from 2 types of electron motion, as shown in Figure 3.2.
pg100_n0031_easy_read: The first type is the movement of electrons around the nucleus of an atom.
pg100_n0032_easy_read: The second type of motion is the spin of electrons around their own axes.
pg100_n0033_easy_read:
These motions of charged particles each create a magnetic effect.
Because of this, an atom behaves like a tiny magnet.
pg101_n0007_easy_read: Figure 3.2: The orbit of a spinning electron around the nucleus of an atom
pg101_n0009_easy_read:
In many atoms, these magnetic effects cancel each other out.
In other atoms, they do not cancel completely.
pg101_n0013_easy_read:
When a magnet is near different objects, some objects are attracted or repelled.
Other objects are not affected.
pg101_n0014_easy_read: Objects that are attracted are said to have induced magnetism.
pg101_n0015_easy_read:
A material can become a magnet when it is close to or touching a magnet.
This process is called induction.
pg101_n0016_easy_read: Induced magnetism can be temporary or permanent after the magnet is removed.
pg101_n0017_easy_read: The type of material being magnetised decides how long the induced magnetism lasts.
pg101_n0018_easy_read:
For example, iron has temporary magnetism.
Materials like steel keep their magnetism for a long time.
pg101_n0019_easy_read: Materials that are not affected by a magnet are called non-magnetic materials.

pg101_n0041_easy_read: Magnetic materials are materials that can be magnetised even by weak magnets.
pg101_n0042_easy_read: Materials that are attracted to a magnet and can be strongly magnetised are called ferromagnetic materials.
pg101_n0043_easy_read:
Ferromagnetic materials contain:
- iron
- nickel
- cobalt
pg101_n0044_easy_read:
These materials are grouped as magnetically hard or magnetically soft.
This depends on how well they keep their magnetism after magnetisation.
pg101_n0046_easy_read:
Magnetically hard materials such as steel do not lose their magnetism easily.
But they are difficult to magnetise.
pg101_n0047_easy_read: Magnetically hard materials are used to make permanent magnets.
pg101_n0048_easy_read:
Soft magnetic materials like iron can be magnetised easily.

pg107_n0034_easy_read: People make magnets by lining up the tiny atomic magnets in a material.
pg107_n0035_easy_read: The process of making a magnet is called magnetisation.
pg107_n0036_easy_read: Demagnetisation is the process of removing or destroying the magnetism in a magnetised material.
pg107_n0040_easy_read:
The atoms in most materials act like tiny magnets.
These tiny magnets are called atomic dipoles.
pg107_n0041_easy_read:
If the material is not magnetised yet, its atomic dipoles line up at random.
This forms magnetic domains, as shown in Figure 3.16.
pg107_n0045_easy_read: Figure 3.16: Random alignment of atomic dipoles in unmagnetised material
pg108_n0005_easy_read: A material is magnetised when the N poles of its atomic dipoles face in the same direction.
pg108_n0008_easy_read: Magnetisation is the process of lining up the atomic dipoles in a material in 1 direction. This creates an overall effect of attraction or repulsion.
pg108_n0010_easy_read: The domains can show an overall magnetic effect even without an external magnetic field.
pg108_n0011_easy_read: When an external magnetic field is applied, all dipoles line up in the direction of that field.
pg108_n0012_easy_read: In this way, the material becomes strongly magnetised in a direction parallel to the magnetising field, as shown in Figure 3.17.
pg108_n0015_easy_read: Figure 3.17: Atomic dipoles lined up in a magnetised material
pg108_n0017_easy_read: Materials that can be made to line up in this way are either ferromagnetic or paramagnetic.
pg108_n0018_easy_read: Ferromagnetic materials, such as steel, nickel, and cobalt, can become permanent magnets. Paramagnetic materials, such as aluminium and chromium, can only be magnetised weakly. They lose their magnetism when the external field is removed.
pg108_n0019_easy_read:
The domains in these materials can be lined up in 1 of these ways:
- heating or vibration
- stroking
- the electric method
pg108_n0021_easy_read: In the 1st method of magnetisation, an external magnetic field is needed.
pg108_n0022_easy_read: If you place an object in an external magnetic field, some alignment will happen.
pg108_n0023_easy_read: Heating or vibrating the object can increase the alignment. This happens because the atomic dipoles move and then line up.
pg108_n0024_easy_read: Many natural magnetic materials first form as part of lava (molten rock).
pg108_n0025_easy_read: If the lava contains ferromagnetic minerals, the atoms line up with the Earth’s magnetic field while the rock is still liquid and vibrating.
pg108_n0026_easy_read: As the rock cools and becomes solid, the alignment becomes permanent.

pg112_n0012_easy_read: Demagnetisation is the process of removing the magnetic property of a material.
pg112_n0014_easy_read: This process destroys the dipole alignment in the magnetised material.
pg112_n0015_easy_read: You can do this process in the following ways:
pg112_n0019_easy_read: If a permanent magnet is heated or vibrated without an external field, its magnetisation can be destroyed.

pg113_n0037_easy_read: To keep magnets magnetic for a long time, follow these practices:

pg116_n0045_easy_read:

pg117_n0004_easy_read: Magnetic lines of force enter the south pole and return to the north pole. They form a closed loop.

pg117_n0020_easy_read: 6. Magnetic lines of force pass through magnetic and non-magnetic materials.

pg122_n0003_easy_read:
Earth has 2 geographic poles, north and south.
Its axis of rotation defines them.
Earth also has 2 magnetic poles, north and south.
Its magnetic field defines them.
pg122_n0004_easy_read:
The magnetic pole in the Northern Hemisphere is magnetically a south pole.
It is called the Magnetic South Pole (MSP).
The magnetic pole in the Southern Hemisphere is called the Magnetic North Pole (MNP).

pg122_n0012_easy_read:

- magnitude
- direction
pg122_n0013_easy_read: The SI unit for the magnitude of a magnetic field is the tesla, T.
pg122_n0014_easy_read:
The magnitude of Earth’s magnetic field changes from place to place.
It ranges from 25µT to 65µT.
pg122_n0015_easy_read: You can use a compass to find the direction of Earth’s magnetic field.
pg122_n0016_easy_read:
A compass is a device with a magnetised needle.
The needle can turn freely in a horizontal plane.
It lines up with the horizontal part of Earth’s magnetic field.
pg122_n0017_easy_read:
The head of a compass needle is a magnetic north pole.
The tail is a magnetic south pole.
pg122_n0019_easy_read:
The compass needle points toward the north pole.
This means it points toward Earth’s MSP.
pg122_n0020_easy_read: So, a compass needle points in the general north direction of Earth, as shown in Figure 3.46.
pg122_n0021_easy_read:
For this reason, the magnetic north pole of the compass needle is called a north-seeking pole.
The general direction it shows is often called "magnetic north".
pg122_n0028_easy_read:
If you hang a magnet so it can swing freely in a horizontal direction, it moves back and forth for a short time.
Then it comes to rest in an approximate N–S direction.
pg122_n0029_easy_read:
The magnet comes to rest with its axis in a vertical plane.
This plane is called the magnetic meridian.
pg123_n0003_easy_read: Like a compass needle, the pole that points north is the north-seeking pole (N pole). The other pole is the south-seeking pole (S pole).

If we place a compass on its side, its needle can turn in a vertical plane.
Then the needle lines up with the Earth's magnetic field.
pg125_n0008_easy_read:
The angle between the direction of the magnetic field and its horizontal part is called the angle of inclination, or dip angle.
It is written as I.
pg125_n0010_easy_read:
This angle is positive when the magnetic field vector points downward, as in the Northern Hemisphere.
This angle is negative when the magnetic field vector points upward, as in the Southern Hemisphere.
pg125_n0011_easy_read: The angle of inclination goes from 0° at the magnetic equator to 90° at the magnetic poles.
pg125_n0012_easy_read:
We measure it with a dip needle.
A dip needle is a magnetised needle on a pivot.
The pivot lets the needle turn freely in a vertical plane, as shown in Figure 3.53.
pg125_n0016_easy_read:
In practice, a compass lines up the dip needle with the horizontal part of the magnetic field.
Then the dip needle turns vertically to line up with the total magnetic field.
pg125_n0017_easy_read:
The magnetic dip creates a vertical turning effect.
This makes the needle in a compass turn vertically.
pg125_n0018_easy_read:
This vertical turning creates friction in the pivot.
This friction makes it harder for the needle to turn freely.
pg125_n0019_easy_read:
To balance the dip, a small mass is added to 1 end of the needle.
This mass creates an opposite gravitational turning effect.
This keeps the needle balanced vertically.
pg125_n0020_easy_read:
In a compass for the northern hemisphere, the vertical component points down.
So the mass is added to the tail end of the needle.
pg125_n0021_easy_read:
In a compass for the southern hemisphere, the vertical component points up.
So the mass is added to the head end of the needle.

pg130_n0026_easy_read: Light is a form of energy that makes vision possible.
pg130_n0028_easy_read: Light has some clear features that make it different from other forms of energy.
pg130_n0032_easy_read: 1. Light comes out from its source.
pg130_n0033_easy_read: Lines called light rays show the direction of light.
pg130_n0035_easy_read: 2. Light travels in a straight line.
pg130_n0036_easy_read: This means we can see light as a beam of light.
pg130_n0037_easy_read: A beam is a group of rays.
pg130_n0040_easy_read: Objects gain energy when they absorb light.
pg130_n0041_easy_read: For example, solar panels absorb light.
pg131_n0003_easy_read: They take energy from the Sun (solar energy) and change it into electrical energy.
pg131_n0005_easy_read: Light does not need a material medium to travel.
pg131_n0006_easy_read: 5. Light travels at 3 times 10 to the power of 8 metres per second. This is the highest speed recorded on Earth.
pg131_n0010_easy_read: Light sources can be put into 2 main types: natural and artificial.
pg131_n0011_easy_read: Some objects are luminous. This means they make their own light. Other objects are non-luminous. They only reflect or scatter light from other sources.
pg131_n0012_easy_read: Bioluminescence is a natural event in some glowing organisms. It is common especially in dark forests.

Rectilinear propagation of light is a basic principle.
It means that light travels in straight lines in a uniform medium.
pg134_n0016_easy_read:
This principle is very important when people design optical devices, such as cameras, telescopes, and lasers.
These devices need light to follow exact paths to work properly.
pg134_n0017_easy_read:
The idea of rectilinear propagation of light helps us understand how light behaves.
So it is important in science and in practical uses.

Light travels through matter in different ways.
This ability changes from one substance to another.
pg134_n0036_easy_read:
When light travels through matter, it is called transmitted.
This means passed through.
pg134_n0037_easy_read:
When we talk about light transmission, materials are put into 3 groups:
- transparent materials
- translucent materials
- opaque materials
pg134_n0040_easy_read: Transparent materials allow light to pass through them.
pg134_n0041_easy_read: You can see through transparent materials clearly, as shown in Figure 4.3.
pg135_n0004_easy_read:
Examples are:
- glass panes of windows
- glass slabs
- prisms
- clear plastics
pg135_n0008_easy_read: Figure 4.3: Light passing through transparent material
pg135_n0010_easy_read: Translucent materials let only some light pass through them. They do not let enough light through to make a clear image.
pg135_n0011_easy_read: This happens because light rays spread out when they pass through the material, as shown in Figure 4.4.
pg135_n0012_easy_read: Oiled paper and tinted frosted glass are examples of translucent materials.
pg135_n0013_easy_read: Tinted glass is used in car windows.
pg135_n0014_easy_read: Some glass windows in houses are frosted for privacy.
pg135_n0015_easy_read: You cannot see clearly through a translucent material.
pg135_n0019_easy_read: Figure 4.4: Light passing through translucent material
pg135_n0021_easy_read: Opaque materials are materials that block all light, as shown in Figure 4.5.
pg135_n0022_easy_read:
These are examples of opaque materials:
- a block of concrete
- wood
- a book
- a wall
- a human body

pg135_n0036_easy_read: When an opaque object is in the path of a beam of light, a dark area forms behind the object.
pg135_n0037_easy_read: Little or no light reaches this area because the opaque object does not let light pass through it.
pg135_n0038_easy_read: This area is called a shadow.
pg135_n0039_easy_read: A shadow forms because light travels in straight lines.
pg135_n0040_easy_read: Shadows have sharp edges, as shown in Figure 4.6.
pg136_n0003_easy_read: The type of shadow changes with the size of the light source.

pg136_n0005_easy_read: An extended source of light makes a shadow that is not even.

pg136_n0008_easy_read: The Sun is an example of an extended source of light.
pg136_n0009_easy_read: The shadow from an extended source of light is blurred at the edges.

pg137_n0043_easy_read: We see objects because they reflect the light that falls on them.
pg137_n0044_easy_read:
When light rays fall on the surface of an object, the light is:
- absorbed
- transmitted
- reflected
pg137_n0045_easy_read: Sometimes, 2 or more of these processes happen together.
pg137_n0046_easy_read: When light hits a surface, the way the light is reflected depends on the type of surface.
pg137_n0049_easy_read: Reflection of light is when light rays bounce back after they hit a smooth, polished surface like a mirror.
pg137_n0051_easy_read:
People usually cannot see behind themselves.
But with a mirror, they can see an object that is coming from behind.
pg137_n0052_easy_read:
This happens because light from the object falls on the mirror.
Then the mirror reflects the light back to the observer’s eyes.
pg138_n0003_easy_read: So, when light bounces back from a mirror, this is called reflection.
pg138_n0004_easy_read: We can see an object because the object gives off light or reflects light.
pg138_n0006_easy_read: When you use a plane mirror, a reflected ray bounces off the mirror.
pg138_n0007_easy_read: A plane mirror is a thin piece of glass. Its bottom or back surface is covered with silver to make a shiny surface that reflects light.
pg138_n0008_easy_read: Figure 4.9 shows how light rays reflect from a plane mirror.
pg138_n0009_easy_read: A polished metal surface can also reflect light rays like a plane mirror.
pg138_n0015_easy_read: Figure 4.9: Reflection of light on a plane mirror
pg138_n0019_easy_read:
There are 2 types of reflection:
- regular, or specular, reflection
- irregular, or diffuse, reflection
pg138_n0023_easy_read: In regular reflection, the surface is very smooth. So the image of the object is very clear.
pg138_n0024_easy_read: In regular reflection, all the reflected rays go in 1 direction.
pg138_n0025_easy_read: The rays are also parallel, as Figure 4.10 shows.
pg138_n0026_easy_read:
Examples of these surfaces are:
- mirrors
- polished metal surfaces
- highly reflective aluminium sheets
pg138_n0028_easy_read: When you look at the image of an object in a plane mirror, light rays come from the object. The rays travel in parallel in a straight line to the mirror.
pg138_n0029_easy_read: After reflection, the same rays reach the eye. They seem to come from the image, so the image looks very sharp.
pg138_n0037_easy_read: Irregular reflection is reflection that happens when light rays hit a rough surface.
pg138_n0038_easy_read: Figure 4.11 shows this. The incident light rays reflect in different directions.
pg138_n0039_easy_read: In irregular reflection, the reflected rays are not parallel. They spread in many directions.
pg138_n0048_easy_read: Reflection is a basic part of how light behaves. It is also a foundation for the study of
pg139_n0004_easy_read: When light hits a surface, it changes direction in a clear way. It follows rules called the laws of reflection.
pg139_n0005_easy_read: These laws explain how light acts when it hits reflective surfaces, such as mirrors (Figure 4.12). They also show the path of the reflected rays.
pg139_n0006_easy_read: These laws are important for understanding how optical systems work. They are also useful in astronomy and in everyday technology, such as periscopes, cameras, and fibre optics.
pg139_n0007_easy_read: Activity 4.4 helps you explore the laws of reflection of light by experiment.

pg139_n0024_easy_read: The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.
pg139_n0025_easy_read: This means the angle where the incoming light ray hits a surface is the same as the angle where the light ray reflects away.
pg139_n0028_easy_read: The incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal to the reflective surface are all in the same plane.
pg139_n0030_easy_read: This means the reflection stays in 1 flat plane. This plane is made by the light ray and the line that is at 90° to the surface at the point where the light hits.

pg141_n0019_easy_read: A plane mirror is a simple piece of glass with a flat surface.
pg141_n0020_easy_read: The only difference from other glass is that the back of the mirror has been silvered.
pg141_n0021_easy_read: The image formed by a plane mirror has several characteristics.
pg141_n0025_easy_read: 1. The image formed is virtual (not real).
pg141_n0027_easy_read: When an object is in front of a plane mirror, its image appears behind the mirror.
pg141_n0028_easy_read: This image is called virtual, or not real, because it is in a place where light does not reach, even though it seems to.
pg141_n0029_easy_read: To the observer, it only seems that the light comes from this point.
pg141_n0033_easy_read:
If you stand in front of a plane mirror, your image looks upright.
Your head appears at the top and your feet appear at the bottom.
pg141_n0034_easy_read: This is because plane mirrors form upright images, not inverted images.
pg141_n0036_easy_read: 3. The image is the same size as the object.
pg141_n0038_easy_read: The image of an object in front of a plane mirror is the same size as the object.
pg141_n0039_easy_read: The ratio of image size to object size is called magnification.
pg141_n0040_easy_read: Plane mirrors make images with a magnification of 1.
pg141_n0042_easy_read: 4. The image is the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front of the mirror.
pg141_n0044_easy_read: If you stand 3 metres from a plane mirror, you must focus 3 metres behind the mirror to see your image.
pg141_n0046_easy_read: 5. The image has a left-right reversal.
pg141_n0048_easy_read: If you look at your image in a plane mirror, you will notice that it appears laterally inverted.
pg141_n0049_easy_read: This means that, for example, when you raise your left hand, the image seems to raise its right hand.
pg141_n0050_easy_read: If you are wearing a shirt with the word WAY, it will appear as YAW.
pg142_n0003_easy_read: The order and direction of the letters are reversed.
pg142_n0005_easy_read:
These letters look the same in a plane mirror:
- A
- H
- I
- M
- O
- T
- U
- V
- W
- X
- Y
pg142_n0007_easy_read: This means that if we cut the letters in half, both halves will look the same.
pg142_n0008_easy_read: The letter will not look different when it is flipped sideways.
pg142_n0010_easy_read: Lateral inversion means that the image turns 180° around the vertical axis. So the right side of the object looks like the left side, and the left side looks like the right side.
pg142_n0011_easy_read: For example, if a card has the word REEL on it, the mirror shows it as ⅃ƎƎЯ.

pg163_n0005_easy_read: Curved mirrors have many uses in daily life.
pg163_n0006_easy_read:
Some uses need concave mirrors.
Other uses need convex mirrors.
pg163_n0010_easy_read:
Convex mirrors give a wide view compared to other mirrors.
They make images look smaller.
pg163_n0011_easy_read: So, people use convex mirrors when a wide view is more important than a large image.
pg163_n0012_easy_read: Here are some uses of convex mirrors:
pg163_n0014_easy_read: People use convex mirrors as side mirrors on cars.
pg163_n0015_easy_read: This lets the driver see a wide area behind the car, as shown in Figure 4.33.
pg163_n0016_easy_read: However, these mirrors make objects look farther away than they really are.
pg163_n0017_easy_read: This happens because the image always forms between the mirror and the focal point of the mirror, no matter how far away the object is.
pg163_n0018_easy_read: So, images look small, and the brain understands smaller images as being farther away.
pg163_n0020_easy_read: Figure 4.33: A side mirror of a car
pg163_n0022_easy_read:
Reflecting light in streetlights:
A convex mirror acts as a reflector in street lamps.
pg163_n0023_easy_read: Because the convex mirror gives a wide view, light from the lamp spreads over a larger area.
pg163_n0024_easy_read: Figure 4.34 shows light spreading out from the streetlights.
pg163_n0026_easy_read: Figure 4.34: Light spreading out from a streetlight
pg163_n0028_easy_read:
Seeing around corners:
People place convex mirrors at road junctions and at corners in places like parking lots and supermarkets.
pg163_n0029_easy_read: This helps people see around corners and avoid collisions between vehicles or supermarket trolleys.
pg163_n0030_easy_read: Figure 4.35 shows a convex mirror used as a safety mirror at a road junction.
pg163_n0032_easy_read: Figure 4.35: A safety convex mirror around a corner
pg164_n0005_easy_read: Security and investigation: Convex mirrors have a wide field of view. So people use them to watch business places and security areas.
pg164_n0006_easy_read: Figure 4.36 shows an example of a convex mirror used for security.
pg164_n0008_easy_read: Figure 4.36: A convex security mirror in a shop
pg164_n0012_easy_read:
Concave mirrors are useful because they can:
- make images look larger
- focus weak light
- produce a parallel beam of light
pg164_n0013_easy_read: Here are some uses of concave mirrors:
pg164_n0015_easy_read: Headlights in a car: A strong light source is placed at the focal point of a concave mirror. It is in a small space at the back of the headlight.
pg164_n0016_easy_read: Light that hits the mirror from the focus is reflected parallel to the axis of the concave mirror.
pg164_n0017_easy_read: This makes a strong beam of light in front of the car, as shown in Figure 4.37.
pg164_n0021_easy_read: Dentist’s mirror: A concave mirror helps the dentist focus light on the tooth inside the mouth.
pg164_n0022_easy_read: Figure 4.38 shows a dentist’s mirror being used to examine a tooth.
pg164_n0024_easy_read: Figure 4.38: A dentist’s mirror in use
pg164_n0026_easy_read: Shaving mirrors: A concave mirror makes the image larger and upright when the object is between the principal focus and the pole.
pg164_n0027_easy_read: So, people use concave mirrors as shaving mirrors. The mirror makes the face look larger when the face is held within the focus of the mirror.
pg164_n0028_easy_read: Figure 4.39 shows a concave mirror that is used as a shaving mirror.
pg165_n0005_easy_read: Reflecting telescopes: A concave mirror, called the primary mirror, forms images of distant stars at the focal point.
pg165_n0006_easy_read: Then a plane mirror, called the secondary mirror, sends the rays to the side. There, you can see the image through a lens, as shown in Figure 4.40.
pg165_n0016_easy_read: Sometimes, light reflecting from concave surfaces is used for more than light and image formation. The uses are listed below:
pg165_n0017_easy_read: Satellite dishes: A satellite dish is a special antenna. It is made to receive and send signals to and from satellites in orbit.
pg166_n0003_easy_read: Parabolic solar cookers: These solar cookers turn sunlight directly into heat. They do this by concentrating sunlight with reflectors in a parabolic shape.
pg166_n0004_easy_read: Figure 4.42 shows a parabolic solar cooker.

The principles, theories, and concepts of light refraction are an important part of daily life.
They affect natural events and new technology.
pg169_n0008_easy_read:
Key applications are:
- correcting vision
- designing optical instruments
- using optical fibres
- creating different colours with prisms and rainbows
- developing magnifying tools
pg169_n0009_easy_read: In this chapter, you will explore how light refracts through glass prisms and lenses.
pg169_n0010_easy_read: The skills you develop will help you design optical instruments and use them in different situations.
pg169_n0013_easy_read: Why optical fibres are important in daily life
pg169_n0017_easy_read: In the previous chapter, you learnt that light travels in a straight line as it moves through a medium.
pg169_n0018_easy_read: However, when light passes from one medium to another medium, the light beam bends.
pg169_n0019_easy_read: The bending of light is called refraction of light.
pg169_n0020_easy_read: The direction of a ray of light changes as it passes at an angle from one medium into another.
pg169_n0022_easy_read: Refraction happens because different media have different optical densities.
pg169_n0023_easy_read: If light moves more slowly in 1 medium than in another medium, the first medium has a higher optical density than the second medium.
pg169_n0024_easy_read: So, you can find the optical density of a medium by using the speed of light in that medium.
pg169_n0025_easy_read: Refraction happens only at a boundary.
pg169_n0026_easy_read: After light crosses the boundary between 2 media, it continues to travel in a straight line.

pg170_n0038_easy_read: When light passes from a medium like air into another medium like glass, which is optically denser, its speed decreases.
pg170_n0039_easy_read: In contrast, when light passes from an optically denser medium like glass to an optically less dense medium like air, its speed increases.
pg170_n0040_easy_read: The line that is at 90° to the boundary between the 2 media is called the normal line.
pg170_n0041_easy_read:
The light ray in the first medium is called the incident ray.
The light ray in the second medium is called the refracted ray.
pg170_n0042_easy_read:
The angle between the incident ray and the normal line is called the angle of incidence.
It is shown by the letter i.
pg170_n0043_easy_read:
The angle between the refracted ray and the normal line is called the angle of refraction.
It is shown by the letter r.

pg171_n0015_easy_read: Refraction of light in a glass prism
pg171_n0017_easy_read:
Glass prisms have different shapes.
These include:
- rectangular
- triangular
pg171_n0018_easy_read:
Refraction happens when light passes through a prism.
The light bends at the surfaces because its speed changes when it enters and leaves the glass.
pg171_n0019_easy_read:
When light enters the prism from air, it slows down.
It bends towards the normal line.
The normal line is at 90° to the surface where the light enters.
pg171_n0020_easy_read:
When light leaves the prism and goes back into the air, it speeds up.
It bends away from the normal.
pg171_n0022_easy_read: Refraction of light in a rectangular prism
pg171_n0024_easy_read: When a light ray moves from air into a rectangular glass prism, the light bends where it enters the glass.
pg171_n0025_easy_read:
Inside the prism, the light moves in a straight line.
Then it reaches the opposite side.
There, the light bends again as it leaves the glass and goes back into the air.
pg171_n0026_easy_read:
The opposite sides of a rectangular glass prism are parallel.

pg173_n0014_easy_read: When a beam of light passes between 2 different media at an interface, it bends.
pg173_n0015_easy_read:
How much the light bends depends on:
- the optical density of the 2 media
- the angle of incidence of the light beam
pg173_n0016_easy_read: Note that the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction change in proportion to the difference in the optical densities of the 2 media.
pg173_n0017_easy_read: If a light ray passes from a less optically dense medium to a more optically dense medium, the ray bends towards the normal.
pg173_n0018_easy_read: However, if the light ray travels from a medium with higher optical density to a medium with lower optical density, the ray bends away from the normal.
pg173_n0019_easy_read: Experiments show that 2 laws control how a light ray behaves when it hits the interface between 2 media with different optical densities.
pg173_n0020_easy_read: These laws are called the laws of refraction of light.

pg174_n0080_easy_read: You can make several deductions from the results of the experiment above:
pg174_n0083_easy_read: 1. When the pins are set in a line and viewed from 1 side, they appear to be in a line.
pg174_n0084_easy_read: The same happens when you view the pins from the other side.
