This shows the principle of reversibility of light.
This means that "light will follow exactly the same path if its direction of travel is reversed".
pg174_n0086_easy_read:
In a rectangular glass prism, the law of reversibility of light means this:
If i is the angle of incidence from air to glass, and r is the angle of refraction, then r becomes the angle of incidence from glass to air, and i becomes the angle of refraction.
pg174_n0088_easy_read:
2. When a ray of light travels from air to glass, it moves from an optically less dense medium to a denser medium.
At the boundary between the 2 media, the ray bends towards the normal.
pg174_n0089_easy_read: In contrast, when a ray of light travels from glass to air, it moves from an optically denser
pg175_n0003_easy_read: When light moves from a denser medium to a less dense medium, it bends away from the normal.
pg175_n0004_easy_read: 3. The ratio sine of i divided by sine of r stays the same for different angles of incidence.
pg175_n0005_easy_read: 4. Points E and F, the normal line, the incident ray, and the refracted ray are all on the same plane.
pg175_n0006_easy_read: This may have been hard to see at first.
pg175_n0007_easy_read: However, you can see this after you set the pins in a line and lift 1 edge of the glass block above the other edge.
pg175_n0008_easy_read: You will quickly see that pins A, B, C and D are no longer in a straight line.
pg175_n0009_easy_read: These important observations lead to 2 important conclusions. These conclusions are the laws of refraction of light.
pg175_n0011_easy_read: (a) At the point of incidence, the incident ray, the normal line, and the refracted ray are all on the same plane.
pg175_n0012_easy_read: (b) For a particular material, the ratio sine of i divided by sine of r stays constant.
pg175_n0013_easy_read: This law is also called Snell’s law of refraction.
pg175_n0017_easy_read: In Activity 5.4, you observed that for a given material or medium, the ratio sine of i divided by sine of r stays constant, whatever the size of the angle of incidence.
pg175_n0018_easy_read: This constant is called the refractive index of the material or medium.
pg175_n0019_easy_read: It is a dimensionless constant. This means it has no unit. It is written with the Greek letter eta.
pg175_n0020_easy_read: The refractive index of a material shows how the material affects the speed of light as light passes through it.
pg175_n0021_easy_read: Therefore, you can also find the refractive index of a material from the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum, c, to the speed of light in the material, v.
pg175_n0023_easy_read: That is, eta equals c over v.
pg175_n0025_easy_read: More specifically, the ratio eta equals c over v is called the absolute refractive index of a material.
pg175_n0026_easy_read: If the ratio uses the speed of light v sub 1 in 1 material and the speed of light v sub 2 in another material, then eta equals v sub 1 over v sub 2.
pg175_n0028_easy_read: In this case, the ratio is called the relative refractive index.
pg175_n0030_easy_read: Usually, the speed of light in air is taken as the speed of light in vacuum, c.
pg175_n0031_easy_read: Therefore, if light travels from air to water and from air to glass, it has different speeds in water and glass because air, water, and glass have different optical densities.
pg175_n0032_easy_read: If the speed of light in water is v sub 1 and the speed of light in glass is v sub 2, you can calculate the absolute refractive indices of water and glass as follows:
pg175_n0034_easy_read: The absolute refractive index of water:
pg175_n0035_easy_read: eta sub 1 equals c over v sub 1
pg175_n0036_easy_read: This implies that c equals eta sub 1 v sub 1.
pg175_n0038_easy_read: The absolute refractive index of glass:
pg175_n0039_easy_read: eta sub 2 equals c over v sub 2
pg175_n0040_easy_read: This implies that c equals eta sub 2 v sub 2.
pg176_n0003_easy_read: So, c equals eta sub 1 v sub 1 equals eta sub 2 v sub 2
pg176_n0004_easy_read: So, eta sub 1 v sub 1 equals eta sub 2 v sub 2
pg176_n0005_easy_read: We can rearrange this expression as follows:
pg176_n0006_easy_read: eta sub 2 over eta sub 1 equals v sub 1 over v sub 2
pg176_n0007_easy_read: The ratio eta sub 2 over eta sub 1 is the relative refractive index of glass to water.
pg176_n0008_easy_read: This ratio also relates to the ratio of the sines of the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction, as follows.
pg176_n0009_easy_read: eta sub 2 over eta sub 1 equals sine of i divided by sine of r
pg176_n0010_easy_read: So, eta sub 1 sine of i equals eta sub 2 sine of r

When we apply the law of reversibility of light, we get:
g eta sub a equals 1 over a eta sub g
pg176_n0012_easy_read:
Here, g eta sub a and a eta sub g are the relative refractive indices for light travelling:
- from air to glass
- from glass to air

pg177_n0095_easy_read: It is established that when light travels from a lighter medium to a denser medium, eta one is less than eta two, the refracted light ray bends towards the normal.
pg178_n0003_easy_read: When light travels from a denser medium to a lighter medium, eta one is less than eta two, the refracted light ray bends away from the normal.
pg178_n0004_easy_read:
The angle of refraction depends on the angle of incidence.
So, the amount of bending away from the normal also depends on the angle of incidence.
pg178_n0005_easy_read: So, the larger the angle of incidence, the more the light bends away from the normal.
pg178_n0006_easy_read: But when light travels from a denser medium to a less dense medium, how far can the light bend away from the normal?
pg178_n0008_easy_read: The answer is that light can bend only up to 90° without leaving the medium.
pg178_n0009_easy_read: So, there is an angle of incidence at which the angle of refraction is 90°.
pg178_n0010_easy_read:
This angle of incidence is called the critical angle.
It is usually shown by the letter c.
pg178_n0011_easy_read:
When the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle, light is not refracted anymore.
Instead, the light reflects back into the same medium.
pg178_n0012_easy_read: This phenomenon is called total internal reflection.
pg178_n0016_easy_read:
Total internal reflection (TIR) is a physical phenomenon.
In this phenomenon, all the light travelling in an optically denser medium reflects back when it hits the boundary with an optically less dense medium.
pg178_n0020_easy_read: Total internal reflection happens only when both of these 2 conditions are met:
pg178_n0023_easy_read: 1. Light travels from an optically denser medium to a less dense medium.
pg178_n0025_easy_read: 2. The angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle.
pg178_n0027_easy_read: Total internal reflection does not happen unless the incident light travels in the more optically dense medium towards the less optically dense medium.
pg178_n0030_easy_read:
TIR happens for light travelling from water to air.
But it does not happen for light travelling from air to water.
pg178_n0031_easy_read: On the other hand, TIR happens only if the angle of refraction is more than 90°.
pg178_n0032_easy_read: When the angle of incidence is equal to the critical angle, the angle of refraction is 90° (Figure 5.9 (a)).
pg178_n0033_easy_read: Also, when the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle, all the light shows total internal reflection, as shown in Figure 5.9 (b)).

pg179_n0045_easy_read: In the previous discussion, it was shown that light bends when it reaches a boundary between 2 media with different refractive indices.
pg179_n0046_easy_read: After light passes the boundary, it travels in a straight line in the new medium.
pg179_n0047_easy_read: However, this discussion assumed that the media where light travels have uniform optical density.
pg179_n0048_easy_read: But not every medium is uniform, and even air can sometimes be a non-uniform medium.
pg179_n0049_easy_read: When a medium is optically non-uniform, light can refract as it travels through the medium.
pg179_n0050_easy_read: This causes an interesting phenomenon: mirages form.
pg179_n0051_easy_read:
A mirage is an optical phenomenon.
It creates image illusions because light refracts through a non-uniform medium.
pg180_n0003_easy_read: You can often see mirages when you walk on a tarmac road on a sunny day.
pg180_n0004_easy_read: As you walk along the road, you may see what looks like a puddle of water about 100 m ahead of you.
pg180_n0005_easy_read: But when you reach the place where you saw the puddle, you see that the puddle is not there.
pg180_n0006_easy_read: Instead, the puddle seems to be another 100 m farther ahead of you.
pg180_n0007_easy_read: The puddle of water only appears to be there. It is an illusion caused by a mirage.
pg180_n0009_easy_read: Mirages happen on sunny days because the sun heats the road to a high temperature.
pg180_n0010_easy_read: The hot road then heats the air around it. This keeps the air just above the road hotter than the air higher up.
pg180_n0011_easy_read: Hot air is usually optically less dense than cool air.
pg180_n0012_easy_read: So, the air layers just above the road are optically less dense than the air higher above the road.
pg180_n0013_easy_read: This makes the optical medium uneven.
pg180_n0014_easy_read: So, light from the sun passes through the cooler air layers and moves toward the hotter air layers.
pg180_n0015_easy_read: This means that light moves from an optically denser medium to a less dense medium.
pg180_n0016_easy_read: So, light is refracted when it reaches the boundary between the 2 air layers.
pg180_n0018_easy_read: As the light moves through different air layers, it bends more and more upward until it reaches your eyes instead of the road.
pg180_n0019_easy_read: Your brain traces the light back in a straight line along the direction it came to your eyes.
pg180_n0020_easy_read: Figure 5.10 (a) shows an image of the sky. Air with uneven optical density refracts this image, so it looks like a puddle of water just above the road.
pg180_n0021_easy_read: Figure 5.10 (b) shows how an atmospheric mirage forms.
pg180_n0022_easy_read: A mirage can also happen in places with water, such as seas, lakes, and ponds, and in deserts.

pg187_n0016_easy_read: This band is called the spectrum of white light.
pg187_n0017_easy_read:
The colours in the spectrum of white light are:
- red (R)
- orange (O)
- yellow (Y)
- green (G)
- blue (B)

pg187_n0018_easy_read: People often use the abbreviation ROYGBIV to remember the order of these colours.

pg187_n0024_easy_read: Dispersion of light is when white light splits into its different colours after it passes through a material such as a triangular glass prism.
pg187_n0025_easy_read: This happens because when a beam of white light enters a transparent material, each colour bends at a different angle. So, each colour changes direction by a different amount.
pg187_n0026_easy_read: For example, red bends the least, and violet bends the most.
pg187_n0027_easy_read: As a result, white light splits into its colours and forms a spectrum. In Figure 5.16, red is at the top of the spectrum, and violet is at the bottom.
pg187_n0028_easy_read: Each colour has a different wavelength. This wavelength is within the visible part of the electromagnetic spectrum.
pg187_n0032_easy_read:
Light dispersion can also happen when light passes through other transparent materials, such as:
- water droplets
- soap bubbles
pg187_n0033_easy_read: One result of light dispersion by water droplets in the atmosphere is a rainbow.
pg187_n0034_easy_read: A rainbow is a natural phenomenon that happens because white light spreads into different colours.
pg187_n0035_easy_read: A rainbow happens because falling water droplets refract and reflect white light.
pg188_n0005_easy_read: You can see a rainbow when there are water drops in the air and the sun is low behind the observer.
pg188_n0006_easy_read: A rainbow appears because sunlight spreads into different colours when nearly round raindrops bend the light.
pg188_n0007_easy_read: The white light from the sun first bends when it enters the surface of the raindrops.
pg188_n0009_easy_read: When light moves from a less dense medium to a denser medium, it bends towards the normal.
pg188_n0010_easy_read: But the colours do not all bend in the same way.
pg188_n0011_easy_read: Like in a glass prism, red light bends the least and violet light bends the most.
pg188_n0012_easy_read: At the back of the raindrops, some of the separated light reflects back at many angles. The light bends again as it leaves the raindrop.
pg188_n0013_easy_read: In most cases, violet light leaves the raindrop at a smaller angle to the sunlight that enters it than red light does, as shown in Figure 5.17 (a).
pg188_n0014_easy_read: As a result, the observer sees clear bands of colour in the sky. This is called a rainbow. Red light is at the top, and violet light is at the bottom of the spectrum, as shown in Figure 5.17 (b).

pg190_n0011_easy_read: The experiment on recombining the spectrum of light can also be used to observe the recombination of 2 or more separate colours.
pg190_n0012_easy_read: Sir Isaac Newton did this first by using prisms and mirrors.
pg190_n0013_easy_read: He discovered that when light from the red, green, and blue parts of the spectrum is recombined, it forms white light again.
pg190_n0014_easy_read: So, he called red, green, and blue the primary colours.
pg190_n0016_easy_read: Newton also observed that when 2 primary colours are combined, they form other colours.
pg190_n0017_easy_read: For example, when blue light and green light are combined, they form cyan light.
pg190_n0018_easy_read: Also, green light and red light combine to make yellow light. Red light and blue light combine to make magenta light.

pg190_n0021_easy_read: At the end, he organised his findings in a colour wheel. It showed the 3 "primary colours" with the 3 "secondary colours" between them, as shown in Figure 5.20.
pg190_n0023_easy_read: This colour wheel is well known as the Newton colour wheel or disc.
pg190_n0024_easy_read: When the disc turns very fast around its axis, all the colours mix and form white.
pg190_n0025_easy_read: But when the disc slows down, the separate colours can be seen again.
pg190_n0035_easy_read: Magenta was not part of the light spectrum, so where it came from was a mystery.
pg190_n0036_easy_read: Hermann von Helmholtz solved this mystery. He showed that the human eye has 3 types of colour receptors.
pg190_n0037_easy_read: Each primary colour, red, blue, or green, can stimulate only 1 type of receptor.
pg190_n0038_easy_read: Also, the eye sees all the different colours by combining the signals from these receptors inside the eye.
pg190_n0039_easy_read: So, white light is seen when red, blue, and green light enters the eye.
pg190_n0040_easy_read: But when red light and blue light enter the eye, and green light does not, magenta is seen even though the light is not magenta.

pg194_n0021_easy_read: For example, red (R) light and green (G) light add together to make yellow (Y) light.
pg194_n0022_easy_read: Red light and blue light add together to make magenta (M) light.
pg194_n0023_easy_read: Green light and blue (B) light add together to make cyan (C) light.
pg194_n0024_easy_read: Finally, red light, green light, and blue light add together to make white light.
pg194_n0025_easy_read: Also, adding complementary colours of light makes white light.
pg194_n0026_easy_read: The addition of light colours can be shown by these equations:

pg195_n0005_easy_read: The rules of colour addition decide the colour we see when different colours of light mix.
pg195_n0006_easy_read: But to fully understand how we see colour, we also need to understand the rules of colour subtraction.
pg195_n0007_easy_read: Some materials have atoms and molecules that can absorb 1 or more colours of light.
pg195_n0008_easy_read: So, when white light falls on this kind of material, the material absorbs some colours of light and reflects other colours to the observer's eye.
pg195_n0009_easy_read: This is the basis of light colour subtraction.
pg195_n0011_easy_read:
Filters absorb these colours of light:
- Yellow filter absorbs blue light.
- Magenta filter absorbs green light.
- Cyan filter absorbs red light.
pg195_n0024_easy_read: Think about a piece of cloth made of material that can absorb blue light.
pg195_n0025_easy_read: This cloth absorbs blue light and reflects the other colours.
pg195_n0026_easy_read: What colour will this cloth look under white light? How can we explain its appearance?
pg195_n0028_easy_read: Suppose a beam of white light made of blue, green, and red falls on a shirt.
pg195_n0029_easy_read: If the shirt absorbs blue light, the shirt reflects only red and green light.
pg195_n0030_easy_read: We see by reflected light. Also, R+G=Y. So, the shirt appears yellow.
pg195_n0031_easy_read: This example shows the process of colour subtraction.
pg195_n0032_easy_read: In this process, an object's colour depends on which light colours are removed from the original set of colours, as shown in Figure 5.28.
pg195_n0040_easy_read: Figure 5.28: Process of subtraction of light colours
pg195_n0042_easy_read: Figure 5.28 shows the colour subtraction process. We can also show it with this colour subtraction equation:
pg195_n0043_easy_read: W - B = (R + G + B) - B = R + G = Y.
pg195_n0045_easy_read: Suppose the same piece of cloth is lit by a cyan light.
pg195_n0046_easy_read: Cyan light is made of blue and green light. The cloth absorbs blue light. So, blue light is subtracted.

pg195_n0051_easy_read: This shows that an object's colour is not part of the object itself. It depends on the light colours the object reflects.
pg196_n0003_easy_read: because white incident light gives green and red light back.
pg196_n0004_easy_read: In general, these are the rules for subtraction of light colour:
pg196_n0007_easy_read:
1. Red absorbs green light and blue light.
Red reflects red light.
pg196_n0009_easy_read:
2. Blue absorbs green light and red light.
Blue reflects blue light.
pg196_n0011_easy_read:
3. Green absorbs blue light and red light.
Green reflects green light.
pg196_n0013_easy_read:
4. Cyan absorbs red light.
Cyan reflects cyan light (blue + green).
pg196_n0015_easy_read:
5. Magenta absorbs green light.
Magenta reflects magenta light (red + blue).
pg196_n0017_easy_read:
6. Yellow absorbs blue light.
Yellow reflects yellow light (red + green).
pg196_n0019_easy_read: These rules are very important for understanding why objects look the colour they do.
pg196_n0020_easy_read: Figure 5.29 shows a summary of the colour subtraction rules.

pg196_n0026_easy_read:
From the addition and subtraction of light colours, you may see that objects can look like different colours.
This depends on the combination of light that reaches our eyes.
pg196_n0027_easy_read:
This idea is very useful for making colours.
We call this colour mixing.
pg196_n0028_easy_read:
Colour mixing uses the addition and subtraction of light colours.
So, there are 2 main types of colour mixing.
pg196_n0029_easy_read: The 2 main types are additive colour mixing and subtractive colour mixing.
pg196_n0033_easy_read: Additive colour mixing means making a new colour by adding colours to other colours.
pg196_n0034_easy_read: When we add all the different colours of sunlight, we see white light, not many separate colours.
pg196_n0035_easy_read:
This is called additive colour mixing.
It is called additive because all the wavelengths still reach our eyes.
But the colour we see depends on the combination of colours.
pg196_n0037_easy_read:
The primary colours in additive colour mixing are:
- red
- blue
- green
The secondary colours are:
- cyan
- magenta
- yellow
pg196_n0038_easy_read: Additive colour mixing is often used to make colours on televisions and computer monitors with the RGB (red, green and blue) system.
pg196_n0039_easy_read: Activity 5.10 that you did earlier shows the process of additive colour mixing.
pg196_n0043_easy_read:
When colour pigments are mixed, both paints still absorb the same colours as before they were mixed.
The result is
pg197_n0003_easy_read: the colour that both pigments reflect.
pg197_n0004_easy_read:
This process is called subtractive colour mixing.
This is because, when colour pigments mix, each pigment may absorb some colours that the other pigment reflects.
So, fewer colours are seen than before mixing.
pg197_n0005_easy_read:
We only see the light that the paints reflect.
So, in subtractive colour mixing, the primary colours are:
- cyan
- magenta
- yellow
The secondary colours are:
- red
- blue
- green
pg197_n0006_easy_read:
When the primary colours are added, they give black.
This means all colours have been absorbed and no light is reflected.
pg197_n0007_easy_read:
Subtractive colour mixing is commonly used in:
- coloured printers
- making different paints with a CMY system
CMY means cyan, magenta and yellow.
pg197_n0009_easy_read: It is important to note that each primary paint pigment absorbs 1 primary colour of light.
pg197_n0010_easy_read: The colour that a primary paint pigment absorbs is its complementary colour.
pg197_n0020_easy_read: On the other hand, each secondary paint pigment absorbs 2 secondary colours of light.
pg197_n0024_easy_read: (a) Blue paint absorbs cyan and magenta.
pg197_n0026_easy_read: (b) Green paint absorbs yellow and cyan.
pg197_n0028_easy_read: (c) Red paint absorbs magenta and yellow.

pg197_n0057_easy_read: Both additive and subtractive colour mixing are very important for understanding how we see different colours.

pg198_n0005_easy_read:
An easy way to remember the difference is this:
Additive colour mixing happens when we mix lights of different colours.
Subtractive colour mixing happens when we mix paints or other coloured materials.

A piece of glass or other transparent material can have a shape that makes parallel light rays do 1 of 2 things.
They can come together at 1 point, or they can seem to spread out from 1 point.
pg199_n0021_easy_read: A piece of glass with this shape is called a lens.
pg199_n0022_easy_read:
Most lenses are made of glass.
But lenses can also be made from other transparent materials.
pg199_n0023_easy_read: In recent times, more lenses are being made from plastic.
pg199_n0024_easy_read:
A lens is a carefully shaped piece of transparent material.
It bends light rays so that an image forms.
pg199_n0025_easy_read:
We can think of lenses as a set of very small prisms.
Each prism bends light and makes its own image.
pg199_n0026_easy_read: When these prisms work together, they make a bright image focused at 1 point, as shown in Figure 5.30.
pg199_n0028_easy_read: Figure 5.30: A set of prisms arranged to make light rays come together or spread out
pg199_n0036_easy_read: Lenses are different in their shape and in the materials used to make them.
pg199_n0037_easy_read: Based on shape, there are 2 main types of lenses.
pg199_n0038_easy_read:
These 2 types are:
- convex lenses, which are converging lenses
- concave lenses, which are diverging lenses
pg199_n0040_easy_read: A convex lens makes the light rays that pass through it come together.
pg199_n0041_easy_read: A convex lens is thicker in the middle and thinner at the edges, as shown in Figure 5.31.
pg199_n0042_easy_read: At least 1 side of a convex lens curves outward.
pg199_n0043_easy_read: Convex lenses can be divided into smaller groups by their shape.
pg199_n0044_easy_read:
These types are:
- bi-convex lenses
- plano-convex lenses
- convex meniscus lenses
They are shown in Figure 5.31.
pg199_n0045_easy_read: Task 5.5 shows how a convex lens works.

pg200_n0012_easy_read: A concave lens is a lens that spreads out light rays that pass through it.
pg200_n0013_easy_read: A concave lens is thinner in the middle and thicker at the edges.
pg200_n0014_easy_read: At least 1 side of a concave lens curves inward.
pg200_n0015_easy_read:
Types of concave lenses include:
- biconcave lens
- plano-concave lens
- concave meniscus
pg200_n0016_easy_read: Figure 5.32 shows the types of concave lenses.
pg200_n0025_easy_read: To talk about refraction of light rays and how lenses form images, we need to use different terms.
pg200_n0026_easy_read:
Think of 1 face of a lens as part of a spherical surface.
Then the imaginary line that passes through the centre of the sphere and the exact centre of the lens is called the principal axis of the lens.
pg200_n0027_easy_read: A lens also has an imaginary vertical line that divides it evenly into 2 halves.
pg200_n0028_easy_read: This line is called the vertical axis of the lens.
pg200_n0029_easy_read: The point where the vertical axis and the principal axis cross is called the optical centre of the lens.
pg200_n0031_easy_read: Light rays that hit a lens and travel parallel to the principal axis will either come together or spread out.
pg200_n0032_easy_read: In a convex lens, the light rays come together at a point called the focal point or principal focus.
pg200_n0033_easy_read:
In a concave lens, the light rays spread out.
But if you trace them backwards, they seem to come from 1 common point.
This point is also called a focal point.
pg200_n0034_easy_read: In both cases, the focal point is shown by the letter F.
pg200_n0035_easy_read:
The distance between the focal point and the optical centre is called the focal length.
It is shown by the letter f.
pg200_n0037_easy_read: Unlike mirrors, lenses let light pass through either face.
pg200_n0038_easy_read: So, a lens has 2 focal points, 1 on each side of the lens.
pg200_n0039_easy_read:
A lens also has an imaginary point called the centre of curvature.
This is the centre of the sphere that the lens surface is part of.
pg200_n0040_easy_read:
The centre of curvature lies on the principal axis.
Its distance from the optical centre is called the radius of curvature, R.
pg200_n0041_easy_read: The lens has 2 centres of curvature, 1 on each side of the lens.
pg200_n0042_easy_read: The focal point F is real for a convex lens and virtual for a concave lens.
pg201_n0003_easy_read:
Other common terms are:
- real image
- virtual image
- image distance, v
- object distance, u
- magnification, m
pg201_n0004_easy_read: All these terms have the same meaning as in image formation by curved mirrors.
pg201_n0005_easy_read: Figure 5.33 shows the terms used to talk about lenses.
pg201_n0007_easy_read: For thin lenses, the pole and the optical centre are at the same point.
pg201_n0008_easy_read: Also, the plane that passes through the principal focus and is at 90° to the principal axis is called the focal plane.
pg201_n0028_easy_read: Lenses form images because light refracts at both surfaces of the lens.
pg201_n0029_easy_read: When light enters and leaves the lens, it refracts at each boundary.
pg201_n0030_easy_read: The total effect of this refraction at the 2 boundaries is that the light changes direction.
pg201_n0031_easy_read: Because of the shape of a lens, the refracted light rays either meet at a focal point or seem to spread out from a focal point. This forms an image, as shown in Figure 5.30.
pg201_n0036_easy_read: Ray diagrams can show how lenses form images of objects.
pg201_n0037_easy_read: In ray diagrams, lenses are sometimes shown by vertical lines. A mark shows if the lens is a converging lens or a diverging lens.
pg201_n0038_easy_read: Figure 5.34 shows how converging and diverging lenses are represented in ray diagrams.
pg201_n0044_easy_read: Figure 5.34: Representation of converging and diverging lenses in ray diagrams
pg202_n0003_easy_read: Follow some rules when you draw ray diagrams for convex and concave lenses.
pg202_n0004_easy_read: These rules come from the principles of light refraction.
pg202_n0005_easy_read: When a ray of light hits the first surface of a lens, it moves from a less dense medium to a denser medium. So, it bends towards the normal.
pg202_n0006_easy_read: When the ray of light comes out from the other side of the lens, it moves from the denser medium to a less dense medium.
pg202_n0007_easy_read: So, the ray bends away from the normal when it leaves the lens.
pg202_n0008_easy_read: 3 important rules help you draw ray diagrams.
pg202_n0011_easy_read: 1. Convex lens: A ray of light that travels parallel to the principal axis of a convex lens (Figure 5.35(a)) bends to the principal focus.
pg202_n0012_easy_read: Concave lens: A ray of light that travels parallel to the principal axis of a concave lens (Figure 5.35(b)) spreads out. It looks as if it comes from the principal focus.
pg202_n0016_easy_read: Figure 5.35: Refraction of light rays that hit the lens parallel to the principal axis
pg202_n0018_easy_read: 2. A ray of light that passes through the optical centre keeps travelling on the same path in both convex and concave lenses, as shown in Figure 5.36.
pg202_n0021_easy_read: Figure 5.36: Refraction of light rays that pass through the optical centre
pg202_n0023_easy_read: 3. Convex lens: A ray of light that travels through the principal focus of a converging lens is refracted parallel to the principal axis of the convex lens, as shown in Figure 5.37(a).
pg202_n0024_easy_read: Concave lens: A ray of light that seems to travel through the principal focus of a diverging lens is refracted parallel to the principal axis.
pg202_n0025_easy_read: Figure 5.37(b) shows the path of a ray through the principal focus for concave lenses.
pg203_n0007_easy_read: Figure 5.37: Refraction of light rays that pass through the principal focus
pg203_n0009_easy_read: As with spherical mirrors, you only need 2 light rays to find the image formed by a lens.
pg203_n0010_easy_read: We treat the refraction of light by a lens as if it happens on a plane through the optical centre. This plane is perpendicular to the principal axis of the lens.
pg203_n0011_easy_read: When rays spread out after they pass through the lens, extend them backwards to find the virtual image.

pg217_n0010_easy_read: Optical instruments help the human eye see objects that are far away or very small. They make it possible to see stars and microorganisms that we cannot see without them.
pg217_n0011_easy_read: These devices use light, lenses, mirrors, and prisms to make images clearer.
pg217_n0012_easy_read: In this chapter, you will learn how different optical instruments work, including microscopes, telescopes, and cameras.
pg217_n0013_easy_read: The skills you develop will help you choose, use, and even make simple optical instruments for different uses.
pg217_n0020_easy_read: The size of an object that the eye sees depends on the size of the image formed on the retina.
pg217_n0021_easy_read:
The size of the image depends on 2 things:
- the distance from the object to the observer's eye
- the angle the object makes at the eye, called angular size (θ)
pg217_n0022_easy_read: If you want to look closely at a small object, such as an insect, you move the object close to your eye.
pg217_n0023_easy_read: When you do this, you increase the angular size. This makes the image on the retina as large as possible.
pg217_n0024_easy_read: However, your eyes cannot focus clearly on objects closer than about 25 cm from the eye.
pg217_n0025_easy_read: This point is called the near point of the eye.
pg217_n0026_easy_read: When you move an object closer to the near point of the eye, the image on your retina becomes larger.
pg217_n0027_easy_read: But if you move the object closer than the near point, the image becomes fuzzy or blurred. This happens because the lens of the eye can no longer focus the image on the retina.
pg217_n0028_easy_read: So, the closest comfortable distance for viewing an image is when the object is at the near point.
pg217_n0029_easy_read: So, you cannot bring an object closer to the eye than the near point.
pg217_n0030_easy_read: To solve this limit, you can use a converging lens to make the image of an object larger.
pg217_n0031_easy_read: The object can then move even closer to the eye. This makes a large image on the retina.
pg217_n0032_easy_read: A lens used in this way makes a device called a simple microscope.
pg218_n0005_easy_read: A simple microscope has a biconvex lens in a round frame with a handle.
pg218_n0006_easy_read: So, you can hold it in your hand and move it as needed.
pg218_n0007_easy_read: A simple microscope is sometimes called a magnifying glass or a magnifier.
pg218_n0014_easy_read: When you use a simple microscope, put it over the object you want to see.
pg218_n0015_easy_read: To make viewing comfortable, adjust the magnifying glass so the object is at the focal point of the lens.
pg218_n0016_easy_read:
This makes an image of the object that is:
- virtual
- upright
- magnified
pg218_n0017_easy_read: Note that the largest image can form on the retina of the naked eye when the object is at the near point (D ≈ 25 cm).
pg218_n0018_easy_read: So, for a clear image and the largest image on the retina, the magnifier must have a focal length of about 25 cm.
pg218_n0019_easy_read: The image forms at infinity when you adjust the magnifying glass, or the object, so the object is at the focal point of the magnifying glass.
pg218_n0020_easy_read: In this way, the eyes see a magnified image, so smaller details can be seen.

pg221_n0044_easy_read: The magnification of a simple microscope is limited to capital M less than or equal to 9 for realistic focal lengths.

pg221_n0046_easy_read: For example, an object that is 1 mm in size will look like 9 mm when you view it through a magnifying glass.
pg221_n0047_easy_read: However, bacteria are much smaller than 1 mm.
pg221_n0048_easy_read: So, to see a bacterium, you need a magnification greater than 9.
pg221_n0049_easy_read: To do this, people usually use a different microscope with 2 lenses. In this microscope, 1 lens adds to the effect of the other lens.
pg221_n0050_easy_read: This microscope is called a compound microscope.

A compound microscope has 3 systems:
- a lens system
- a lighting system
- a focusing system

pg222_n0006_easy_read: The image from the objective lens becomes the object for the second lens. The second lens is called the eyepiece.
pg222_n0007_easy_read: The eyepiece works like a simple microscope. It makes the final image, which is enlarged and virtual.
pg222_n0009_easy_read: A compound microscope has a revolving nose piece. It lets the user change the objective lens as needed.
pg222_n0010_easy_read: A compound microscope also has a lighting system. This system may also be called the illumination system.
pg222_n0011_easy_read:

- a light-emitting diode (LED)
- natural sunlight
pg222_n0012_easy_read: The microscope also has a mirror and a condenser. They help light pass through the object so the user can view it.
pg222_n0013_easy_read: A compound microscope also has a focusing system.
pg222_n0015_easy_read: This system has coarse and fine adjustment knobs. These knobs move the objective lens away from or towards the object to get a clear image.
pg222_n0016_easy_read: The system also has an inclination joint. It helps tilt the microscope for comfortable viewing.
pg222_n0017_easy_read: Other parts of a compound microscope include the body tube. The body tube separates the objective lens and the eyepiece. It also keeps the optics in line.
pg222_n0018_easy_read: A stage holds the object for viewing. The base supports the whole microscope.

pg222_n0036_easy_read: A compound microscope works on this principle: an image made by 1 optical element can become the object for the second optical element.

pg226_n0036_easy_read: Astronomers use a device called an astronomical telescope to observe the universe and its parts, which are very far from our eyes.

pg227_n0023_easy_read:

pg229_n0042_easy_read: When you visit a national park, you cannot go very close to dangerous animals, such as lions and leopards, for safety reasons.
pg229_n0043_easy_read: To watch these animals closely, you need a device that helps your eyes see distant objects more clearly.
pg229_n0044_easy_read: An optical device used in this situation is called binoculars.
pg230_n0005_easy_read:
Binoculars have 2 telescopes.
The 2 telescopes are exactly the same.
They are side by side and point in the same direction.
pg230_n0006_easy_read: This lets the observer use both eyes to look at distant objects.
pg230_n0007_easy_read:
The main parts of binoculars are:
- the eyepiece
- the objective lens
- prisms
pg230_n0008_easy_read:
The objective lens focuses light from a distant object near the focal point of the eyepiece.
The eyepiece then magnifies the image.
pg230_n0009_easy_read: A pair of prisms turns the image so the eyes see it the right way up.
pg230_n0010_easy_read:
Other parts include the focusing system.
The focusing system moves the lenses back and forth.
pg230_n0011_easy_read: Figure 6.10 shows some parts of binoculars.
pg230_n0020_easy_read: 2 objective lenses are at the ends of the 2 telescopes that make the binoculars.
pg230_n0021_easy_read:
The objective lens collects light from the object the user is looking at.
Then it forms the image of the object at or near the focal point of the eyepiece.
pg230_n0022_easy_read: The eyepiece is like a magnifying glass.
pg230_n0023_easy_read:
The eyepiece takes the small image made by the objective lens.
Then it magnifies the image so the observer can see the object clearly.
pg230_n0024_easy_read:
However, when light is refracted through the objective lens, the light rays cross over.
This makes the image upside down.
pg230_n0025_easy_read:
The eyepiece only magnifies this image.
So the viewer sees the object upside down.
pg230_n0026_easy_read: A pair of prisms can solve this problem.
pg230_n0027_easy_read:
These prisms rotate and reflect the image.
They use the principle of total internal reflection.
pg230_n0028_easy_read: To turn the image by 180 degrees, the prisms are arranged so that each prism turns the image by 90 degrees.
pg230_n0029_easy_read:
Usually, binoculars use 2 types of prisms:
- roof prisms
- porro prisms
pg230_n0030_easy_read: Figure 6.11 shows how the image is turned over in binoculars.
pg230_n0041_easy_read:
Binoculars are made of 2 identical refracting telescopes.
So, the magnifying power of binoculars can be calculated in the same way as for the astronomical telescope.

Here, f sub o is the focal length of the objective lens.
f sub e is the focal length of the eyepiece.
pg231_n0007_easy_read:
2 things determine the quality of images from binoculars:
- the magnification power
- the size of the objective lens
pg231_n0008_easy_read:
The magnification power changes the size of the image.
The size of the objective lens changes the clarity and detail of the image.
pg231_n0009_easy_read:
Commercial binoculars usually have printed information about:
- the size of the objective lens
- the magnification power

Binoculars can focus on distant objects.
So, people use binoculars in many activities to see distant objects clearly and in detail.
pg231_n0025_easy_read: For example, tourists often use binoculars to view animals.
pg231_n0026_easy_read: Also, soldiers use binoculars to view the enemy camp from far away.
pg231_n0028_easy_read: Likewise, surveyors use binoculars to survey and observe the landscape and other features.

The camera is an optical instrument.
People have used it since the discovery of lenses.
pg231_n0042_easy_read:
The word camera comes from Latin.
It means "a room or enclosure".
pg231_n0043_easy_read: So, the main part of a camera is a light-tight enclosure or box.
pg231_n0044_easy_read:
A camera has different components.
These components are inside the light-tight box.
pg231_n0045_easy_read:
Cameras can have different forms, depending on their components.
These forms include:
- film cameras
- digital cameras
- video cameras
pg231_n0046_easy_read:
In this section, we discuss the simplest type of camera.
It is called a lens camera.
pg231_n0050_easy_read:

- a biconvex lens

pg232_n0013_easy_read: The lens forms the image in a camera.
pg232_n0014_easy_read: The focal length of a lens decides the size of the image formed on the film.
pg232_n0015_easy_read: So, there are 4 basic types of lenses.
pg232_n0021_easy_read: A normal lens gives a viewing field of about 50 degrees. It gives a picture with normal size compared to the background. The picture looks natural to the viewer.

The human eye is a natural optical instrument.
It is very important for human life.
pg235_n0013_easy_read:
The human eye belongs to a group of eyes in nature called "camera-type eyes".
This is because the eye works in a similar way to a lens camera.
pg235_n0014_easy_read: The human eye can respond to a range of light frequencies.
pg235_n0015_easy_read: The human eye looks whitish and has a black spot in the centre, as shown in Figure 6.17.
pg235_n0021_easy_read:
The eye is almost round.
It is about 2.5 cm in diameter.
pg235_n0022_easy_read:
The front part of the eye is more curved.
A tough, transparent membrane called the cornea covers it.
pg235_n0023_easy_read: The area behind the cornea contains a liquid called aqueous humour.
pg235_n0024_easy_read:
Next to the aqueous humour, there is a crystalline lens.
It is a capsule that contains fibrous jelly.
The jelly is hard at the centre and softer at the outer parts.
pg235_n0025_easy_read:
Ligaments hold the crystalline lens in place.
The ligaments attach the lens to the ciliary muscles around it.
pg235_n0026_easy_read:
In front of the lens, there is an opening called the pupil.
Its size can change.
pg235_n0028_easy_read:
The iris controls the size of the pupil.
The iris is attached to the ciliary muscles.
pg235_n0029_easy_read: The iris gives the eye its colour.
pg235_n0030_easy_read: The iris acts like the diaphragm in a lens camera.
pg235_n0031_easy_read: Behind the lens, the eye is filled with a thin, watery jelly called the vitreous humour.
pg235_n0032_easy_read:
This jelly helps focus light rays.
It also keeps the shape of the eye.
pg235_n0033_easy_read:
After the vitreous humour, there is a lining on the back inner surface of the eye.
This lining is called the retina.
pg235_n0034_easy_read:
The retina contains light-sensitive cells called cones and rods.
These cells respond to the light that falls on them.
pg235_n0035_easy_read:
Cones and rods connect to millions of nerves.
These nerves join together to form the optic nerve.
pg235_n0036_easy_read: A tough, whitish skin called the sclera protects the eye.

pg236_n0018_easy_read: When light reaches the eye, it passes through the cornea.
pg236_n0019_easy_read: The cornea has a dome shape. It bends the light and helps the eye focus.
pg236_n0020_easy_read: Light passes through the cornea and the aqueous humour. Then it enters the eye through the pupil.
pg236_n0021_easy_read: The iris controls the size of the pupil. This controls how much light enters the eye.
pg236_n0022_easy_read: Next, light passes through the lens.
pg236_n0023_easy_read: The lens works with the cornea. Together, they focus light correctly on the retina.
pg236_n0024_easy_read: Light from the lens travels through the vitreous humour towards the retina.
pg236_n0025_easy_read: The image forms on the retina, as Figure 6.19 shows.
pg236_n0026_easy_read: When light reaches the retina, it forms the image. The photoreceptors on the retina change the light into electrical signals. These signals travel to the brain through the optic nerve.

pg236_n0029_easy_read: The crystalline lens is not homogeneous. Its average index of refraction is 1.437.
pg236_n0030_easy_read: The index of refraction of the crystalline lens is not very different from the index of refraction of the aqueous humour and the vitreous humour.
pg236_n0031_easy_read: So, most of the refraction of light that enters the eye happens at the outer surface of the cornea, as Figure 6.19 shows.
